whyBigDeal: It is one of the first serious paintings of artificial light — the gas jets above the players are the light source and the subject. Seurat built the composition on ratios he believed governed emotional response, treating a fairground booth as a test case for a theory of painting.

title: Gray Weather, Grande Jatte
sceneContext: The Grande Jatte island on an overcast day, painted after the enormous Sunday canvas that made Seurat’s name. He kept returning to the same island in different weather, testing whether his method could handle grey light as well as full sun.
whyBigDeal: Seurat applied paint in separate small touches of unmixed colour, expecting the eye to combine them — a method drawn from contemporary optics that turned out not to work the way the science claimed. The pictures succeed anyway, which is a useful caution about theories and results.

title: Study for "Bathers at Asnières"
sceneContext: A study for *Bathers at Asnières*, painted on a small wood panel outdoors, one of about fourteen such studies for the finished canvas.
whyBigDeal: Seurat made the studies from life and then assembled the large picture in the studio from them, so the spontaneity is entirely in the preparation. He died at thirty-one, having produced perhaps seven major canvases, each preceded by dozens of panels like this one.

title: The Siesta
artistBio: French, Paris 1848–1903 Atuona, Hiva Oa, Marquesas Islands
sceneContext: Tahitian women on a verandah, one ironing, painted during Gauguin's first stay in Polynesia in the early 1890s.
whyBigDeal: The women wear imported cotton dresses and iron them with a European iron, so the picture quietly records a colonised place rather than the untouched paradise Gauguin advertised in his writing. The gap between what he painted and what he claimed is the honest part of the work.

title: Two Women
artistBio: French, Paris 1848–1903 Atuona, Hiva Oa, Marquesas Islands
sceneContext: Painted in the Marquesas in 1901 or 1902, in the last two years of Gauguin's life, when he was ill, in debt and in repeated conflict with the colonial administration.
whyBigDeal: The figures are built from flat areas of unmodelled colour with no attempt at depth, which is the technique that made him legible to Matisse and Picasso a decade later. Gauguin got there by rejecting the Impressionist premise that a painting reports on light.

title: In the Waves (Dans les Vagues)
sceneContext: Painted at Le Pouldu in Brittany in 1889, before Gauguin left Europe. A woman falls forward into green surf shown as a flat sheet of colour.
whyBigDeal: There is no horizon, no sky and no modelling — the sea is a decorative field and the body sits on top of it. Painting a nude without the space around her was a straightforward rejection of the entire Renaissance apparatus, made two years before he left for Tahiti.

title: The Large Tree
sceneContext: Painted in Tahiti in 1891, in Gauguin's first year there, when he was still learning the landscape and living near Papeete.
whyBigDeal: He wrote that he wanted colour to work the way music does, carrying feeling without describing anything. The orange ground here is not what the earth looked like; it is chosen for what it does next to the greens, which is the principle nearly all later modern colour rests on.

title: The Englishman (William Tom Warrener, 1861–1934) at the Moulin Rouge
sceneContext: William Tom Warrener, an English painter living in Paris, shown at the Moulin Rouge leaning toward two women. Toulouse-Lautrec knew him personally.
whyBigDeal: Lautrec drew this from the floor of the club he spent his nights in, not from a studio reconstruction. His lithographic posters for the Moulin Rouge invented much of what advertising still does with flat colour and cropped silhouettes, and the paintings and the posters come from the same evenings.

title: The Sofa
sceneContext: Two women on a sofa in a licensed brothel. Lautrec lived in these houses for weeks at a time in the mid-1890s, keeping a room and working from it.
whyBigDeal: He drew the women off duty — sleeping, waiting, undressing without an audience — rather than performing for a viewer. The pictures are unusual in nineteenth-century art for treating sex work as a job with idle hours in it.

title: The Streetwalker
sceneContext: A woman on the street around 1890, from the years when Lautrec was working through Montmartre subjects nightly.
whyBigDeal: He was drawing from the same milieu that Degas painted, but from inside it rather than from a subscriber's box. The contour line does nearly all the work here, which is why his paintings translate so directly into print — he was thinking in outline before he was thinking in paint.

title: Boating
sceneContext: Painted at Argenteuil in summer 1874, where Manet spent the season alongside Monet and Renoir, working outdoors more than he ever had before.
whyBigDeal: The boat is cropped by all four edges and the river is a flat blue plane with no horizon, which flattens the whole scene into pattern. Manet had absorbed Japanese print composition, and this is the canvas where he applied it hardest.

title: The Dead Christ with Angels
sceneContext: Painted for the Salon of 1864, showing the dead Christ supported by angels, with a wound placed on the wrong side of the body.
whyBigDeal: Critics attacked the picture for showing Christ as an ordinary corpse with dirty feet rather than an idealised body. Manet was testing whether religious subjects could survive being painted with the same unsentimental attention he gave to a barmaid, and the hostility told him they could not, not yet.

title: The Monet Family in Their Garden at Argenteuil
sceneContext: Monet, his wife Camille and their son in the garden at Argenteuil in 1874. Renoir turned up while Manet was painting and set up his own canvas of the same scene.
whyBigDeal: Two versions of this afternoon survive by two different painters, which is rare enough to be useful — you can see exactly where the two men's eyes diverged on identical material. Manet keeps the drawing firm and the blacks strong where Renoir dissolves everything into light.

title: Berthe Morisot with a Muff
sceneContext: Berthe Morisot, painter and Manet's frequent sitter, in a dark winter coat. He painted her eleven times between 1868 and 1874.
whyBigDeal: Morisot was a serious painter in her own right who exhibited with the Impressionists while Manet refused to; the portraits record a professional relationship that the sitter's later marriage to his brother tends to obscure. The black here is doing all the work — Manet's blacks are the reason Matisse called him a colourist.

title: Under the Trees (from "The Public Gardens")
sceneContext: From *The Public Gardens*, a set of nine decorative panels painted in 1894 for the dining room of a Paris apartment.
whyBigDeal: Vuillard painted in distemper on canvas, a matte glue-based paint used for stage scenery, because he wanted wall decoration rather than easel pictures. The Nabis argued that painting should be furniture for a room, and this is that argument built at full scale.

title: Luncheon (Annette and Her Grandmother)
sceneContext: A grandmother and granddaughter at lunch, painted in 1899. Vuillard lived with his mother, a dressmaker, until he was sixty and painted her rooms for decades.
whyBigDeal: The figures nearly dissolve into the wallpaper and tablecloth because pattern is given the same weight as people. Vuillard's mother's workshop supplied the fabrics that fill his interiors, so the domestic clutter is also a record of the trade that supported him.

title: Vase of Flowers
sceneContext: A vase of flowers in pastel, painted around 1905 in Redon's late period, after decades of working almost entirely in black charcoal and lithograph.
whyBigDeal: He spent his first fifty years making dark fantastical images he called his *noirs* and then switched to intense colour in his sixties. The flower pieces are not observations of a bouquet so much as a demonstration that colour could carry the same strangeness the black work had.

title: Jo, La Belle Irlandaise
sceneContext: Joanna Hiffernan, an Irish model who was Whistler's partner, painted by Courbet at Étretat in 1865–66 while the two men were working together on the coast.
whyBigDeal: Courbet made four versions of the picture and kept one until he died. Whistler was painting Hiffernan at the same time in an entirely different register, and the two men's portraits of the same woman in the same months mark the split between realism and aestheticism.

title: The Woman in the Waves
sceneContext: Painted in 1868, a woman thrown backward in breaking surf with her arms raised behind her head. Courbet had been painting the Normandy coast for several years and handled the water here with the same loaded palette knife he used for cliffs and snow.
whyBigDeal: Courbet gives the water and the body the same heavy, palette-knifed paint, so the figure is made of the same material as the sea. It reads as physical fact rather than mythology, which is precisely the transaction that got him attacked for a career.

title: Woman with a Parrot
sceneContext: Painted for the Salon of 1866, where it was accepted and well received after years of Courbet being rejected or condemned.
whyBigDeal: He had submitted deliberately provocative pictures for two decades and finally sent one the jury could take. Courbet was later jailed and bankrupted for his part in the Paris Commune, and died in exile in Switzerland at fifty-eight.

title: Hagar in the Wilderness
sceneContext: Hagar and Ishmael abandoned in the wilderness, painted in 1835 as a Salon submission early in Corot's career.
whyBigDeal: The biblical figures are small and the landscape does the work, which reverses the accepted hierarchy — history painting was supposed to subordinate setting to story. Corot used the required subject as a licence to paint the country he actually wanted to paint.

title: A Woman Reading
sceneContext: A woman reading in a landscape, worked on in 1869 and revised in 1870. Corot repainted the figure late in the picture's life.
whyBigDeal: X-ray shows he changed the pose substantially, which is characteristic — he treated finished pictures as still open. Corot quietly supported younger painters, including Pissarro, and bought work from artists in difficulty, which is part of why the Impressionists claimed him.

title: The Beach at Deauville
sceneContext: The beach at Deauville in 1864, when sea bathing was becoming fashionable and the Normandy coast was filling with Parisians.
whyBigDeal: Boudin painted the holiday crowd rather than the sea, recording a new social habit as it formed. Corot called him the king of skies, and he was the painter who convinced the teenage Monet to work outdoors — the entire Impressionist project has a plausible origin on this beach.

title: Sweeping Snow
sceneContext: A figure sweeping snow, painted in the 1890s by Hassam after his return from Paris to the United States.
whyBigDeal: Hassam brought Impressionist technique back to America and applied it to New York and New England, and became commercially successful doing it. He later tried to have his estate distributed to American museums specifically to keep the style in circulation, which worked better than the paintings' reputation did.

title: Surmananda Ragaputra of Hindol, from a Ragamala
medium: Gum tempera, ink, and gold on paper
sceneContext: A Ragamala folio from the Pahari courts of the Punjab hills around 1750. Surmananda is a ragaputra, a 'son' of the parent mode Hindol, one of the subordinate melodies in the system.
whyBigDeal: Ragamala means garland of melodies: each painting visualises a musical mode as a person, a season, an hour and a mood, so a musician and a painter are describing the same thing in different media. No other tradition built a picture cycle on the structure of its own music.

title: Sindhu (Saindhava) Ragaputra of Shri Raga, from a Ragamala
medium: gum tempera, ink, and gold on paper
sceneContext: A ragaputra of Shri Raga, painted in the Punjab hill states around 1680–90. Shri Raga is an evening mode associated with winter and with kingship.
whyBigDeal: The hill courts were small, often a single valley, and each developed a recognisable hand while working from shared texts. That is why Pahari painting can be sorted by kingdom the way Italian painting sorts by city — the same subject, painted forty miles apart, comes out visibly different.

title: Todi Ragini, from a Ragamala Series
medium: Gum tempera and gold on paper
sceneContext: Todi Ragini painted at Murshidabad in Bengal around 1755, when the Mughal provincial court there was the richest in India and about to be taken by the East India Company.
whyBigDeal: Todi is always shown the same way: a woman with a veena in a forest, with deer drawn to her by the music. The iconography is fixed by convention, so what changes between versions is everything else — and comparing them is how you read the difference between one workshop and another.

title: Kausa Ragaputra of Malkos, from a Ragamala
medium: Gum tempera, ink, and gold on paper
sceneContext: Kausa, a ragaputra of Malkos, from a Pahari Ragamala of about 1750. Malkos is a late-night mode, traditionally sung in the small hours.
whyBigDeal: The ragas carry strict times of day, and performing one outside its hour was considered a mistake rather than a preference. A painted Ragamala therefore doubles as a reference book — it fixes the correct mood and moment for a mode that otherwise exists only while someone is playing it.

title: Maru Ragini, from a Ragamala (Garland of Melodies)
medium: Gum tempera, ink, and gold on paper
sceneContext: Maru Ragini from Rajasthan, 1650–80. Maru shows the lovers Dhola and Maru riding a camel together in flight across the desert.
whyBigDeal: The subject is a Rajasthani folk romance rather than a Sanskrit classical source, which is unusual — most Ragamala imagery descends from courtly poetry. Its presence in the set records regional oral tradition being admitted into a formal system.

title: Dipak Raga, One of the Thirty-Six Melodies (Ragamala): Personifying Love
medium: Gum tempera and ink on paper
sceneContext: Dipak Raga from Himachal Pradesh, about 1690. Dipak means lamp, and the mode is personified here as a lover surrounded by light.
whyBigDeal: Legend held that Dipak was so powerful that singing it correctly would ignite lamps, and eventually the singer. Painters had to render a mode defined by the fire it supposedly caused, which is a peculiar brief: depict a sound by depicting its damage.

title: Shri Raga, from a Ragamala (Garland of Melodies)
medium: Gum tempera and gold on paper
sceneContext: Shri Raga from Rajasthan, dated 1695. Shri is a principal mode, associated with the cool season and with a prince attended by musicians.
whyBigDeal: A dated folio is rare and useful, because most Indian painting is placed by style rather than record. Firm dates like this one anchor whole groups of undated pictures, which is why they matter out of proportion to the individual painting.

title: A Woman Charms Snakes in the Wilderness: Asavari Ragini, from a Ragamala
medium: gum tempera and gold on paper
sceneContext: Asavari Ragini from Rajasthan, early 1700s. Asavari is always a woman of the forest seated on a rock or sandalwood tree, charming snakes.
whyBigDeal: The figure is described in the texts as a tribal woman, an outsider to the court that commissioned the picture. The convention preserved a low-status subject inside high-status art for centuries — the courts kept painting a woman they would not have received.

title: Women worshiping a Shiva linga: Devagandhari Ragini of Hindol Raga, from a Ragamala
medium: gum tempera and gold on paper
sceneContext: Devagandhari Ragini of Hindol, painted in the Punjab hills around 1700, showing women in worship before a Shiva linga.
whyBigDeal: Ragamala painting fused devotional practice with music theory: a mode is illustrated by an act of worship, so the picture is simultaneously about sound, season and ritual. The categories that seem separate to us were one subject to the people who made these.

title: A Heroine and Her Paramour: Malavi Ragini, from a Ragamala
medium: gum tempera, ink, and gold on paper
sceneContext: Malavi Ragini from Rajasthan, about 1695, showing a heroine with her lover on a terrace. Malavi belongs to the family of evening modes, and Ragamala painters gave each ragini a fixed situation that identified it as reliably as a caption would.
whyBigDeal: Rajput Ragamala sets were produced in the hundreds, usually thirty-six folios to a set, so a workshop was painting a fixed sequence again and again. Repetition at that scale is what produced the extreme economy of these pictures — a mood established with four colours and a flat ground.

title: Woman Addressing a Peacock: Gujari Ragini of Megh, from a Ragamala
medium: gum tempera and gold on paper
sceneContext: Gujari Ragini of Megh from Rajasthan, about 1680. Megh is the monsoon mode, and Gujari is shown addressing a peacock.
whyBigDeal: The peacock calls before rain, so it stands in for the monsoon itself and for the return of an absent lover. Indian painting uses this compression constantly — one bird carrying weather, longing and a musical mode at once — which is why the pictures reward slow looking.

title: Lovers on a Terrace: Ramakali Ragini of Hindol, from a Bundi Ragamala
medium: gum tempera and gold on paper
sceneContext: Ramakali Ragini of Hindol from a Bundi Ragamala of about 1610, one of the earliest surviving Rajput sets.
whyBigDeal: Bundi's early Ragamalas were painted just as Mughal workshops were absorbing European perspective. These stayed flat and saturated, refusing the imported illusionism, and the refusal was a choice — Bundi painters had seen the alternative and declined it.

title: Sindhu Raga
medium: Gum tempera and ink on paper
sceneContext: Sindhu Raga, painted in Rajasthan about 1720, one folio from a set that would originally have run to thirty-six paintings covering the full system of modes.
whyBigDeal: By the eighteenth century, Ragamala sets were being made for merchants and minor landholders, not only for rulers. The market widened and the pictures got quicker and brighter, which is usually described as decline and is better understood as a change of customer.

title: Patamanjari Ragini of Dipak, from a Ragamala
medium: Gum tempera and ink on paper
sceneContext: Patamanjari Ragini of Dipak, painted in the Punjab hills around 1740–50. Patamanjari is a mode of separation and evening.
whyBigDeal: Pahari painting reaches its peak in exactly these decades, largely through the family workshop of Pandit Seu and his sons Manaku and Nainsukh. Their influence spread across the hill states through relatives and pupils, so a single family shapes most of what survives.

title: Krishna Fluting
sceneContext: Krishna playing the flute, painted in Rajasthan in the late seventeenth century. The scene is the standard one: the god alone with his instrument, the cowherd women somewhere beyond the frame, already listening.
whyBigDeal: The flute is the whole theology in one object: its sound is said to call the cowherd women away from their households, which devotional poetry treats as the model for the soul abandoning everything for God. The image is doctrine compressed into an instrument.

title: Krishna celebrates Holi
medium: gum tempera, gold, and silver on paper
sceneContext: Krishna at Holi, painted in the Punjab hills around 1770. Holi marks the arrival of spring with thrown coloured powder and water, and Krishna is traditionally shown starting the game with Radha and the cowherd women.
whyBigDeal: Holi is the one festival in which social rank is deliberately suspended, and painting Krishna inside it gives divine licence to the reversal. The pictures were made for the courts whose hierarchy the festival temporarily dissolved.

title: "Portrait of Raja Bikramajit (Sundar Das)", Folio from the Shah Jahan Album
medium: Ink, opaque watercolor, and gold on paper
sceneContext: Raja Bikramajit, born Sundar Das, a Hindu official who rose to command Mughal armies. Painted by Bichitr around 1620 for the album later assembled for Shah Jahan.
whyBigDeal: Bichitr was among the few Mughal painters to sign work and to place himself in it. The Shah Jahan Album paired paintings with calligraphy on facing pages, so a portrait was designed to be seen beside a written page — the picture was never meant to hang alone.

title: Rishyashringa addresses the courtesans, from the "Shangri" Ramayana
medium: Gum tempera and ink on paper
sceneContext: From the 'Shangri' Ramayana, a large Pahari series of about 1700–1725 named after the Shangri branch of the Kulu royal family who owned it.
whyBigDeal: The set runs to hundreds of folios by several hands over decades, so it functions as a record of a workshop changing across a generation. Rishyashringa, the ascetic lured from the forest by courtesans, opens the epic with a story about the power of exactly the court world the painting was made for.

title: Pradyumna and Samvara fight with maces, from the "Large Basohli Bhagavata Purana"
medium: Gum tempera, ink, and gold on paper
sceneContext: From the Large Basohli Bhagavata Purana of about 1760–65, showing Krishna's son Pradyumna fighting the demon Samvara, who had abducted him as an infant and raised him without knowing who he was.
whyBigDeal: Basohli painting uses fragments of iridescent green beetle wing set into the surface for jewels, so the pictures change as you move past them. It is a literal use of light that no pigment could reproduce, and it only works in the room, not in reproduction.

title: Radha Worships Krishna as Kali
artistBio: India, Kalighat district, Kolkata, West Bengal
sceneContext: A Kalighat painting from Kolkata, late nineteenth century, showing Radha in the form of Kali. These were made in the lanes around the Kalighat temple and sold to pilgrims as inexpensive souvenirs of a visit.
whyBigDeal: These were made fast and cheap on mill paper with brush and watercolour, by hereditary scroll-painters who had moved to the city for work. The sweeping single-stroke line was an economic necessity that turned into a style, and it fed directly into twentieth-century Indian modernism through Jamini Roy.

title: Queen Kaikeyi reminds King Dasharatha about the sacrifices of King Bali and King Shivi, folio 39 from the Ayodhya Kanda (Book of Ayodhya) of a Ramayana (Rama's Journey)
medium: gum tempera, ink, and gold on paper
sceneContext: Queen Kaikeyi pressing King Dasharatha to honour an old promise, the moment that sends Rama into exile. Rajasthan, about 1710.
whyBigDeal: The entire Ramayana turns on a debt the king had forgotten he owed. Indian painting returns to this scene constantly because it locates catastrophe in a domestic conversation rather than in a battle.

title: Krishna Lifting Mount Govardhan, from a Persian translation of the Bhagavata Purana, c. 1625
medium: gum tempera, ink, and gold on paper
sceneContext: Krishna lifting Mount Govardhan, from a Persian translation of the Bhagavata Purana made in the Deccan in the 1700s.
whyBigDeal: Hindu scripture translated into Persian for a Muslim court, illustrated by painters trained in both traditions. That kind of crossing was ordinary in Indian courts and is routinely written out of later accounts of the period.

title: Sugriva challenges his brother Vali, King of the Forest Dwellers, to a duel, folio 10 from the Kishkindha Kanda (Book of Kishkindha) of a Ramayana (Rama’s Journey)
medium: Gum tempera, ink, and gold on paper
sceneContext: Sugriva challenging his brother Vali to single combat, from a Pahari Ramayana of about 1700–1720. Rama has agreed to kill Vali from hiding, and the fight is staged so that he can.
whyBigDeal: The brothers are identical, so Rama cannot tell them apart and has to wait for a garland to mark one before shooting. The painters had to make two figures readable as the same person while keeping the picture legible — a problem of design set by the plot.

title: Sita asks Rama to fetch the golden deer, from the “Shangri” Ramayana
medium: Gum tempera, ink, and gold on paper
sceneContext: Sita asking Rama to catch the golden deer, from the 'Shangri' Ramayana of about 1700–1725. The deer is the demon Maricha in disguise, sent to draw Rama away from her.
whyBigDeal: The deer is a demon in disguise, and her request is the hinge that leads to her abduction. Painting it means showing a scene that looks like a domestic request and is actually the trap closing.

title: Radha’s Confidante Brings Her to Krishna, based on poetry of Bihari (Indian, 1595–1663)
medium: Gum tempera, ink, and gold on paper
sceneContext: Illustrating the Hindi poetry of Bihari, whose *Satsai* of seven hundred couplets was among the most-painted texts in northern India. Rajasthan, about 1790–1800.
whyBigDeal: Bihari wrote extremely compressed verses, each a single image, which suited painters exactly — one couplet became one picture without adaptation. The pairing of a terse poetic form with a small painted format is why the *Satsai* was illustrated so often.

title: Celebrations of Krishna's Birth, from a Bhagavata Purana
medium: Gum tempera and gold on paper
sceneContext: The celebrations at Krishna's birth, from a Pahari Bhagavata Purana of about 1725–30. Krishna is born in a prison cell and carried out the same night to a cowherd household, where the rejoicing takes place.
whyBigDeal: The Bhagavata Purana was the most illustrated text in India for three centuries. Krishna is born in a prison cell and smuggled out the same night, so the celebration shown here is happening in the wrong household — the painters are illustrating a joy built on a substitution.

title: Ravana addresses Sita in the garden of Lanka, from Chapters 53 and 54 of the Aranya Kanda (Book of the Forest) of a Ramayana (Rama’s Journey)
medium: Gum tempera, gold, and silver on paper
sceneContext: Ravana confronting Sita in the garden at Lanka, where she is held captive, from a Pahari Ramayana of about 1725.
whyBigDeal: Sita is kept in a grove rather than a cell because Ravana cannot touch her without consent, a constraint the epic states explicitly. The painting has to convey imprisonment through a garden, which is why these versions put so much weight on the surrounding trees.

title: The Birth of Krishna, from a Sursagar of Surdas (Indian, c. 1480–1580)
medium: Gum tempera, ink, and gold on paper
sceneContext: The birth of Krishna, from a Sursagar of Surdas, painted in Rajasthan 1705–10. Surdas was a blind sixteenth-century poet whose devotional songs are still sung.
whyBigDeal: A blind poet's descriptions of Krishna's childhood became one of the most-painted texts in India. What the pictures illustrate is not something seen but something imagined and sung, which the painters treated as no obstacle at all.

title: Krishna Exacts a Toll from the Milkmaids: Dana-Lila, from a Bhagavata Purana
medium: gum tempera and gold on paper
sceneContext: Krishna and the cowherds blocking the milkmaids' path to demand a toll, from a Bhagavata Purana of about 1600 — among the earliest surviving Rajput sets.
whyBigDeal: The Dana-Lila is a flirtation with a theological reading: what Krishna demands is devotion, and the toll is the surrender of the self. Painters liked it because a doctrinal point arrives as a roadside argument.

title: Krishna Rajagopalaswamy, king of the cowherds
medium: Opaque watercolor and hand-colored silver on paper
sceneContext: Krishna as Rajagopalaswamy, painted at Tirupati in Andhra Pradesh in the late eighteenth century for the temple town's pilgrim trade.
whyBigDeal: South Indian temple painting worked to a different brief from courtly miniature: images for worship rather than for an album, made to be seen by crowds at a distance. The frontality and scale come from that function.

title: Battle between monkeys and demons, from the “Shangri” Ramayana
medium: Gum tempera and ink on paper
sceneContext: The battle between the monkey army and Ravana's demons, from the 'Shangri' Ramayana of about 1700. Rama's forces are animals, fighting a city with fortifications and flying machines.
whyBigDeal: Rama's army is made of animals, and the epic's climactic war is fought by monkeys and bears against a technologically superior enemy. Painters used the mass battle scenes to work at a density of small figures rarely attempted in courtly portraiture.

title: Krishna and Radha Quarreling: Shatha Nayaka, from a Rasikapriya
medium: Gum tempera and gold on paper
sceneContext: Krishna and Radha quarrelling, illustrating the Shatha Nayaka — the deceitful hero — from Keshavdas's Rasikapriya. Rajasthan, about 1680.
whyBigDeal: Keshavdas wrote a taxonomy of lovers — types of hero and heroine, sorted by circumstance and mood — and painters worked through it category by category. It is a manual of emotional states, illustrated as systematically as a botanical plate.

title: Iltifat Khan
medium: Brush drawing with pigment on paper
sceneContext: A Mughal court portrait of about 1640, from the reign of Shah Jahan, when imperial portraiture had settled into strict profile against a plain ground.
whyBigDeal: Mughal portraiture aimed at exact likeness at a time when the courts of Europe were doing much the same thing, but in strict profile and without shadow. The convention makes the sitter identifiable while flattening him into pattern, which is a deliberate balance rather than a limitation.

title: A Lady Playing the Tanpura
medium: Ink, opaque and transparent watercolor, and gold on paper
sceneContext: A lady with a tanpura, painted at Kishangarh in Rajasthan around 1735. The tanpura is a drone instrument, played to hold a single sustained pitch under a singer rather than to carry a melody.
whyBigDeal: Kishangarh painting under Raja Sawant Singh produced the most stylised faces in Indian art — enormously elongated eyes, arched brows, a pointed chin — largely through the painter Nihal Chand. The ruler was himself a devotional poet, and the court's house style is inseparable from his verse.

title: Portrait Jewel of Emperor Jahangir
medium: Gum tempera and gold on paper
sceneContext: A portrait of Jahangir made to be worn as a jewel, from his court in the early 1600s.
whyBigDeal: Jahangir gave portrait jewels to favoured nobles, who wore them in their turbans as a visible mark of access. The picture is therefore an instrument of politics that happens to be a painting — status made portable and displayed on the body.

title: Maharana Jagat Singh II Hunting
artistBio: Jugarsi, son of Jiva (Indian, active mid-1700s)
medium: Gum tempera and gold on paper
sceneContext: Maharana Jagat Singh II of Mewar hunting, painted by Jugarsi, son of Jiva, in 1747. Mewar court painters were salaried staff who recorded the ruler's activities as they happened, dated and identified.
whyBigDeal: Mewar court painting recorded specific events on specific dates, functioning as a court diary. That makes these pictures usable as historical evidence in a way most Indian painting is not — the hunt happened, and the painter was expected to get it right.

title: Princess and attendant in trompe l’oeil window
medium: Gum tempera, ink, and gold on paper
sceneContext: A princess at a window, painted by Aqil Khan at Lucknow around 1765, using a trompe l'oeil frame.
whyBigDeal: Lucknow's court absorbed European illusionism as Mughal power collapsed, and the painted window frame is that borrowing made explicit. Provincial courts were often more experimental than the imperial workshop precisely because they had less to conserve.

title: Portrait of Murad Bakhsh (1624–61)
medium: gum tempera and gold on paper
sceneContext: Prince Murad Bakhsh, the youngest of Shah Jahan's four sons, painted by Balchand around 1635 when the boy was about eleven. The borders were added later when the sheet was mounted into an album.
whyBigDeal: Murad was executed in 1661 after losing the war of succession to his brother Aurangzeb. Mughal portraiture recorded the whole imperial family young, so the albums are full of faces whose fates were decided decades after the sitting.

title: A prince riding a composite elephant
medium: Gum tempera, ink, and gold on paper
sceneContext: A prince riding a composite elephant, painted at Golconda in the Deccan around 1590. The elephant's body is assembled from human and animal figures.
whyBigDeal: Composite animals were a Persian and Deccani speciality — an image that resolves into a different image the closer you get. It asks for exactly the kind of looking a screen at a distance discourages, and rewards walking up to it.

title: "Suhrab Slain by Rustam", Folio from a Shahnama (Book of Kings) of Firdausi
medium: Ink, opaque watercolor, and gold on paper
sceneContext: Rustam killing his own son Suhrab without recognising him, from a Shahnama of about 1610. The Shahnama is Persia's national epic, in wide circulation in India.
whyBigDeal: It is the epic's most-illustrated scene and its bleakest: the recognition comes only after the wound. Indian workshops illustrated the Persian classics as thoroughly as their own, and the two traditions are hard to separate by this date.

title: Sultan Ibrahim ibn Adham of Balkh Visited by Angels
medium: gum tempera and gold on paper
sceneContext: Sultan Ibrahim ibn Adham of Balkh, a king who abandoned his throne to become an ascetic, visited by angels. Rajasthan, about 1740.
whyBigDeal: The renunciant king is a story shared across Islamic, Hindu, Buddhist and Jain traditions in India — the Buddha's biography has the same shape. Painting it at a Rajput court meant depicting the abandonment of exactly the life the patron led.

title: Rustam Takes Aim at Ashkabus, from a Shah-nama (Book of Kings)
medium: Gum tempera and ink on paper
sceneContext: Rustam taking aim at Ashkabus, from a Sultanate Shah-nama of about 1425–50, made in the Deccan or Malwa.
whyBigDeal: Sultanate painting predates the Mughals by more than a century and is far rarer. It shows Persian models being absorbed by Indian workshops before the imperial style existed, which makes surviving folios disproportionately important for understanding what came next.

title: Portrait of Islam Khan Mashhadi
medium: Opaque watercolor and gold on paper
sceneContext: Islam Khan Mashhadi, a Mughal noble who served as governor and later as Shah Jahan's chief minister, painted by Payag in the seventeenth century.
whyBigDeal: Payag was among the most technically ambitious Mughal painters, working with unusually dark tonality and night effects. Where most court portraiture is evenly lit and even-handed, his pictures use shadow, which was a deliberate departure.

title: "Death of Farud", Folio from a Shahnama (Book of Kings) of Firdausi
medium: Ink, opaque watercolor, and gold on paper
sceneContext: The death of Farud, from a Shahnama of about 1610. Farud is killed by his own family's army after a misunderstanding.
whyBigDeal: The Shahnama returns repeatedly to kin killing kin by mistake, and Mughal patrons — whose own successions were settled by fratricide — commissioned illustrated copies throughout. The epic was read at courts that were living its plot.

title: Portrait of Suraj Singh Rathor, Raja of Marwar and Maternal Uncle of Shah Jahan: A Page from the Prince Khurram Album
medium: Gum tempera and gold on paper
sceneContext: Suraj Singh Rathor, Raja of Marwar and maternal uncle of the future Shah Jahan, painted by Bishandas around 1600. Marwar was one of the Rajput states allied to the Mughals by marriage.
whyBigDeal: Jahangir sent Bishandas to Persia specifically to paint Shah Abbas from life, calling him unequalled at likeness. An emperor dispatching a painter abroad as an instrument of diplomacy is a fair measure of how seriously portraiture was taken.

title: "Four Portraits: (upper left) A Raja (Perhaps Raja Sarang Rao), by Balchand; (upper right) 'Inayat Khan, by Daulat; (lower left) 'Abd al-Khaliq, probably by Balchand; (lower right) Jamal Khan Qaravul, by Murad", Folio from the Shah Jahan Album
medium: Ink, opaque watercolor, and gold on paper
sceneContext: Four separate portraits mounted together on a single album page, the upper left painted by Balachand around 1610–15. Mughal albums paired such pages with facing sheets of calligraphy.
whyBigDeal: Mughal albums combined paintings of different dates and hands on one page within new borders, so an album page is a curated object rather than a single work. Later owners rearranged them, and much Mughal painting survives in an order nobody originally intended.

title: Sultan Muhammad 'Adil Shah and Ikhlas Khan Riding an Elephant
medium: Ink, opaque watercolor, and gold on paper
sceneContext: Sultan Muhammad 'Adil Shah of Bijapur riding an elephant with Ikhlas Khan, painted by Haidar 'Ali about 1645.
whyBigDeal: Ikhlas Khan was an African minister who effectively governed Bijapur — one of several Africans, mostly brought as slaves, who reached the top of Deccan states. He is shown at the sultan's scale, which in this system is a precise statement of power.

title: Maharana Jawan Singh of Mewar (r. 1828–38) Holding a Falcon
medium: gum tempera, pearls, silk, and gold on paper
sceneContext: Maharana Jawan Singh of Mewar holding a falcon, painted by Ghasi around 1835. Falconry was a court activity that doubled as portraiture: the bird identifies the sitter's rank as clearly as his jewellery does.
whyBigDeal: Ghasi worked for both the Mewar court and British patrons, including the resident James Tod, producing architectural studies alongside court portraits. The double employment is typical of the 1830s, when Indian painters were serving two systems at once.

title: Lineage Portrait of an Abbot
sceneContext: A lineage portrait of a Tibetan abbot, painted in central Tibet about 1350. The figure sits enthroned with the teachers he received transmission from ranged above and around him.
whyBigDeal: Tibetan Buddhism transmits authority through teacher-to-pupil lineage, so portraits function as legal documents of succession rather than as commemoration. The named figures establish a claim, which is why identification matters more than likeness.

title: Portrait of the Indian Monk Atisha
sceneContext: Atisha, the Bengali monk who travelled to Tibet in 1042 and reformed Buddhism there. Painted in Tibet in the early to mid-twelfth century.
whyBigDeal: Atisha left the great monastic university of Vikramashila in Bihar and never returned. Within two centuries Buddhism was effectively extinct in the country of its origin and continuous in Tibet, so paintings like this preserve an Indian tradition outside India.

title: Bejeweled Buddha Preaching
medium: Gum tempera, ink, and gold on cloth
sceneContext: A bejewelled Buddha preaching, painted in Nepal in 1648. The Buddha is shown crowned and ornamented rather than in monastic robes, a form associated with his role as a cosmic rather than historical teacher.
whyBigDeal: Newar artists of the Kathmandu Valley supplied painting and metalwork to Tibet for a thousand years, and much of what is called Tibetan art was made by them or by their pupils. The valley was a workshop for a religion practised over the mountains.

title: Nagarjuna (c. 150–250 CE) with a Buddhist Master
sceneContext: Nagarjuna, the second-century Indian philosopher, seated with a Buddhist master. Painted in Nepal in the fourteenth century, some twelve hundred years after the man it depicts.
whyBigDeal: Nagarjuna's argument that nothing possesses independent existence underlies most later Mahayana thought. Portraying a philosopher whose position is that no fixed essence exists is a problem the tradition solved by convention rather than by likeness.

title: Eleven-Headed, Thousand-Armed Bodhisattva of Compassion (Avalokiteshvara)
medium: Gum tempera and ink on cotton
sceneContext: The eleven-headed, thousand-armed Avalokiteshvara, painted in western Tibet about 1500. Each hand holds an implement or bears an eye, and the heads rise in tiers above the shoulders.
whyBigDeal: The eleven heads come from a story in which his head splits from grief at the scale of suffering he cannot relieve, and is remade so he can perceive more. The multiplication is an argument about the limits of compassion, drawn rather than stated.

title: Portrait of Shakyashribhadra with His Life Episodes and Lineage
sceneContext: Shakyashribhadra, a Kashmiri scholar who reached Tibet in 1204, shown with episodes from his life and his lineage. Painted in Tibet in the early to mid-fourteenth century.
whyBigDeal: He arrived as the Islamic conquest of northern India was destroying the monastic universities, carrying texts and ordination lineages that would otherwise have been lost. The painting records a transfer of institutional memory across the Himalayas.

title: Tsong Khapa, Founder of the Geluk Order
medium: Gum tempera and gold on cotton
sceneContext: Tsong Khapa, founder of the Geluk order, painted in central Tibet about 1440–70, within living memory of his death in 1419.
whyBigDeal: The Geluk order became the dominant school of Tibetan Buddhism and produced the line of Dalai Lamas. This is a portrait of an institution's founder made while the institution was still establishing itself.

title: Green Tara
artistBio: Aniko (Nepalese, active in Tibet mid- to late 1200s)
medium: thangka; gum tempera, ink, and gold on sized cotton; mount: silk
sceneContext: Green Tara, attributed to Aniko, the Nepalese artist who went to Tibet as a teenager and then to the court of Kublai Khan. About the 1260s.
whyBigDeal: Aniko became head of imperial artistic production for the Yuan dynasty, running workshops across China. A Newar teenager from the Kathmandu Valley ended up directing the visual output of the Mongol empire, and this panel dates from the beginning of that journey.

title: Portraits of Two Lineage Masters of the Kagyu Order: Phagmo Drupa (1110–1170) and Tashipel (1142–1210)
sceneContext: Phagmo Drupa and a second master of the Kagyu order, painted in central Tibet in the thirteenth or early fourteenth century.
whyBigDeal: The Kagyu order transmitted its teaching orally from master to pupil, and its paintings record the chain of that transmission. Removing a figure from the sequence would break the claim, so the pictures are maintained as much as admired.

title: Tantric Buddha Vairochana as Vajrasattva
medium: gum tempera, ink, and gold on cloth
sceneContext: Vairochana in his tantric form as Vajrasattva, painted in central Tibet about 1150–1200. He holds the vajra and bell, the paired implements of tantric practice, crossed at the chest.
whyBigDeal: Twelfth-century Tibetan painting still shows its Indian sources directly, before the tradition consolidated into something recognisably its own. Pieces this early are the best surviving evidence of what the lost Buddhist painting of eastern India looked like.

title: Painting from a Kalpa-sutra: Queen Trishala Reclining
medium: Gum tempera and gold on paper; 18th century gold flecked border
sceneContext: Queen Trishala reclining, from a Jain Kalpasutra painted in Gujarat about 1450–75. She is the mother of Mahavira, the last Jain tirthankara.
whyBigDeal: Jain communities commissioned illustrated manuscripts as acts of merit and stored them in temple libraries, which is why so many survive when comparable Hindu and Buddhist manuscripts do not. Preservation here is a by-product of a religious practice, not of connoisseurship.

title: A Mughal courtier
medium: Gum tempera and gold on paper, mounted with gold-sprinkled borders
sceneContext: A courtier at Akbar's court, painted about 1575, with borders added later.
whyBigDeal: Akbar was illiterate and built his authority partly through pictures, running a workshop of over a hundred painters, most of them Hindu, under Persian masters. The Mughal style was manufactured deliberately and quickly, as policy.

title: Chand Bibi Hawking with Attendants in a Landscape
medium: Opaque watercolor, gold, and silver on card-weight paper
sceneContext: Chand Bibi hawking, painted about 1700. She ruled Ahmednagar as regent and personally led its defence against Akbar's armies in 1595.
whyBigDeal: She was killed by her own troops during the second siege. The hawking portrait, painted a century later, is a posthumous invention — she is remembered through an image of leisure by the empire that destroyed her state.

title: A group of women in ecstasy before Madhava, folio 4 from a Madhavanala-Kamakandala
medium: gum tempera and gold on paper
sceneContext: From a *Madhavanala Kamakandala*, a Hindi romance, painted in the Punjab hills about 1720.
whyBigDeal: The story turns on a musician whose playing overwhelms his listeners, and the painting has to show sound overpowering a room. Indian painters solved this by depicting the effect rather than the cause — bodies losing composure, not an instrument.

title: Birth of Mahavira, folio 40 (verso) from a Kalpa-sutra
medium: gum tempera, ink, and gold on paper
sceneContext: The birth of Mahavira, from a Jain Kalpasutra painted in Gujarat about 1400.
whyBigDeal: Western Indian manuscript painting uses a rigid convention of the projecting further eye on a face shown in profile, held for centuries. It is not an inability to foreshorten; it is a fixed sign for a face, maintained deliberately long after alternatives were available.

title: Taking of the toll, Dana-Lila
medium: Gum tempera and gold on paper
sceneContext: The Dana-Lila, Krishna demanding a toll from the milkmaids, painted in the Punjab hills about 1760.
whyBigDeal: Comparing this with the Rajasthani version of the same episode from a century and a half earlier shows the two traditions diverging: the hills soften the palette and open up the landscape where Rajasthan keeps the ground flat and hot.

title: Heroine with attendant and a pair of deer
sceneContext: A heroine with her attendant and a pair of deer, painted in the Punjab hills about 1710–20.
whyBigDeal: Paired deer are a standing sign for lovers in Indian poetry and painting, placed in the picture to say something about the human figures. The landscape in these works is rarely neutral — it is carrying the commentary.

title: Akbar supervising the capture of wild elephants at Malwa in 1564, painting 90 from an Akbar-nama (Book of Akbar) of Abu’l Fazl (Indian 1551–1602)
medium: ink with use of colors and gold on paper, mounted on an album page with borders of gold-decorated buff and blue paper (recto); calligraphy by Faqir Ali (verso)
sceneContext: Akbar supervising the capture of wild elephants at Malwa in 1564, painted by Farukh Chela about 1602–3 for an illustrated history of the reign.
whyBigDeal: The *Akbarnama* was an official chronicle illustrated as it was written, with named painters assigned to named events. It is state history produced as a picture book, and the attribution notes in the margins let us reconstruct exactly who painted what.

title: The Fabulous Creature Buraq
medium: Opaque watercolor and gold on paper
sceneContext: Buraq, the winged steed with a human face that carried Muhammad on the night journey to Jerusalem and through the heavens. Painted about 1660–80.
whyBigDeal: Indian Islamic painting depicted Buraq freely while generally veiling or omitting the Prophet himself. The creature became the acceptable stand-in for an unpicturable event, and is now among the most recognisable images in South Asian Islamic art.

title: Lovers Embracing
medium: Gum tempera and gold on paper
sceneContext: Lovers embracing, painted at the Mughal court about 1630.
whyBigDeal: Mughal painting is dominated by portraits, court scenes and natural history; intimate subjects are comparatively rare and were made for private albums. The audience for a picture like this was a handful of people turning pages, not a court.

title: Devananda's Fourteen Auspicious Dreams Foretelling the Birth of Mahavira: Folio from a Kalpasutra Manuscript
sceneContext: Devananda's fourteen dreams foretelling Mahavira's birth, by the Master of the Jaunpur Kalpasutra, about 1465.
whyBigDeal: Jain doctrine holds that the embryo was transferred between two mothers, so the dreams are dreamt by the wrong woman. The painters had to illustrate a prophecy that turns out to have been delivered to the incorrect recipient.

title: Juggler
sceneContext: A juggler, painted about 1840 for a British patron in Lucknow or Delhi.
whyBigDeal: Company School painters were trained in Mughal workshops and retrained to supply Europeans with catalogues of Indian trades, castes and costumes. The pictures are documentary in intent and were shaped by what the buyer wanted recorded.

title: Man Dyeing Cloth
medium: Gum tempera and ink on paper
sceneContext: A man dyeing cloth, painted in Lucknow in the early 1830s as part of a series on Indian occupations.
whyBigDeal: Indian painters lost their court patrons as Mughal power collapsed and found British ones with entirely different requirements — watercolour on English paper, plain backgrounds, one trade per sheet. The style changed because the customer did.

title: Portrait of Hafiz Abd al-Rahim Khan, from the Fraser Album
medium: Gum tempera and gold on paper
sceneContext: Hafiz Abd al-Rahim Khan, from the Fraser Album, painted in Delhi about 1815–20.
whyBigDeal: William Fraser and his brother commissioned Delhi painters to portray individual soldiers and villagers at life-size scale, named and specific. The results are unlike anything else from the period: ordinary people given the treatment reserved for nobles.

title: Women playing at cross-dressing
medium: ink heightened with colors on paper
sceneContext: Women at play in male dress, painted at Golconda in the Deccan about 1680–1700.
whyBigDeal: Deccan painting is more inward and more strange than Mughal work, with a taste for reverie and inversion that the imperial style discouraged. The southern sultanates were absorbed by the Mughals within decades of this being painted.

title: A marbled picture of Rustam catching Rakhsh
medium: Gum tempera and gold on paper
sceneContext: Rustam catching the horse Rakhsh, made about 1650 at Bijapur using marbled paper.
whyBigDeal: The image is built by floating pigment on liquid, transferring it to paper, and then cutting and assembling the marbled sheets into figures. It is collage from a controlled accident, three centuries before European artists tried anything comparable.

title: An African Lyre Player (recto)
medium: Gum tempera, ink, and gold on paper
sceneContext: An African lyre player, painted in the Deccan about 1640–60.
whyBigDeal: Africans reached the Deccan in large numbers, many through the slave trade, and some rose to command armies and govern states. Deccan painting records their presence as ordinary, which the later historical record largely does not.

title: A European Couple
medium: Gum tempera and gold on paper
sceneContext: A European couple, painted at Bijapur about 1610–27 by the artist known as the 'Bodleian Painter'.
whyBigDeal: Deccan painters saw Europeans through imported prints rather than in person, and copied costume details from engravings without the context. The pictures are a record of one culture reading another entirely through printed matter.

title: Italian Landscape
sceneContext: Painted in Rome about 1630 by a Frenchman who spent almost his whole career there, sketching outdoors in the countryside around the city and composing the finished pictures in the studio.
whyBigDeal: Claude invented the formula that European landscape painting used for the next two centuries — framing trees at the sides, a receding middle distance, the sun near the horizon. English landowners later remodelled real parks to look like his paintings, which is an unusual direction for influence to run.

title: Tobias and the Angel
sceneContext: Tobias and the archangel Raphael, painted by Guardi in the 1750s as one of a set of organ-loft panels for the church of the Angelo Raffaele in Venice.
whyBigDeal: The panels sat high above a church floor, so Guardi painted them loosely, for legibility at distance rather than close inspection. He spent most of his career on view paintings for tourists, and this religious commission is a reminder that the souvenir trade was the exception in his training, not the rule.

title: Christ on the Cross
sceneContext: Painted in Toledo around 1600–1610, late in El Greco's career, when he was running a busy workshop supplying altarpieces across Castile.
whyBigDeal: He trained in Crete as an icon painter, then worked in Venice and Rome before settling in Spain, and the elongated bodies come partly from Byzantine convention rather than from Italian anatomy. He was dismissed for centuries as eccentric and only recovered when the Expressionists recognised what he was doing.

title: Portrait of a Woman
sceneContext: Painted in Florence about 1550 by Bronzino, court painter to Cosimo I de' Medici, who used him to produce portraits of the ruling family for diplomatic distribution.
whyBigDeal: Bronzino's sitters have skin like enamel and expressions that give nothing away, which was the point — Medici portraiture was designed to project control rather than personality. The coldness modern viewers read as psychological distance was a political specification.

title: Christ Crowned with Thorns (Ecce Homo), and the Mourning Virgin (Mater Dolorosa)
medium: Oil on canvas, transferred from wood
sceneContext: A devotional diptych of about 1530–40 pairing Christ crowned with thorns and the grieving Virgin, made in Bruges for private prayer.
whyBigDeal: The two panels were meant to be held open in the hands, close to the face, so the viewer looked at Christ's suffering and Mary's grief simultaneously and at conversational distance. It is a piece of religious technology, designed for a specific bodily use.

title: Children Dancing
sceneContext: Children dancing, painted in France about 1650 by one of the Le Nain brothers, who worked so closely together that individual attribution remains unsettled.
whyBigDeal: The brothers painted French peasants without caricature or moralising at a time when rural poverty was normally shown as comic. Their reputation collapsed after their deaths and was rebuilt in the nineteenth century by Courbet's generation, who found in them a precedent for painting ordinary people seriously.

title: Saint Peter Repentant
sceneContext: Saint Peter weeping after denying Christ, painted in Lorraine in 1645 and signed and dated — unusual for La Tour, whose chronology is otherwise guesswork.
whyBigDeal: He built almost his whole output around a single candle inside the picture, which does all the lighting. La Tour was completely forgotten for nearly three hundred years and only reconstructed in 1915, when a scholar began gathering pictures scattered under other names.

title: The Penitent Magdalen
sceneContext: The Magdalen with a skull and a candle flame, painted about 1640. La Tour returned to this subject at least four times with slight variations.
whyBigDeal: The candle is both light source and subject: it measures the time she has left, which is what the skull states more bluntly. Reducing a religious painting to one figure, one flame and two objects strips out everything the Counter-Reformation normally required.

title: The Holy Family with Mary Magdalen
sceneContext: Painted in Toledo about 1590–95, during El Greco's most productive Spanish years.
whyBigDeal: He priced his work aggressively and sued patrons who underpaid, leaving a paper trail of lawsuits that tells us more about his life than about his art. The litigation records are the main reason we can date his career at all.

title: Scenes of Witchcraft
sceneContext: From a group of witchcraft scenes painted about 1645–49 for a Florentine patron.
whyBigDeal: Rosa specialised in subjects the academies considered improper — witches, bandits, wild landscapes — and marketed himself as an outsider while working steadily for wealthy collectors. The Romantics took him at his word and made him a hero, which he had spent his career arranging.

title: Saint John the Baptist in a Landscape
sceneContext: John the Baptist in a wilderness, painted in Bruges about 1445 by Petrus Christus, who took over the leading workshop in the city after Jan van Eyck's death.
whyBigDeal: Christus was among the first Northern painters to use a single vanishing point, adopting from Italy a system van Eyck had managed without. His pictures document the moment two separate solutions to depth were traded across the Alps.

title: Lazarus and the Rich Man
sceneContext: The parable of Lazarus and the rich man, painted in Venice about 1550 by Bassano, who worked in the small mainland town of Bassano del Grappa rather than in the city.
whyBigDeal: He filled biblical scenes with livestock, kitchen pots and farm labour, which let him paint the countryside he lived in while satisfying a religious commission. The formula sold extremely well and his four sons turned the workshop into a production line.

title: Portrait of a Woman
sceneContext: Painted in Florence about 1518 by Andrea del Sarto, whom Vasari called the painter without errors — a compliment that has followed him around ever since as a slight.
whyBigDeal: Vasari's verdict fixed his reputation as technically flawless and lacking ambition, and Robert Browning built a well-known poem on that reading. It is a case of an artist's standing being set almost entirely by one line from a near-contemporary.

title: The Immaculate Conception
sceneContext: The Immaculate Conception, painted in Seville about 1680. Murillo painted the subject more than twenty times.
whyBigDeal: The doctrine was fiercely contested and not made official Church teaching until 1854, so these paintings were arguments in a live theological dispute. Seville was the centre of the campaign, and Murillo's workshop supplied the imagery that eventually won.

title: The Baptism of Christ
sceneContext: The Baptism of Christ, painted in Cranach's Wittenberg workshop in the 1530s.
whyBigDeal: Cranach was Luther's close friend, printed his tracts, and produced the visual language of the Reformation while continuing to take Catholic commissions. He was also the town's apothecary, a printer and twice its mayor — the painting was one business among several.

title: Abraham Welcoming the Three Angels
sceneContext: Abraham welcoming the three angels, from Guardi's set of organ-loft panels for the Angelo Raffaele in Venice, 1750s.
whyBigDeal: Guardi worked in his brother-in-law Tiepolo's shadow for decades and only found his own market late. Venice's painters at this date were competing for a shrinking pool of local patrons while the city's political power drained away.

title: Rest on the Flight into Egypt
sceneContext: The Holy Family resting during the flight into Egypt, painted in Rome in the early 1640s.
whyBigDeal: Claude kept a book of drawings of every finished painting, the *Liber Veritatis*, specifically to prove which pictures were his when forgeries began circulating. It is one of the earliest systematic attempts by an artist to police his own attribution.

title: María Teresa (1638–1683), Infanta of Spain
sceneContext: The Infanta María Teresa, daughter of Philip IV, painted 1651–54 and sent abroad as part of marriage negotiations. She married Louis XIV of France in 1660.
whyBigDeal: Court portraits functioned as diplomatic documents, so the likeness had to be accurate enough to be relied on by a foreign court. Velázquez was painting evidence, and the elaborate hair and dress record what the Spanish court wanted a prospective husband to see.

title: Saint Ambrose
sceneContext: Saint Ambrose, painted about 1796–99, in the years around the illness that left Goya completely deaf.
whyBigDeal: The deafness in 1793 separated his career in two: the court painter before, and the maker of the *Caprichos* and the Black Paintings after. This sits at the hinge, still a commission for a church, from a man already producing private work nobody had asked for.

title: Martyrdom of Saint Andrew
sceneContext: The martyrdom of Saint Andrew, painted by Guido Reni in the early seventeenth century.
whyBigDeal: Reni was the most sought-after painter in Italy in his lifetime and the most reviled by the following century, dismissed as sentimental by Ruskin's generation. Few reputations have swung so far in both directions, and neither verdict has much to do with the pictures.

title: The Virgin and Child Appearing to Saint Francis of Assisi
sceneContext: The Virgin appearing to Saint Francis, painted in Naples in the 1680s by Giordano, nicknamed *Luca fa presto* — Luke works fast.
whyBigDeal: He was said to be able to paint in the manner of Titian, Raphael or Rubens on request, and did so openly rather than as forgery. Extreme facility of that kind was admired then and read as emptiness later, which says more about changing ideas of originality than about him.

title: Adoration of the Magi
sceneContext: The Adoration of the Magi, painted in 1642, the year Reni died heavily in debt.
whyBigDeal: He gambled compulsively and worked at speed to cover his losses, which is the practical explanation for much of the thinly painted late work. The biography is not incidental — the pictures were made to pay creditors.

title: Portrait of a Man with a Rosary
sceneContext: A man holding a rosary, painted about 1508 while Cranach was court painter to Frederick the Wise of Saxony.
whyBigDeal: Cranach ran the largest workshop in Germany, signing pictures with a winged serpent badge that functioned as a trademark rather than a signature. Distinguishing his hand from his employees' is a problem that remains unresolved for much of the output.

title: Portrait of Charles I (1600–1649)
sceneContext: Charles I of England, after Van Dyck, who was the king's principal painter from 1632 until his own death in 1641.
whyBigDeal: Van Dyck invented the image of Stuart monarchy so successfully that the king was executed in 1649 partly for the absolutism the portraits projected. Few painters have shaped a political reputation so directly, or seen it destroyed so quickly.

title: Sketch for a Ceiling
sceneContext: An oil sketch for a ceiling, painted by Tiepolo in the 1750s.
whyBigDeal: Ceiling commissions were sold on the strength of sketches like this, so the small painting is the sales document and the contract. Tiepolo's finished ceilings in Würzburg and Madrid are the last great decorative schemes before the market for them disappeared.

title: Friedrich III (1463–1525), the Wise, Elector of Saxony
artist: Lucas Cranach the Elder and Workshop
medium: Oil on beech, with letterpress-printed paper labels
sceneContext: Frederick the Wise, Elector of Saxony, painted in 1533 by Cranach's workshop, eight years after the sitter's death.
whyBigDeal: Frederick protected Luther from arrest and made the Reformation politically survivable. Cranach produced posthumous portraits of him in quantity, effectively manufacturing a Protestant founder-image for distribution — the workshop was doing propaganda at scale.

title: Portrait of Agostino Barbarigo
sceneContext: Agostino Barbarigo, a Venetian noble, painted by Veronese after about 1571.
whyBigDeal: Veronese was summoned before the Inquisition in 1573 over a Last Supper containing dwarfs, drunkards and dogs. He refused to repaint it and simply retitled it *The Feast in the House of Levi*, which the tribunal accepted — an early instance of an artist winning a censorship fight on a technicality.

title: Scenes of Witchcraft: Day
sceneContext: From Rosa's *Scenes of Witchcraft* series, about 1645–49, depicting the daylight hours of a witches' sabbath.
whyBigDeal: Witchcraft prosecutions were still active across Europe when these were painted, so the subject was contemporary rather than folkloric. They were made as private cabinet pictures for collectors who found the material entertaining, at a time when others were being executed for it.

title: The Sacrifice of Isaac
sceneContext: The sacrifice of Isaac, from Guardi's organ-loft series for the Angelo Raffaele, Venice, 1750s.
whyBigDeal: The panels are attributed jointly to Francesco and his brother Gianantonio, and separating their hands is unresolved. Venetian workshops of this period were family firms in which individual authorship was not the organising idea.

title: Allegorical Figure
sceneContext: An allegorical figure painted about 1636 by Strozzi, a Genoese who had been a Capuchin friar before leaving the order to support his mother and sister.
whyBigDeal: The order pursued him legally for years after he left, and he eventually moved to Venice to escape it. He was painting these full-blooded, warmly lit figures while under sustained pressure from the Church he had walked out of.

title: Philip IV (1605–1665), King of Spain
sceneContext: Philip IV of Spain, probably 1624, from the first years after the twenty-four-year-old Velázquez was appointed court painter.
whyBigDeal: The appointment gave him an exclusive right to paint the king and effectively removed him from the open market for the rest of his life. He produced comparatively few pictures as a result, and spent much of his time on palace administration.

title: Madonna and Child with Saints
sceneContext: A Madonna and Child with saints, painted in 1607 by Ludovico Carracci in Bologna.
whyBigDeal: Ludovico and his cousins Annibale and Agostino founded an academy in Bologna that taught drawing from life at a time when most training was copying. Their curriculum became the model for the European art academy for the next two hundred and fifty years.

title: Scenes of Witchcraft: Morning
sceneContext: From Rosa's *Scenes of Witchcraft*, about 1645–49, showing the sabbath breaking up at morning.
whyBigDeal: Rosa also wrote satirical verse attacking patronage and staged his own theatrical performances. He is one of the earliest painters to construct a public persona as a rebel, and to have it work commercially.

title: Nymphs and a Satyr (Amor Vincit Omnia)
sceneContext: Nymphs and a satyr, painted in Rome about 1625–27, in Poussin's first years in the city after arriving from Normandy.
whyBigDeal: He spent almost his whole career in Rome painting for a small circle of learned collectors, mostly on a scale that suited a private study rather than a church. That deliberate choice of audience is why his pictures assume you already know the text.

title: The Life of the Virgin
sceneContext: Scenes from the life of the Virgin, painted in Bruges after 1521 by Isenbrant, who ran one of the city's largest workshops.
whyBigDeal: Bruges was silting up and losing its trade to Antwerp exactly as Isenbrant was working, so the workshop was producing conservative devotional pictures in a city that was economically finished. The style stayed deliberately old-fashioned because the customers wanted it that way.

title: Portrait of King Charles II of England
sceneContext: Charles II of England in 1653, painted by Champaigne during the king's exile in France after his father's execution.
whyBigDeal: He would not be restored to the throne for another seven years. Portraits of exiled claimants were made to keep a claim alive in foreign courts, so the picture is an argument that a monarchy still existed when it did not.

title: Saint Mary Magdalen
sceneContext: Mary Magdalen, painted about 1630 by Vouet after fourteen years in Italy, where he had absorbed Caravaggio and then moved past him.
whyBigDeal: Vouet returned to Paris in 1627 and effectively founded the French school of the seventeenth century, training Le Brun and Le Sueur. Almost every French painter of the next generation passed through his studio.

title: Ruins in a Rocky Landscape
sceneContext: Ruins in a rocky landscape, painted about 1640.
whyBigDeal: Rosa's wild landscapes gave the eighteenth century its category of the sublime — the pleasurable terror of nature that later drove Romantic painting. Travellers on the Grand Tour looked for real scenery that resembled his invented views.

title: The Holy Family with Saint John the Baptist and Saint Margaret
sceneContext: The Holy Family with the young Baptist and Saint Margaret, painted in Florence about 1488–93 by Filippino Lippi, son of the painter-friar Fra Filippo.
whyBigDeal: Filippo was a friar who abducted a nun, Lucrezia Buti, from the convent he was chaplain to; Filippino was their son, and the Medici obtained a papal dispensation releasing both parents from their vows. This picture exists because a scandal was politically fixed.

title: The Penitence of Saint Jerome
artistBio: Netherlandish, Dinant or Bouvignes, active by 1515–died 1524 Antwerp
sceneContext: Saint Jerome in penitence, painted about 1515 by Patinir, who worked in Antwerp.
whyBigDeal: Patinir is the first European painter to treat landscape as the main subject and the figures as small incidents inside it. Dürer, who met him, described him as a good landscape painter — the earliest use of the term for a specialism rather than a background.

title: Virgin and Child with the Young Saint John the Baptist
sceneContext: A Virgin and Child with the young Baptist, painted in Florence about 1490, from Botticelli's busy workshop years.
whyBigDeal: Within a few years Botticelli fell under the influence of the preacher Savonarola, whose bonfires consumed luxury objects and possibly some of his own pictures. His late work turns harsh and archaic, and he died poor and unfashionable in a city that had moved on.

title: The Judgment of Paris
sceneContext: The Judgment of Paris, painted about 1528, with the three goddesses in the costume and setting of a German court rather than a classical one.
whyBigDeal: Cranach's mythological nudes were made for Protestant princes at the same moment their courts were suppressing religious imagery. Classical subjects supplied a legal loophole: painting the body was acceptable when the excuse was Greek.

title: Hunting near Hartenfels Castle
medium: oil, originally on wood, transferred to masonite
sceneContext: A stag hunt near Hartenfels Castle, painted in 1540 with the Elector of Saxony and his guests as participants.
whyBigDeal: Court hunts were staged events in which deer were driven into water and killed from boats, and the painting records the arrangement precisely. It functions as documentation of a political occasion as much as a sporting picture.

title: Nymph of the Spring
sceneContext: A nymph beside a spring, painted about 1545–50 by Cranach the Younger, who took over his father's workshop and its signature.
whyBigDeal: The composition was produced repeatedly by the workshop with small variations, usually with an inscription warning the viewer not to disturb her sleep. It is a manufactured product line, and the moralising label is part of the packaging.

title: Panel from a Triptych: St. Anthony Abbot
sceneContext: Saint Anthony Abbot, one panel of a triptych painted in 1458 by Fra Filippo Lippi, a Carmelite friar.
whyBigDeal: Painted the year after the scandal of his relationship with Lucrezia Buti became public. Cosimo de' Medici, who employed him, is said to have locked him in a room to make him work and gave up when Lippi climbed out on knotted sheets.

title: The Coronation of the Virgin
sceneContext: The Coronation of the Virgin, painted after 1595 by Annibale Carracci, probably during his years in Rome working for Cardinal Farnese.
whyBigDeal: Annibale's Farnese Gallery ceiling was ranked beside the Sistine for two centuries. He was paid a fraction of what he expected for it, fell into depression, and painted almost nothing in his last years.

title: The Supper at Emmaus
sceneContext: The Supper at Emmaus, painted in Venice about 1720 by Piazzetta, who worked notoriously slowly and left many commissions unfinished.
whyBigDeal: He used deep shadow and a restricted palette while Venice was turning to the bright, high-keyed manner of Tiepolo. Being out of step with a small market cost him work, and he died in poverty despite heading the city's painting academy.

title: Pontifical Ceremony in SS. Giovanni e Paolo, Venice, 1782
sceneContext: A pontifical ceremony in the church of SS. Giovanni e Paolo in Venice in 1782, painted by Guardi.
whyBigDeal: Pope Pius VI's visit to Venice was one of the last state occasions of the Republic, which Napoleon abolished fifteen years later. Guardi recorded the ceremonies of a government in its final decade, for buyers who wanted souvenirs of it.

title: Christ with Joseph of Arimathea
sceneContext: Christ with Joseph of Arimathea, painted about 1525 by Savoldo, a Brescian who worked largely in Venice.
whyBigDeal: Savoldo painted silvered, night-lit surfaces decades before Caravaggio and had almost no following. He is a reminder that innovations do not automatically propagate — the same effects had to be invented again later to have any influence.

title: Terminus, the Device of Erasmus
artistBio: Hans Holbein the Younger (German, active England and Switzerland, 1497/98–1543)
sceneContext: *Terminus*, the personal device of Erasmus, painted by Holbein about 1532. The Roman boundary god carried the motto 'I yield to no one'.
whyBigDeal: Erasmus adopted a god of boundaries as his emblem while spending his life refusing to take sides between Luther and Rome. Holbein carried Erasmus's letters of introduction to England, which is how he ended up painting the Tudor court.

title: Virgin and Child
sceneContext: A Virgin and Child painted in Bruges about 1470–80 by Memling, a German who settled in the city and became its wealthiest painter.
whyBigDeal: Memling appears on Bruges tax rolls among the richest citizens, which is rare evidence of a fifteenth-century painter's actual standing. He produced small devotional panels for Italian bankers stationed in the city, who carried them home.

title: Panel from a Triptych: The Archangel Michael
sceneContext: The Archangel Michael, from the 1458 triptych by Fra Filippo Lippi.
whyBigDeal: Michael weighs souls at the Last Judgement, so his armour and scales are inventory rather than decoration. Fifteenth-century viewers read these attributes as fluently as text, which is why the pictures could be so economical.

title: The Rest on the Flight into Egypt
sceneContext: The rest on the flight into Egypt, painted 1537–40 by Jan Massys, son of Quentin Massys.
whyBigDeal: Jan was banished from Antwerp for a decade on suspicion of Protestant sympathies and worked in Italy and France before being allowed back. Religious pictures made in that period were produced by painters whose own confession could get them exiled.

title: Portrait of a Man, Possibly Girolamo Rosati
sceneContext: A man, possibly Girolamo Rosati, painted 1533–34 by Lorenzo Lotto.
whyBigDeal: Lotto kept an account book for his last twenty years listing prices, debts and unsold pictures, which survives. It shows a painter of real ability failing commercially and eventually retiring to a religious house at Loreto — the clearest financial record we have of a Renaissance career going wrong.

title: The Nativity
sceneContext: The Nativity, painted in Bruges about 1485–90 by Gerard David, who became the city's leading painter after Memling.
whyBigDeal: David was the last major figure of the Bruges school before the city's economy collapsed and Antwerp took over. Netherlandish painting did not decline so much as relocate, following the money north.

title: Pope Pius VI Descending the Throne to Take Leave of the Doge in the Hall of SS. Giovanni e Paolo, 1782
sceneContext: Pope Pius VI taking leave of the Doge of Venice, painted about 1783.
whyBigDeal: Guardi painted several versions of this ceremony, all from the same drawings rather than from the event. His view paintings were commercial products made to order, and the number of variants of a single scene reflects demand rather than repeated observation.

title: Ceres and Bacchus
sceneContext: Ceres and Bacchus, painted in the seventeenth century after Spranger, who worked at the court of Rudolf II in Prague.
whyBigDeal: Rudolf assembled one of the strangest collections in Europe — art, automata, astronomical instruments and alleged unicorn horn — and largely stopped governing. The elongated, erotic mythologies his painters supplied were made for a single obsessive private viewer.

title: Johann I (1468–1532), the Constant, Elector of Saxony
artist: Lucas Cranach the Elder and Workshop
medium: Oil on beech, with letterpress-printed paper labels
sceneContext: Johann the Constant, Elector of Saxony, painted 1532–33 by the Cranach workshop.
whyBigDeal: Johann formalised the Lutheran church in his territory and signed the protest that produced the word Protestant. Cranach's workshop supplied paired portraits of these rulers in quantity, functioning as the party's visual identity.

title: Portrait of a Man
sceneContext: A man, painted about 1650, from Velázquez's second stay in Rome.
whyBigDeal: On that visit he painted Pope Innocent X and his own servant Juan de Pareja, an enslaved man of North African descent whom he freed shortly afterwards and who became a painter himself. The Roman portraits are the most technically free work Velázquez ever produced.

title: Boy Drinking
sceneContext: A boy drinking, painted 1582–83 when Annibale Carracci was in his early twenties in Bologna.
whyBigDeal: Painting an ordinary boy drinking from a glass, at this date and this scale, had almost no precedent. The Carracci academy's insistence on drawing from life produced subjects that had no place in the existing hierarchy of genres.

title: Portrait of a Woman
sceneContext: A woman, painted about 1520 by Quentin Massys in Antwerp.
whyBigDeal: Massys ran the leading workshop in a city that had just overtaken Bruges as northern Europe's financial centre, and he painted bankers and money-changers as readily as saints. The commercial subjects were new and reflected exactly who now had money.

title: Diana and Her Nymphs Departing for the Hunt
sceneContext: Diana and her nymphs setting out to hunt, painted about 1615 in Rubens's Antwerp studio.
whyBigDeal: Rubens ran a workshop that functioned as a factory, priced pictures according to how much he had personally painted, and worked simultaneously as a diplomat for the Spanish Netherlands. He was knighted by two kings for negotiation rather than for painting.

title: Adoration of the Magi
sceneContext: An Adoration of the Magi from Titian's workshop in the sixteenth century.
whyBigDeal: Titian ran the most successful painting business in Europe for sixty years, with Charles V and Philip II as clients, and produced versions of popular compositions to order. Separating his hand from his assistants' in these repetitions is still contested.

title: Virgin and Child with Saints and Donors
artistBio: Giovanni Battista Cima da Conegliano (Italian, c. 1459–1518)
sceneContext: A Virgin and Child with saints and donors, painted about 1515 by Cima da Conegliano.
whyBigDeal: The donors are portrayed at the same scale as the saints, kneeling inside the sacred scene they paid for. Placing a paying customer inside a holy event was standard practice and reveals precisely how the transaction was understood.

title: Virgin and Child with Angels
medium: tempera and gold on wood panel
sceneContext: A Virgin and Child with angels, painted about 1460 by Fra Filippo Lippi.
whyBigDeal: Lippi's Virgins were reportedly modelled on Lucrezia Buti, the nun he took from the convent. Vasari says Botticelli, his pupil, absorbed the type directly, and the faces do descend visibly from teacher to student.

title: The Fall of Simon Magus
sceneContext: The Fall of Simon Magus, painted about 1745–50 by Batoni in Rome.
