whyBigDeal: Batoni made his living painting British aristocrats on the Grand Tour posed beside classical ruins, producing perhaps two hundred such portraits. History paintings like this one were what he considered his real work and what the market wanted least.

title: The Crucifixion with a Carthusian Monk
sceneContext: The Crucifixion with a Carthusian monk, painted in 1460 by Rogier van der Weyden, the most influential Northern painter of his century.
whyBigDeal: Carthusians live in near-total silence in individual cells, and this panel was made for that kind of solitary use. Van der Weyden's compositions were copied across Europe for a hundred years, largely through pictures made for private cells that almost nobody saw.

title: Portrait of Anne Louis Goislard de Montsabert, Comte de Richbourg-le-Toureil
sceneContext: The Comte de Richebourg, painted in 1734 by Largillière, who painted well over a thousand portraits across a very long career.
whyBigDeal: He worked for the Parisian financial and merchant class rather than for Versailles, which is why his sitters are so often people whose names mean nothing now. The output is a portrait of a rising class rather than of a court.

title: Portrait of Cardinal Guillaume Dubois
sceneContext: Cardinal Dubois, painted in 1723 by Rigaud, the leading portraitist of the French court.
whyBigDeal: Dubois rose from very modest origins to be Louis XV's chief minister and a cardinal, and died the year this was painted. Rigaud kept detailed account books recording every sitter and fee, which makes French portraiture of this period unusually well documented.

title: The Martyrdom of Saint Barbara
sceneContext: The martyrdom of Saint Barbara, painted about 1510, before Cranach's involvement with the Reformation.
whyBigDeal: Barbara was beheaded by her own father, who was then struck by lightning — which made her the patron saint of gunners and miners. Cranach was painting Catholic martyrdoms in the decade before he became the Reformation's principal image-maker.

title: The Holy Family on the Steps
sceneContext: The Holy Family on the steps, painted in 1648, from Poussin's austere late manner.
whyBigDeal: He arranged the figures according to geometric proportion, using wax models on a small stage to fix the lighting before painting. Cézanne said he wanted to redo Poussin from nature, and Cubism's debt runs back through that remark.

title: Madonna Adoring the Child
sceneContext: A Madonna adoring the Child, from Botticelli's workshop about 1490–95.
whyBigDeal: The workshop produced devotional Madonnas in quantity for Florentine households, and demand was high enough that the compositions were repeated with variations. These were domestic objects, made for a room rather than an altar.

title: Portrait of Infante Don Luis de Borbon
sceneContext: The Infante Don Luis de Borbón, painted about 1776 by Mengs, court painter in Madrid.
whyBigDeal: Mengs and his friend Winckelmann effectively invented Neoclassicism as a theory before there was much painting to support it. He was the most admired painter in Europe at his death and almost immediately forgotten — a reputation built on ideas rather than pictures.

title: St. Francis Kneeling before Christ on the Cross
sceneContext: Saint Francis kneeling before Christ on the cross, painted 1437–44 by Sassetta for the high altarpiece of San Francesco at Borgo San Sepolcro.
whyBigDeal: The altarpiece was dismembered and sold off in the nineteenth century and its panels are now scattered across several countries. Reconstructing what these objects originally looked like is a large part of what the study of early Italian painting consists of.

title: Virgin and Child in a Landscape
sceneContext: A Virgin and Child in a landscape, painted in 1531 by Gossaert, who had travelled to Rome in 1508 and brought Italian models north.
whyBigDeal: He was among the first Netherlandish painters to make classical nudes a regular subject, which permanently changed what northern patrons expected. The trip to Rome functioned as a technology transfer.

title: Two Children Teasing a Cat
sceneContext: Two children teasing a cat, by Annibale Carracci.
whyBigDeal: There is no story, no moral and no classical source — just two children and an unwilling animal. Painting something with no subject at all was close to unthinkable in Bologna at this date, and it took two centuries for the idea to become ordinary.

title: The Immaculate Conception
sceneContext: The Immaculate Conception, painted by Guido Reni in 1627 for a Spanish patron.
whyBigDeal: The Spanish crown lobbied Rome for decades to have the doctrine made official and commissioned imagery to press the case. Reni's version was copied throughout Spain and the Americas and set the standard form the subject took.

title: The Return of the Holy Family to Nazareth
sceneContext: The Holy Family returning to Nazareth, painted about 1627 in Rome.
whyBigDeal: Poussin caught a serious illness in 1629 and was nursed by the family of a French cook in Rome, whose daughter he married. He had no children, no workshop and few pupils, and painted almost entirely for a private clientele of scholars.

title: Sketch for "The Assumption of the Virgin" (for St. James, Zbraslav, near Prague)?
sceneContext: An oil sketch for an Assumption of the Virgin painted about 1744 for a church at Zbraslav in Bohemia.
whyBigDeal: Venetian painters supplied ceilings and altarpieces across central Europe in this period, working from sketches for buildings they never visited. The finished work was executed at a distance, from a small painting agreed in advance.

title: Study for "Antiochus and Stratonice"
sceneContext: A study for *Antiochus and Stratonice*, painted about 1746. The subject is a prince who falls ill from love for his stepmother, diagnosed by a doctor who notices his pulse.
whyBigDeal: The story was popular because it let painters depict a diagnosis — the doctor reading a body for evidence of a concealed emotion. It is a subject about the visibility of feeling, which is precisely the problem the painter faces.

title: The Triumph of the Church
sceneContext: A study for *The Triumph of the Church*, part of a tapestry series designed by Rubens after 1628 for a convent in Madrid, commissioned by the Infanta Isabella.
whyBigDeal: Rubens designed the whole cycle as an argument for the Eucharist against Protestant doctrine, and it was woven in Brussels for a Spanish convent. He was working as a Catholic propagandist and a diplomat at the same time, and the two roles were not separable.

title: Coronation of the Virgin
medium: tempera and gold on wood panel
sceneContext: The Coronation of the Virgin, painted in the 1420s by Fra Angelico, a Dominican friar who painted under religious vows.
whyBigDeal: He worked at San Marco in Florence painting frescoes in individual monks' cells that no visitor would ever see. Making his best work for an audience of one or two people, as an act of devotion, is a straightforward inversion of how patronage normally functioned.

title: Saint Nicholas of Bari
medium: Tempera and gold leaf on wood panel
sceneContext: Saint Nicholas of Bari, painted in 1472 by Crivelli, who left Venice after a conviction for adultery and spent his career in the provincial Marches.
whyBigDeal: He applied real gems and gilded gesso in relief to the panel surface, so the paintings are partly sculpture. Working far from the centre let him keep an ornate late-Gothic manner going long after Venice had abandoned it.

title: Study for "The Bear Hunt" (for the Alcázar, Madrid)
sceneContext: A study for *The Bear Hunt*, one of a series of hunting scenes designed for Philip IV's hunting lodge outside Madrid around 1639.
whyBigDeal: Rubens sent oil sketches to Spain and had assistants execute the large canvases there, an arrangement that let one studio supply courts across Europe. Much of the Torre de la Parada series was destroyed by fire, so the sketches are what survives.

title: The Football Players
medium: Hanging scroll; ink and light color on silk
sceneContext: Court officials playing cuju, an ancient Chinese kickball game, painted in the Southern Song around 1200 by Ma Yuan, a painter attached to the imperial academy at Hangzhou.
whyBigDeal: Ma Yuan was nicknamed 'one-corner Ma' for pushing his subject into a single corner and leaving the rest empty. That empty space is not unfinished — Song theory treated it as the part of the picture the viewer completes, which is a genuinely different idea of what a painting is.

title: Landscape
sceneContext: A landscape by Wang Hui, who was summoned to Beijing to direct the enormous scrolls recording the Kangxi emperor's southern inspection tours.
whyBigDeal: Wang Hui built pictures by quoting the brushwork of named earlier masters, a practice closer to musical variation than to copying. Chinese painting treated the history of the art as a working vocabulary, so a landscape could be an argument about lineage.

title: Paintings after Ancient Masters: Mr. Five Willows (Wuliu), Tao Yuanming
medium: album leaf, ink and color on silk
sceneContext: Mr Five Willows — the poet Tao Yuanming, who resigned his official post rather than bow to an inspector and retired to farm. Painted by Chen Hongshou in the seventeenth century.
whyBigDeal: Tao's resignation became the standard image of principled withdrawal from government, painted for centuries by men who had made or were contemplating the same choice. Chen himself became a monk after the Ming fell rather than serve the Qing.

title: Listening to the Qin
medium: hanging scroll; ink and light color on silk
sceneContext: Listening to the qin, painted by Tang Yin, who was barred from the imperial examinations for life after being implicated in a cheating scandal in 1499.
whyBigDeal: The ban ended the official career he had trained for, and he supported himself selling paintings — an unusual and slightly disreputable position for an educated man. The scandal made him a professional artist against his intentions.

title: Chinese Beauty
medium: Hanging scroll; ink and color on silk
sceneContext: A Chinese beauty painted in Japan by Kubo Shunman around 1800. Chinese subjects were an established genre for Japanese painters who had never been to China.
whyBigDeal: Japan was closed to almost all foreign contact for over two centuries, so China reached its painters through imported books and older pictures. The result is an image of a country assembled entirely from secondhand material.

title: River Village:  Fisherman's Joy
medium: Fan painting mounted as album leaf; ink and color on silk
sceneContext: A fan painting by Zhao Mengfu, about 1302, later mounted as an album leaf. Zhao was a Song imperial descendant who took office under the Mongol Yuan dynasty.
whyBigDeal: Serving the conquerors of his own family's dynasty made him permanently controversial, and Chinese critics argued about his character for centuries. He also argued that painting should recover the plainer manner of earlier centuries, which set the direction for the next five hundred years.

title: Bamboo and Insects
medium: Album leaf; fan painting, ink on silk
sceneContext: Bamboo and insects on a round silk fan, painted in the Southern Song in the late twelfth century.
whyBigDeal: Song academy painters worked at this scale with extraordinary precision, on objects that were used — fans were carried and waved. The most refined painting of the period was made for things people held in their hands, not hung on walls.

title: Bamboo, Rock, and Tall Tree
sceneContext: Bamboo, rock and a tall tree by Ni Zan, who gave away his considerable property in the 1350s and spent his last twenty years living on a boat.
whyBigDeal: He painted almost nothing but the same spare riverbank, never including a single human figure. Later collectors judged a family's taste by whether it owned a Ni Zan, so the paintings of a man who renounced property became a marker of wealth.

title: Playing the Qin in a Secluded Valley
medium: hanging scroll; ink and light color on paper
sceneContext: Playing the qin in a secluded valley, painted in 1548 by Wen Zhengming, who failed the civil service examination nine times before finally being recommended for a post.
whyBigDeal: He resigned after three years in Beijing and returned to Suzhou to paint for the next thirty. His long life and enormous output made him the central figure of the Wu school, and the failure that preceded it is documented in his own writing.

title: One Hundred Children at Play
medium: Album leaf; ink and color on silk
sceneContext: One hundred children at play, an album leaf from the Song dynasty. The subject was a standing wish for numerous sons.
whyBigDeal: Paintings like this were functional objects given at weddings and births, carrying a specific hope rather than illustrating a scene. The hundred children is a target, not an observation.

title: Catching Fireflies Beneath a Willow Tree (left)
sceneContext: The left sheet of an Utamaro triptych of about 1796–97, showing women and children catching fireflies under a willow.
whyBigDeal: Triptychs were sold as three separate sheets and could be bought singly, so the composition had to work whole and in parts. Publishers were designing for a market that might never assemble the picture as intended.

title: Women Watching a Girl Dance on Shells (From the series Fashionable Presentations of Three Horses)
sceneContext: Women watching a girl dance, printed in 1784 by Torii Kiyonaga, whose tall, calm figures set the standard that Utamaro then reacted against.
whyBigDeal: Kiyonaga's prints established the proportions later printmakers took as normal. Ukiyo-e was a commercial publishing industry with rapid stylistic turnover, and dominance of the kind he had rarely lasted more than a decade.

title: Scholar Reclining and Watching Rising Clouds, Poem by Wang Wei
sceneContext: A scholar reclining and watching clouds, with a poem by the Southern Song emperor Lizong, about 1256. Painted by Ma Lin, son of Ma Yuan.
whyBigDeal: The emperor's calligraphy is part of the object, so painting and imperial handwriting share one surface. In China calligraphy ranked above painting, which makes the inscription the higher-status half of what you are looking at.

title: The Courtesan Karahama of Yamashiroya Performing the Tea Ceremony (from the series Models for Fahions: New Designs as Fresh as Young Leaves)
sceneContext: The courtesan Karahama of the Yamashiroya house, printed by Isoda Koryūsai in the late 1770s.
whyBigDeal: Prints of named courtesans functioned as advertising for the licensed quarter as well as pictures to own. The women were indentured and could not leave; the prints celebrating them were part of the economy that held them there.

title: Landscape after Guo Zhongshu
sceneContext: A landscape after Guo Zhongshu by Bada Shanren, a prince of the fallen Ming who feigned madness and became a monk after the dynasty collapsed in 1644.
whyBigDeal: He reportedly wrote the character for 'dumb' on his door and stopped speaking for years. His paintings of birds and fish with hostile, staring eyes are usually read as coded resistance to the Qing, made by a man whose survival depended on appearing insane.

title: The Minister Toru Daijin Standing by a Lake Beneath a Crescent Moon, from the series A True Mirror of Chinese and Japanese Poetry
sceneContext: The minister Tōru, from Hokusai's series of large prints of about 1834–35.
whyBigDeal: Hokusai changed his professional name more than thirty times, often selling the old name to a pupil. He called himself 'the old man mad about painting' and said nothing he did before seventy was worth counting — he was seventy-four when he made this.

title: Reminiscences of Qinhuai River
medium: Album leaf; ink and color on Song paper
sceneContext: Reminiscences of the Qinhuai River, an album leaf by Shitao, another Ming imperial descendant who survived the conquest as a monk.
whyBigDeal: Shitao wrote that method should arise from the painter rather than the tradition, attacking the copying of old masters that dominated his century. It is one of the few outright manifestos in Chinese painting, and he lost patrons for it.

title: Mother and her Children in Front of a Freestanding Screen of a Chinese Lion
medium: Woodblock print (surimono); ink and color on paper
sceneContext: A surimono of 1786 by Utamaro showing a mother and children before a standing screen.
whyBigDeal: Surimono were privately commissioned prints, produced outside the commercial market for poetry clubs and given as gifts. Because there was no price pressure they used metallic pigments and blind embossing that ordinary prints could not afford.

title: A Vignette of Life on the Frontier
medium: Folding fan; ink and color on paper
sceneContext: A folding fan showing frontier life, painted about 1717–22 by Jiao Bingzhen, an astronomer at the Qing court who worked with Jesuit missionaries.
whyBigDeal: He learned European perspective from the Jesuits and applied it inside Chinese painting, producing a hybrid the court encouraged and Chinese critics largely ignored. Two systems of depth met in one man's work and did not merge.

title: Album of Seasonal Landscapes, Leaf H (previous leaf 8)
medium: album leaf; ink and light color on paper
sceneContext: A leaf from an album of seasonal landscapes by Xiao Yuncong, dated 1668.
whyBigDeal: Album leaves were viewed one at a time, in sequence, by a small group passing the album between them. The format assumes an intimate, slow, social kind of looking that a wall-hung picture cannot produce.

title: Watching the Deer by a Pine Shaded Stream
medium: Album leaf; ink and light color on silk
sceneContext: Watching deer by a pine-shaded stream, an album leaf by Ma Yuan from the Southern Song.
whyBigDeal: The Southern Song court had lost northern China to the Jin and ruled from Hangzhou, and its academy painters produced small, exquisite, melancholy landscapes throughout. The intimacy of the format is inseparable from the political contraction that produced it.

title: Portrait of An Qi
medium: hanging scroll; ink and color on paper
sceneContext: A portrait of the collector An Qi, painted by Wang Hui in 1715 when the painter was in his eighties.
whyBigDeal: An Qi was a salt merchant of Korean descent whose collection catalogue is still used to trace the ownership of Chinese paintings. Portraits of collectors are effectively documentation of the market that preserved the rest of the material.

title: The Mountain of Five Cataracts
sceneContext: The Mountain of Five Cataracts, painted about 1630 by Chen Hongshou.
whyBigDeal: Chen deliberately distorted proportion and archaised his figures, working against the naturalism his contemporaries valued. He also designed playing cards and book illustrations, moving between elite painting and commercial print without apparent difficulty.

title: Listening to the Bamboo
medium: hanging scroll, ink on sutra paper
sceneContext: Listening to bamboo, by Wen Zhengming, painted on satin.
whyBigDeal: Bamboo bends without breaking and stays green in winter, so it stands for the scholar who survives political pressure without compromising. Painting it was a statement about conduct, which is why it was painted so relentlessly.

title: Catching Fireflies Beneath a Willow Tree (right)
sceneContext: The right sheet of Utamaro's firefly-catching triptych, about 1796–97.
whyBigDeal: Utamaro was later shackled and imprisoned for fifty days for a print depicting a sixteenth-century military ruler, which the Tokugawa authorities took as a comment on their own. He died two years afterwards, and the censorship is generally held responsible.

title: The Rush Gatherer, from the series A True Mirror of Chinese and Japanese Poetry
sceneContext: The rush gatherer, from Hokusai's series *A True Mirror of Chinese and Japanese Verse*, 1834–35.
whyBigDeal: The series pairs figures with classical poems, aimed at buyers who would recognise the verse. Ukiyo-e is often described as popular art, but a good deal of it assumed a literate audience able to catch a reference.

title: Bamboo and Ducks by a Rushing Stream
medium: hanging scroll; ink and light color on silk
sceneContext: Bamboo and ducks by a rushing stream, attributed to Ma Yuan, Southern Song.
whyBigDeal: Attribution in Chinese painting is unusually unstable, because copying a master was a respected exercise and copies were often inscribed with his name in good faith. A great deal of what is catalogued as Song is later homage.

title: Album of Miscellaneous Subjects, Leaf 2
medium: album leaf, ink and color on silk
sceneContext: A leaf from Fan Qi's *Album of Miscellaneous Subjects*, painted in Nanjing in the early 1650s.
whyBigDeal: Fan Qi worked in Nanjing in the years immediately after the Ming collapse, when the city had been the southern capital and was reduced to a provincial town. The painters who stayed produced small, private, unofficial work.

title: Sunset Glow over a Fishing Village, from Eight Views of Xiao-Xiang
medium: Hanging scroll from a set of eight; ink and color on silk
sceneContext: Sunset over a fishing village, from Sesshū's set of Eight Views of the Xiao and Xiang Rivers. Sesshū was a Zen monk who travelled to China in 1467.
whyBigDeal: The Eight Views is a Chinese poetic sequence that Japanese painters worked for centuries, mostly without seeing the rivers. Sesshū actually went, which was rare, and returned saying that the Chinese painters of his day had little to teach him.

title: Puppy with Dandelions
sceneContext: A puppy among dandelions, painted by Sōtatsu in the early seventeenth century.
whyBigDeal: Sōtatsu ran a fan-painting shop in Kyoto rather than holding a court appointment, and worked in pooled ink that spreads and dries unevenly by design. Allowing the material to determine the edge of a form was a deliberate surrender of control.

title: Heron on a Willow Branch
medium: Two-panel folding screen; ink, color, lacquer, and gold on silk
sceneContext: A heron on a willow branch, on a two-panel screen by Maruyama Ōkyo, late eighteenth century.
whyBigDeal: Ōkyo sketched birds and plants from life at a time when Japanese painting was overwhelmingly copied from models, and he studied imported Dutch prints for perspective. His school dominated Kyoto painting for a century on the strength of that one decision.

title: Plum Tree
sceneContext: A plum tree by Ogata Kōrin, about 1700. Kōrin came from a wealthy Kyoto textile family and was bankrupt by middle age.
whyBigDeal: He trained in his family's kimono business, and the flattened, boldly cropped designs in his paintings come directly from textile pattern. The Rinpa manner named after him is essentially fabric design applied to screens.

title: Beauty with Fireflies
medium: Hanging scroll; ink and color on silk (ivory roller ends)
sceneContext: A beauty with fireflies, painted by Kubo Shunman in the early nineteenth century.
whyBigDeal: Shunman was a poet as well as a printmaker and worked largely in restrained greys when the market wanted strong colour. Painters who supplied the poetry circles could afford that restraint because they were not selling to the street.

title: Winter and Summer Flowers
medium: One of a pair of six-panel folding screens; ink, color, and gold on paper
sceneContext: Winter and summer flowers, one of a pair of six-panel screens by Kaihō Yūshō, about 1600. Yūshō was born a samurai and became a painter in middle age.
whyBigDeal: His family was destroyed in the wars of the sixteenth century and he entered a monastery before taking up painting seriously. Screens like this were made for the warlords who had done the destroying.

title: Flowers and Trees of the Four Seasons (right screen)
medium: Six-panel folding screen; ink, color, gold, silver, and gilding on paper
sceneContext: Flowers and trees of the four seasons, the right screen of a pair by Watanabe Shikō, early eighteenth century.
whyBigDeal: Screens were room dividers, moved and reconfigured, so the painting had to work as architecture. A Japanese interior was assembled from these surfaces rather than built with permanent walls.

title: Oath of the Peach Garden, from Romance of the Three Kingdoms
medium: hanging scroll; ink and color on silk
sceneContext: The Oath of the Peach Garden from the Chinese *Romance of the Three Kingdoms*, painted about 1780 by Matsumura Goshun.
whyBigDeal: Goshun trained under the poet-painter Buson and then joined Ōkyo, merging literati looseness with observation from life. The Shijō school that resulted was the practical compromise between the two dominant Kyoto positions.

title: Horse Stable
medium: One of a pair of six-panel folding screens; ink, color, and gold on paper
sceneContext: A horse stable, one of a pair of six-panel screens from the early sixteenth century by an unrecorded painter.
whyBigDeal: Stable screens were made for warrior households, where horses were both military equipment and status. Naming the artist mattered less than the subject — much of the finest Japanese screen painting is anonymous.

title: The Courtesan Senzan of Chojiya Strolling with her Kamuro Yasono and Yasoji and Two Shinzo
sceneContext: The courtesan Senzan of the Chōjiya house walking with her attendants, printed by Kiyonaga in 1786.
whyBigDeal: The kamuro accompanying her were children apprenticed to the house who would in most cases become courtesans themselves. The prints record the system's full hierarchy without comment, which is part of what makes them difficult.

title: Goose and Reeds; Willows in the Moonlight
medium: Pair of six-panel folding screens; ink, color and gold on paper
sceneContext: A pair of six-panel screens by Maruyama Ōkyo, the right painted in 1774 and the left nearly twenty years later in 1793, showing geese among reeds and willows under a moon.
whyBigDeal: The two halves were made almost two decades apart and are meant to hang as one work, so Ōkyo had to match a composition he had painted as a younger man. Screens were often completed piecemeal as a patron's money allowed.

title: Painting the Eyes on a Snow Rabbit
medium: Hanging scroll; ink and color on silk
sceneContext: Painting the eyes on a snow rabbit, by Isoda Koryūsai, about 1780.
whyBigDeal: Koryūsai was a samurai who gave up his rank to work as a commercial printmaker — a substantial loss of status. He was among the most prolific designers of his generation and then abruptly stopped, having been granted an honorary Buddhist title.

title: Gibbons in a Landscape
medium: Pair of six-panel screens; ink on paper
sceneContext: Gibbons in a landscape, from a pair of screens by Sesson Shūkei, about 1570. Sesson worked in the provinces and never went to the capital.
whyBigDeal: There are no gibbons in Japan. Painters worked from Chinese pictures, so generations of Japanese artists painted an animal none of them had seen — the errors are inherited faithfully from the models.

title: Peafowl and Phoenixes
medium: Pair of six-panel screens; ink, color, and gold on gilded paper
sceneContext: Peafowl and phoenixes, a pair of six-panel screens by Tosa Mitsuyoshi, late sixteenth century.
whyBigDeal: The Tosa school held the hereditary post of court painter and specialised in Japanese subjects while the rival Kano school took Chinese ones. The division of labour was formalised and lasted for centuries.

title: Farmer Returning Home in Autumn
medium: Hanging scroll; ink and light color on silk
sceneContext: A farmer returning home in autumn, painted in 1781 by Yosa Buson, who is better known as one of the great haiku poets.
whyBigDeal: Buson made his living from painting and his reputation from poetry, and treated the two as one practice. The literati ideal held that a cultivated man wrote, painted and composed without specialising in any of them.

title: A Beauty
medium: hanging scroll; ink and color on silk
sceneContext: A beauty, painted about 1810 by Fujimaro, a pupil of Utamaro.
whyBigDeal: Successful print designers took pupils who used a syllable of the master's name, so a workshop identity was carried in the signatures. It functioned as a brand, and disentangling individual hands from it is often impossible.

title: The Actor Ichikawa Raizo as Soga No Goro
sceneContext: The actor Ichikawa Raizō as Soga no Gorō, printed by Katsukawa Shunshō in the mid-1770s.
whyBigDeal: Shunshō was the first to give kabuki actors recognisable individual faces instead of a generic mask with a crest for identification. Fans wanted a specific performer, and the market rewarded likeness.

title: First Bonito of the Year
sceneContext: The first bonito of the year, printed by Kunisada in the 1840s. The season's first catch commanded extravagant prices in Edo.
whyBigDeal: Kunisada was the best-selling print designer of the nineteenth century by a wide margin and is still the least regarded, dismissed as commercial. Volume and reputation have run in opposite directions in ukiyo-e criticism ever since.

title: Amusements at Higashiyama in Kyoto
medium: Pair of six-panel folding screens; ink, color, gold, mica, and gold leaf on paper
sceneContext: Amusements at Higashiyama in Kyoto, a pair of six-panel screens from the Kano Sadanobu studio, early 1620s.
whyBigDeal: Screens of the city recorded specific streets, shops and festivals, and are used now as evidence for what Kyoto physically looked like. They were made as luxury goods and survive as documentary sources.

title: Chōdayu of the Okamotoya from the series ?
sceneContext: A courtesan of the Okamotoya house, printed by Keisai Eisen in the early nineteenth century.
whyBigDeal: Eisen wrote that the taste of his time had coarsened, and his own figures are heavier and more worldly than Utamaro's. Late ukiyo-e is often described as decadent, which is largely a description of a market widening beyond its original buyers.

title: Courtesan and Attendants
medium: hanging scroll; ink and color on paper
sceneContext: A courtesan with attendants, painted about 1748–51 by Engetsudō.
whyBigDeal: Painted ukiyo scenes cost many times what a print did and were bought by people who could have afforded better-regarded art. The subject, not the medium, was what marked this material as low.

title: Drunken Asaina
medium: Fan mounted as hanging scroll; ink and color on paper
sceneContext: Drunken Asaina, a fan painting by Hokusai mounted as a hanging scroll, about 1810.
whyBigDeal: Hokusai worked on any surface a customer would pay for — fans, lanterns, banners, grains of rice, and once a portrait of Daruma said to be over a hundred metres long. He was a working commercial artist for seventy years.

title: Palindromic Poems (Kaibunka): Kyo
medium: Right-hand sheet of a triptych of woodblock prints; ink and color on paper
sceneContext: From Harunobu's *Palindromic Poems*, about 1768.
whyBigDeal: Harunobu was central to the invention of the full-colour print around 1765, which required separate blocks in exact registration for each colour. It was a technical advance driven by a fashion for privately commissioned calendars.

title: Operating on Guan Yu's Arm
medium: hanging scroll; ink, color, and gold on silk
sceneContext: The surgeon Hua Tuo operating on the general Guan Yu's arm, painted in the 1840s by Katsushika Ōi, Hokusai's daughter.
whyBigDeal: She lived and worked with her father for most of his life and probably painted parts of pictures signed with his name. Only about ten works are securely hers, and she is thought to have handled light and shadow more boldly than he did.

title: The Four Accomplishments
medium: One of a pair of six-panel folding screens; ink and slight color on paper
sceneContext: The Four Accomplishments — music, chess, calligraphy and painting — on a screen by Kano Shōei, late sixteenth century.
whyBigDeal: The Kano school ran as a hereditary dynasty for over three hundred years, adopting talented pupils into the family to keep the succession going. It is the longest continuous workshop in the history of art anywhere.

title: Paulownias and Chrysanthemums
medium: Two-panel folding screen; ink and color on gilded paper
sceneContext: Paulownias and chrysanthemums on a two-panel screen by Sakai Hōitsu, early nineteenth century.
whyBigDeal: Hōitsu was born into a daimyo family, became a monk, and set out to revive Kōrin's manner a century after Kōrin's death, publishing woodblock books of his designs. Rinpa is a tradition assembled retrospectively by an admirer rather than passed hand to hand.

title: The Hour of the Snake (from the series A Clock for Young Women)
sceneContext: The Hour of the Snake, from Utamaro's series pairing times of day with women of different social classes, about 1796.
whyBigDeal: Utamaro's close-up half-length format was a publishing innovation that let a print carry a face at legible size. It is the change that made ukiyo-e portraits of women recognisable as individuals.

title: The Strange Occurrence of Ukiyo Matahei and his Famous Paintings
sceneContext: Ukiyo Matahei and his famous paintings, a diptych printed by Kuniyoshi in 1853.
whyBigDeal: Kuniyoshi filled his prints with monsters, tattooed heroes and coded political satire, and was repeatedly investigated by the censors. He is the direct ancestor of a good deal of modern Japanese graphic style.

title: Bamboo and Rocks in Clearing Skies
medium: Two-panel folding screen; ink on paper
sceneContext: Bamboo and rocks in clearing skies, on a two-panel screen by Ike Taiga, mid-eighteenth century.
whyBigDeal: Taiga and his wife Gyokuran were both painters and lived in famous disorder, reportedly selling their possessions to buy materials. He was a leading figure of the Japanese literati movement, which imported the Chinese scholar-painter ideal into a society that had no scholar-officials.

title: The Moon-Viewing Promontory, from One Hundred Views of Famous Places in Edo
sceneContext: The Moon-Viewing Promontory, from Hiroshige's *One Hundred Famous Views of Edo*, 1857.
whyBigDeal: The series was published in the last years before Japan opened to the West, and copies reached Paris within a decade. Van Gogh copied two of them in oil, and the flat colour and abrupt cropping fed directly into European painting.

title: Birds and Flowers
medium: Pair of six-panel folding screens; ink, color, and gold on paper
sceneContext: Birds and flowers, a pair of six-panel screens by Kano Mitsunobu, late sixteenth century.
whyBigDeal: Gold-leaf grounds were used partly because castle interiors were dark, and the leaf threw candlelight back into the room. The most opulent-looking convention in Japanese painting began as a lighting solution.

title: Thirty-Six Poetic Immortals
medium: two-fold screen; ink, color, and gold on paper
sceneContext: The Thirty-Six Poetic Immortals on a two-fold screen by Tatebayashi Kagei, mid-eighteenth century.
whyBigDeal: The canon of thirty-six poets was fixed in the eleventh century and painted for the next eight hundred years, with the same figures in the same order. It is a literary canon maintained as a picture.

title: Ichikawa Ebizō IV (Danjurō) as Takemura Sadanoshin in The Loving Wife's Parti-Colored Reins
sceneContext: The actor Ichikawa Ebizō IV, printed by Sharaku in 1794.
whyBigDeal: Sharaku produced around 140 prints in ten months and then vanished; nothing certain is known about who he was. The portraits are unflatteringly specific about ageing actors' faces, which is the usual explanation for why they sold badly and why he stopped.

title: Portrait of Ōzora Buzaemon
medium: hanging scroll; ink and color on paper
sceneContext: A portrait of Ōzora Buzaemon, painted in 1827 by Watanabe Kazan. The sitter was an unusually tall man exhibited as a curiosity in Edo.
whyBigDeal: Kazan used Western shading learned from Dutch books and later wrote criticising Japan's isolation policy. He was arrested for it, sentenced to house arrest, and killed himself in 1841 to spare his lord further trouble.

title: Calligraphy and Painting Party
medium: hanging scroll; ink and color on paper
sceneContext: A calligraphy and painting party, painted by Kawanabe Kyōsai in 1880. These were public events at which artists performed in front of a paying audience, usually drinking heavily.
whyBigDeal: Kyōsai was arrested in 1870 for a caricature made at one of these gatherings and flogged. He worked through the collapse of the shogunate and the arrival of Western art, satirising both.

title: Monkeys by a Stream
medium: hanging scroll; ink and color on paper
sceneContext: Monkeys by a stream, painted about 1796 by Nagasawa Rosetsu, Ōkyo's most unruly pupil.
whyBigDeal: Rosetsu was expelled from Ōkyo's studio more than once and died at forty in circumstances that contemporaries suspected were poisoning. He painted enormous, loose compositions that his teacher's school of careful observation could not contain.

title: Returning Sails off a Distant Shore, from Eight Views of Xiao-Xiang
medium: Hanging scroll from a set of eight; ink and color on silk
sceneContext: Returning sails off a distant shore, from Sesshū's Eight Views set.
whyBigDeal: Sesshū's reputation was so complete that later painters competed to claim descent from him, and forgeries and false lineages proliferated. Establishing which paintings are actually his remains an open problem.

title: Kenshu, Monk with Shrimp
sceneContext: Kenshu, a monk with a shrimp, painted by Sōtatsu in the early seventeenth century. The monk was said to have eaten shrimp in defiance of monastic rules.
whyBigDeal: Zen painting favoured subjects that undercut piety, on the grounds that attachment to rules is itself an obstacle. The picture is a joke with a doctrinal point, which is a combination Zen art relies on constantly.

title: Winter Day
medium: Six-panel folding screen, ink, gold, and silver on paper
sceneContext: Winter Day, a six-panel screen painted by Maruyama Ōkyo in 1784.
whyBigDeal: Ōkyo used tone rather than outline to describe snow and mist, which was close to heresy in a tradition built on brushed line. His pupils took the observational method and largely dropped the argument that came with it.

title: Landscape with Fishermen
medium: hanging scroll; ink and slight color on silk
sceneContext: A landscape with fishermen by Yi Bul-hae, painted in Korea in the seventeenth century.
whyBigDeal: Joseon painting is far less known outside Korea than Chinese or Japanese work of the same centuries, largely because so much was destroyed in the Japanese invasions of the 1590s and again in the twentieth century. Survival, not quality, explains the difference in visibility.

title: Winter Landscape
medium: hanging scroll; ink and slight color on silk
sceneContext: A winter landscape by Yeoseol, painted in Korea in the sixteenth century.
whyBigDeal: Korean painters absorbed Chinese models and then diverged from them, keeping compositions long after China had abandoned them. Joseon painting is often the best surviving evidence of what earlier Chinese painting looked like.

title: Snowscape with Figures
sceneContext: A snowscape with figures, painted in 1584 by Kim Si.
whyBigDeal: Kim Si was a member of the yangban scholar-official class who painted as an accomplishment rather than a trade. In Korea as in China, professional painters ranked below amateurs, and the amateurs were the ones whose names were kept.

title: Nine-Dragon Falls
sceneContext: Nine-Dragon Falls, painted in the late nineteenth century by Han Unpyeong.
whyBigDeal: Korean painters of this period turned to the actual mountains of Korea instead of idealised Chinese scenery, a movement begun by Jeong Seon in the eighteenth century. Painting your own landscape rather than an imported one was a nationalist argument as much as an aesthetic one.

title: Landscape of the Four Seasons
medium: Pair of six-panel screens; ink and slight color on paper
sceneContext: Landscape of the four seasons, a pair of six-panel screens by Yi Sumun, late fifteenth century. Yi is thought to have travelled to Japan and worked there.
whyBigDeal: Korean painters carried Chinese models into Japan and shaped Japanese ink painting at a formative moment. The transmission ran through Korea rather than directly, which Japanese accounts have not always acknowledged.

title: Portrait of a Government Official
medium: Hanging scroll; ink and color on silk
sceneContext: A portrait of a government official, painted in 1921 by Chae Yongshin during the Japanese occupation of Korea.
whyBigDeal: Chae kept the exacting Joseon portrait tradition going into the twentieth century, after the dynasty had been abolished and the country annexed. He was painting officials of a state that no longer existed.

title: Books and Scholars’ Accoutrements
medium: ten-panel folding screen; ink and color on silk
sceneContext: *Chaekgeori* — books and scholars' accoutrements — on a ten-panel folding screen from the late nineteenth century by Yi Taek-gyun.
whyBigDeal: The genre shows shelves of books and imported objects in a Korean adaptation of Western perspective, and spread from the palace to ordinary households. It is a still life of aspiration: a display of the learning the owner wished to be credited with.

title: Orchids and Rocks
medium: Eight-panel folding screen; ink on silk
sceneContext: Orchids and rocks on an eight-panel screen painted 1897–98 by Yi Ha-eung, the Daewongun — regent of Korea and father of the last king but one.
whyBigDeal: He ruled Korea for a decade, pursued a policy of near-total isolation, and painted orchids throughout. His ink orchids were sought after in his lifetime, which is a hard thing to separate from the fact that he held power.

title: Egret and Reeds
sceneContext: An egret among reeds, painted in the late nineteenth century by Yang Ki-hun.
whyBigDeal: Yang worked in the last decades of the Joseon dynasty and taught the generation that had to decide what Korean painting would be under Japanese rule. The question of whether to keep the ink tradition or adopt Western oil was settled largely by force.

title: Mountain Market, Clear with Rising Mist
sceneContext: Mountain market, clear with rising mist — another of the Eight Views of the Xiao and Xiang, painted in the early sixteenth century by an unrecorded Japanese artist.
whyBigDeal: The eight titles are fixed and each specifies a weather condition, so painters were working to a written brief about atmosphere. It is a set of standing commissions issued by a poem, and answered for eight hundred years.

title: The Doge's Palace, Venice
sceneContext: The Doge's Palace painted in 1826 by Bonington, an Englishman who trained in France and died of tuberculosis at twenty-five.
whyBigDeal: He worked in watercolour and oil interchangeably and carried watercolour's transparency into oil, which Delacroix — who shared a studio with him — took up directly. An enormous amount of French Romantic handling traces back to a painter who was dead before he turned twenty-six.

title: Gray Day on the Bay
sceneContext: A grey day on Shinnecock Bay, painted about 1886 by William Merritt Chase on eastern Long Island.
whyBigDeal: Chase ran a summer school at Shinnecock where students painted outdoors in the dunes, training a generation of American painters in French methods without their leaving the country. Teaching, not his own canvases, was his largest effect.

title: Point Judith, Rhode Island
sceneContext: Point Judith, Rhode Island, painted 1867–68 by Martin Johnson Heade.
whyBigDeal: Heade painted salt marshes obsessively — more than a hundred of them — at a moment when American landscape painting wanted mountains and waterfalls. Choosing flat, unspectacular coastal ground was a deliberate refusal of the national taste for grandeur.

title: "Isfandiyar's Third Course: He Slays a Dragon", Folio 434v from the Shahnama (Book of Kings) of Shah Tahmasp
medium: Opaque watercolor, ink, silver, and gold on paper
sceneContext: Isfandiyar killing a dragon, from a Shahnama made about 1530 in Safavid Iran. The hero's third labour is fought from inside a spiked chest mounted on a chariot.
whyBigDeal: The Shahnama runs to some fifty thousand couplets and took Firdausi thirty years. Illustrated copies were among the most expensive objects a Persian court could commission, with dozens of painters, calligraphers and gilders working for years on a single manuscript.

title: Haverstraw Bay
sceneContext: Haverstraw Bay on the Hudson, painted in 1868 by Sanford Robinson Gifford.
whyBigDeal: Gifford built his pictures around a single suffusing light rather than around topography, sometimes glazing the whole surface to unify it. The group later labelled Luminist were not a movement and never called themselves one — the name was applied a century afterwards.

title: Portrait of Franklin H. Delano
sceneContext: Franklin H. Delano, painted about 1881 by Eastman Johnson. The sitter was a great-uncle by marriage of Franklin Delano Roosevelt.
whyBigDeal: Johnson had studied at Düsseldorf and in Rembrandt's Netherlands before returning to paint American subjects. He co-founded the Metropolitan Museum, which is a reminder that the institutions holding this art were built by the painters themselves.

title: Portrait of Nushirwan the Just (verso) from a Shahnama (Book of Kings) of Firdausi (940–1019 or 1025)
medium: opaque watercolor, ink, and gold on paper
sceneContext: Nushirwan the Just, the Sasanian king held up as the model ruler in Persian literature, from a Shahnama of 1330–35.
whyBigDeal: This manuscript was made under the Ilkhanids, the Mongol dynasty ruling Iran, who commissioned Persian national epics to legitimise themselves as heirs to the Persian kings. Conquerors were buying the visual language of the conquered.

title: The Troubadour
sceneContext: A troubadour, painted 1868–73 by Daumier late in life, when failing eyesight was ending his career.
whyBigDeal: Daumier made some four thousand lithographs for the Paris press and was jailed for six months for caricaturing the king. His paintings were almost unknown in his lifetime; he was a journalist whose private work turned out to matter more.

title: Greek Cavalry Men Resting in Forest
sceneContext: Greek cavalrymen resting, painted in 1858. Delacroix had made the Greek war of independence a subject thirty years earlier.
whyBigDeal: His *Massacre at Chios* of 1824 turned a contemporary atrocity into a large public painting, which was new. Political events had previously entered art as allegory; Delacroix's generation began painting them as news.

title: "The Concourse of the Birds", Folio 11r from a Mantiq al-Tayr (Language of the Birds)
medium: Ink, opaque watercolor, gold, and silver on paper
sceneContext: The Concourse of the Birds, from Attar's *Mantiq al-Tayr*, painted about 1600 by Habiballah of Sava.
whyBigDeal: The poem describes thirty birds searching for a king and discovering they are themselves the answer — the Persian for 'thirty birds' is also the name of the bird they seek. It is a pun carrying the whole theological argument, which is why the poem could not be translated without losing it.

title: Sleeping Youth (verso), Illustration from a Single Page Manuscript
medium: opaque watercolor and gold on paper
sceneContext: A sleeping youth by Riza-yi Abbasi, the leading painter at the Safavid court of Shah Abbas in the early seventeenth century.
whyBigDeal: Riza abandoned the court for several years to live among wrestlers and low company, and his contemporaries wrote about it disapprovingly. He also shifted Persian painting from manuscript illustration toward single-figure drawings sold separately — a change of format that was also a change of market.

title: Mount Starr King, Yosemite
medium: oil on canvas on panel-back stretcher
sceneContext: Mount Starr King in Yosemite, painted in 1866 by Bierstadt, who had travelled west with a survey expedition.
whyBigDeal: His enormous western canvases were exhibited singly as ticketed attractions and helped build public support for the national parks. Yosemite was protected in 1864, and paintings like this were part of the argument that produced it.

title: Harbor of Boston, with the City in the Distance
sceneContext: Boston harbour, painted about 1846–47 by Fitz Henry Lane, who had been unable to walk since infancy and worked from a boat.
whyBigDeal: Lane was a commercial lithographer before he painted, and the precision comes from that training. He was entirely forgotten until the 1930s and is now central to accounts of American painting — a reputation created a century after his death.

title: Deserted Wharf (The Old Mill at Cos Cob)
sceneContext: The old mill at Cos Cob, Connecticut, painted before 1899 by Twachtman.
whyBigDeal: Twachtman sold almost nothing and taught to survive, and his pictures grew paler and more abstract as his career went on. He died at forty-nine having been called by his friends the most original painter among them and by the market almost nothing at all.

title: Fir Trees and Storm Clouds
medium: oil on paper mounted on canvas
sceneContext: Fir trees and storm clouds, painted about 1870 by Bierstadt.
whyBigDeal: Bierstadt's reputation collapsed in his own lifetime as taste turned against theatrical scale, and he died largely forgotten in 1902. The pictures that had drawn paying crowds became embarrassing within thirty years.

title: Marguerite-Juliette Pierret
sceneContext: Marguerite-Juliette Pierret, painted about 1827. She was the wife of Delacroix's closest friend, Jean-Baptiste Pierret.
whyBigDeal: Delacroix kept a journal for most of his adult life which is one of the most useful documents any painter has left — on colour, on method, on his contemporaries. Much of what we know about French painting of the period comes from a private diary he never meant to publish.

title: Approaching Storm from the Alban Hills
sceneContext: An approaching storm in the Alban Hills outside Rome, painted in 1871 during Inness's second long stay in Italy.
whyBigDeal: Inness followed the theology of Swedenborg and believed a landscape should convey a spiritual state rather than a place. He repainted canvases for years and destroyed work he judged to have failed at it.

title: Cottages Near Larchant
sceneContext: Cottages near Larchant, by Théodore Rousseau, leader of the painters who settled at Barbizon on the edge of the Fontainebleau forest.
whyBigDeal: Rousseau was rejected by the Salon so consistently through the 1830s and 40s that he was nicknamed *le grand refusé*. The Barbizon painters campaigned to have part of the forest protected from logging, and succeeded in 1861 — arguably the first nature reserve created at the request of artists.

title: Bahram Gur Slays a Dragon (verso), from a Shahnama (Book of Kings) of Firdausi (940–1019 or 1025), known as the Great Mongol Shahnama
medium: opaque watercolor, ink, and gold on paper
sceneContext: Bahram Gur killing a dragon, from the Ilkhanid Shahnama of 1330–35.
whyBigDeal: The manuscript this comes from was cut up and sold leaf by leaf in the twentieth century by a dealer who found the pages were worth more separately. A great many Persian manuscripts survive only as scattered folios for that reason.

title: Mount Vesuvius at Midnight
sceneContext: Vesuvius erupting at midnight, painted in 1868 by Bierstadt.
whyBigDeal: Vesuvius was in near-continuous eruption through the nineteenth century and was a fixed stop on the Grand Tour, painted by dozens of artists. Volcanic spectacle was to that century roughly what space photography is to ours.

title: Storm Clouds
sceneContext: Storm clouds, painted in 1880 by Twachtman before his years in France.
whyBigDeal: He trained in Munich, where the method was dark tonal painting laid on quickly, then went to Paris and abandoned all of it for a pale, high-keyed manner. Few painters visibly changed their entire technique twice.

title: La Cervara, the Roman Campagna
sceneContext: La Cervara in the Roman Campagna, painted about 1830–31 during Corot's first Italian stay.
whyBigDeal: Corot made small oil studies outdoors in Italy and larger composed pictures in the studio afterwards, and the studies are now generally held to be the better work. That reversal of value between preparation and product runs through the whole century.

title: Ruins of an Ancient City
medium: oil on paper, mounted on canvas
sceneContext: Ruins of an ancient city, painted about 1810–20 by John Martin.
whyBigDeal: Martin's apocalyptic panoramas were engraved and sold in enormous numbers, reaching an audience no gallery could. His brother Jonathan set fire to York Minster in 1829 believing he was acting on divine instruction, which shadowed the painter's reputation for the rest of his life.

title: Bahram Gur Visits the Princess of India in the Black Pavilion (recto): Illustration and Text, Persian Verses, from a manuscript of the Khamsa of Nizami, Haft Paykar [Seven Portraits]
artistBio: Iran, possibly Tabriz or Shiraz, Timurid Period, early 15th century
medium: opaque watercolor and ink on paper
sceneContext: Bahram Gur in the Black Pavilion, from Nizami's *Haft Paykar*, painted about 1400–1410. The king visits a pavilion of a different colour on each day of the week.
whyBigDeal: Each pavilion has its own colour, planet, princess and story, so the poem is built as a system rather than a plot. Persian painters illustrating it had to keep a colour scheme running across seven separate pictures.

title: Whalers
sceneContext: Whalers, painted about 1845 by Turner, exhibited when he was seventy.
whyBigDeal: Turner's late work was widely thought to show failing powers, and one critic said he painted with tinted steam. Ruskin defended him in five volumes of *Modern Painters*, and the reputation that resulted was largely Ruskin's construction.

title: Venice, from the Porch of Madonna della Salute
sceneContext: Venice from the porch of the Madonna della Salute, painted about 1835.
whyBigDeal: Turner left nearly three hundred paintings and nineteen thousand works on paper to the nation, on condition they be kept together. The bequest was litigated by his relatives, partially honoured, and is the reason so much of his output is in one place.

title: "The Seven Sleepers of Ephesus", Folio from a Falnama (Book of Omens)
medium: Ink, opaque watercolor, and gold on paper
sceneContext: The Seven Sleepers of Ephesus, from a *Falnama* or Book of Omens, made in Safavid Iran in the 1550s.
whyBigDeal: Falnamas were oversized manuscripts used for divination: you opened one at random and read your fortune from the picture. The paintings are unusually large and strange because they were made to be consulted rather than read in sequence.

title: Mlle. Alexandrine-Julie de la Boutraye
sceneContext: Mlle Alexandrine-Julie de la Boutraye, painted about 1832–34, shortly after Delacroix returned from six months in Morocco.
whyBigDeal: The Moroccan journey supplied him with subjects for the rest of his life, and he filled seven notebooks there. He argued afterwards that the classical world he had been trained to imagine was still alive in North Africa, which was both an artistic and a political claim.

title: George Washington at Princeton
artistBio: Charles Willson Peale (American, born The Thirteen Colonies, 1741–1827)
sceneContext: Washington at Princeton, painted about 1779 by Charles Willson Peale, who had fought at Trenton and Princeton himself.
whyBigDeal: Peale painted Washington from life seven times and produced dozens of replicas to meet demand. He also founded one of the first American museums, named his sons Raphaelle, Rembrandt and Titian, and put a mastodon skeleton on display beside the portraits.

title: The Third-Class Carriage
sceneContext: The Third-Class Carriage, painted in 1864. Daumier made several versions of passengers in the cheapest railway compartments.
whyBigDeal: Rail travel had created a new social situation — strangers of the same class pressed together in silence for hours — and Daumier was among the first to treat it as a subject. The picture is about a form of modern experience that had not existed a generation earlier.

title: Monsieur Martin
sceneContext: Monsieur Martin, painted in 1840 when Millet was twenty-six and supporting himself with portraits in Cherbourg.
whyBigDeal: He turned to peasant subjects only after moving to Barbizon in 1849, and they were attacked as socialist agitation. *The Gleaners* was read by conservative critics as a threat, because it showed the rural poor exercising a customary right the landowners were then trying to abolish.

title: Royal Reception in a Landscape, right folio from a double-page frontispiece of a Shahnama (Book of Kings) of Firdausi (940–1019 or 1025)
medium: opaque watercolor, gold, and silver on paper
sceneContext: A royal reception in a landscape, the right half of a double-page frontispiece from a manuscript dated 1444.
whyBigDeal: Frontispieces opened a manuscript across two facing pages, so the composition had to work as a single image split by the binding. Persian painters designed for the gutter as a deliberate structural element.

title: The Wood Chopper
sceneContext: The wood chopper, painted in 1849, from Inness's early Hudson River manner before Barbizon changed his handling.
whyBigDeal: Inness had epilepsy and almost no formal training, and he later dismissed his own early detailed work as mere transcription. The pictures collectors most wanted from him were the ones he thought least of.

title: The Old Road to the Sea
sceneContext: The old road to the sea, painted about 1893 at Shinnecock.
whyBigDeal: Chase lived expensively, kept a famously theatrical studio full of props, and was chronically in debt. The relaxed prosperity his paintings project was a professional performance sustained on borrowed money.

title: Orchid Blossoms
sceneContext: Orchid blossoms, painted in 1873. Heade travelled to Brazil to paint hummingbirds and orchids and planned a book of chromolithographs.
whyBigDeal: The book was never published because the printing could not reproduce the colours he wanted. He kept painting the subject for another thirty years, so a failed publishing project produced one of the odder bodies of work in American art.

title: Yusuf and Zulaykha (recto), from an Anthology of Persian Verses, including the Haft Awrang (Seven Thrones) of Jami: The Fifth Throne
artistBio: Iran, Shiraz or Mashhad, Safavid period (1501–1722)
medium: Gum tempera, ink, and gold on paper
sceneContext: Yusuf and Zulaykha, from an anthology of Persian verse copied about 1556–65. The story appears in both the Bible and the Quran.
whyBigDeal: Persian poets read it as an allegory of the soul's desire for God, so a story of attempted seduction is illustrated as devotional literature. The doubled reading is the point rather than a cover for it.

title: An Episode from the Story of the Sasanian King Khusrau and His Beloved Shirin, from a Khamsa (Quintet) of Nizami (1141–1209) (verso)
medium: opaque watercolor, ink, gold, and silver on paper
sceneContext: An episode from the story of Khusrau and Shirin, painted 1540–70. Their romance is one of the central narratives of Persian poetry.
whyBigDeal: Nizami's version turns on the sculptor Farhad, who is set an impossible task to win Shirin and is then falsely told she is dead. The tale of the artisan destroyed by a court is one Persian painters, employed by courts, returned to repeatedly.

title: Harvest Time
sceneContext: Harvest time, painted in 1864 during the American Civil War.
whyBigDeal: Inness was a pacifist and an abolitionist who painted almost nothing of the war directly. Quiet agricultural landscapes made in those years were not a retreat from the subject so much as a deliberate alternative to it.

title: Count Demetrius de Palatiano in Suliot Costume
sceneContext: Count Demetrius de Palatiano in Suliot costume, painted by Delacroix.
whyBigDeal: Delacroix borrowed the costume and used it repeatedly in the studio, so the same clothes appear on several different sitters. A good deal of nineteenth-century exoticism is a small wardrobe reused.

title: Woman  Applying Henna
medium: Ink, opaque watercolor, and gold on paper
sceneContext: A woman applying henna, painted in Safavid Iran in the late sixteenth century.
whyBigDeal: Single-figure paintings of this kind were sold to individual buyers rather than bound into manuscripts, and they show ordinary activity rather than epic narrative. The shift in format opened a subject range the manuscript tradition had no room for.

title: Moses Seymour Jr.
sceneContext: Moses Seymour Jr., painted in 1789 by Ralph Earl, who painted many of his Connecticut portraits while imprisoned for debt.
whyBigDeal: Earl had fled to England as a Loyalist during the Revolution and returned afterwards to paint the leading families of a country he had opposed. He died of alcoholism at forty-nine.

title: Lormes:  Goat-Girl Sitting Beside a Stream in a Forest
sceneContext: A goat-girl beside a stream at Lormes, painted in 1842 in the Morvan.
whyBigDeal: Corot travelled and painted almost every summer for fifty years and gave away money and pictures freely, supporting Daumier when he went blind and Millet's widow. His generosity is as well documented as his output.

title: Albert Wolff in His Study
sceneContext: The critic Albert Wolff in his study, painted in 1881 by Bastien-Lepage.
whyBigDeal: Wolff was the most feared reviewer in Paris and had savaged the Impressionists in print. Bastien-Lepage, who had absorbed their light while keeping academic drawing, was painting the man whose approval that compromise was designed to keep.

title: The Oak Tree
medium: oil on paper mounted on wood panel
sceneContext: The oak tree, by Théodore Rousseau.
whyBigDeal: Rousseau painted individual trees as portraits, returning to the same specimens in the Fontainebleau forest over years. Treating a tree as a sitter rather than as scenery was a genuine reordering of what landscape was for.

title: The Race Track (Death on a Pale Horse)
sceneContext: The Race Track, or Death on a Pale Horse, painted between about 1896 and 1908 by Albert Pinkham Ryder.
whyBigDeal: Ryder is said to have begun it after a waiter he knew killed himself having lost his savings on a horse. He worked pictures for decades, piling on varnish and unstable mediums, so most of his surviving canvases have darkened and cracked badly.

title: A Winter Sky
sceneContext: A winter sky, painted in 1866.
whyBigDeal: Inness said a painting's aim was to awaken an emotion, and that finish and detail worked against it. He was arguing against precisely the Hudson River clarity that had made his own early reputation.

title: Portrait of Lisa Colt Curtis
sceneContext: Lisa Colt Curtis, painted in 1898 by Sargent at the height of his portrait practice.
whyBigDeal: Sargent gave up society portraiture around 1907, calling it a pimp's profession, and turned to watercolour and murals. He was refusing the most lucrative work available to any painter alive at the time.

title: Return from the Fields
sceneContext: Return from the fields, painted about 1846–47 by Millet before he settled at Barbizon.
whyBigDeal: Millet was a farmer's son from Normandy and the only major painter of peasants who had done the work. Van Gogh copied his compositions repeatedly and called him the essential modern painter.

title: View of Florence
sceneContext: View of Florence, painted in 1837 by Thomas Cole after his European travels.
whyBigDeal: Cole founded what became the Hudson River School and simultaneously warned in print that American scenery was being destroyed by settlement. The landscape tradition he began was elegiac from its first year.

title: Royal Reception in a Landscape, left folio from the double frontispiece of a Shahnama (Book of Kings) of Firdausi (Persian, about 940–1019 or 1025)
medium: opaque watercolor, ink, gold and silver on paper
sceneContext: The left half of the 1444 double-page frontispiece.
whyBigDeal: Manuscripts of this quality record the names of calligrapher, illuminator and binder as often as the painter, and sometimes only the calligrapher. In Persian book production the writing was the senior craft.

title: Rustam meets the challenge of Ashkabus, from a Shah-nama (Book of Kings) of Firdausi (Persian, about 934–1020)
medium: opaque watercolor and gold on paper
sceneContext: Rustam meeting the challenge of Ashkabus, painted about 1590–1600. Rustam shoots the champion's horse first, then the man.
whyBigDeal: Rustam appears in the Shahnama across five hundred years of story time and eventually kills his own son without knowing him. He is a hero the epic treats with steady ambivalence, which the paintings reproduce without comment.

title: Marie Samary of the Odéon Theater
sceneContext: The actress Marie Samary of the Odéon, painted about 1881.
whyBigDeal: Bastien-Lepage died of stomach cancer at thirty-six, three years after this. He was one of the most admired painters in Europe at the time, and his reputation did not survive the century — the middle position he occupied between the academy and Impressionism stopped being interesting once the argument was settled.

title: "Sam Seals His Pact with Sindukht", Folio 85v from the Shahnama (Book of Kings) of Shah Tahmasp
medium: Opaque watercolor, ink, silver, and gold on paper
sceneContext: Sam sealing his pact with Sindukht, from a Shahnama of about 1525–30 — the Shah Tahmasp copy, the most lavish Persian manuscript ever produced.
whyBigDeal: It has 258 illustrations by the best painters of the age and took some twenty years. It was given to the Ottoman sultan as a diplomatic gift, and in the twentieth century its owner broke it up and sold the leaves individually.

title: The Story of Nushirwan and his Minister, "The Third Discourse on Diverse Events and Disorder in Life" from a  Khamsa (Quintet) of Nizami (1141–1209) (verso)
sceneContext: The story of Nushirwan and his minister, from a manuscript of 1555–65.
whyBigDeal: The tale has the king overhear two owls discussing how his misgovernment has produced enough ruined villages to serve as their dowry. Persian mirrors-for-princes deliver political criticism through animals, which is how it could be delivered at all.

title: Left side of a double-page album folio: Outside a Royal Encampment (recto)
medium: opaque watercolor and gold on paper
sceneContext: Outside a royal encampment, attributed to Bihzad, the most celebrated painter of the Persian tradition, about 1485 at Herat.
whyBigDeal: Bihzad's name became so valuable that it was added to paintings he did not make for centuries afterwards, and very few works are securely his. He is simultaneously the most famous Persian painter and one of the least firmly documented.

title: The Peaceable Kingdom
sceneContext: The Peaceable Kingdom, painted about 1816–18 by Edward Hicks, a Quaker minister and sign painter.
whyBigDeal: He painted the subject — Isaiah's prophecy of predator and prey lying down together — more than sixty times, with Penn's treaty with the Lenape in the background. His own Quaker meeting disapproved of him painting at all, and the repetitions track a lifelong argument with his faith.

title: Bahram Visits the White Domed Pavilion on Friday (recto)
medium: opaque watercolor, ink, and gold on paper
sceneContext: Bahram in the White Pavilion on Friday, from the *Haft Paykar*, about 1560–80.
whyBigDeal: The seven pavilions run from black to white across the week, ending in purity, so the sequence is a moral progression disguised as an itinerary of pleasures. The poem gets to instruct while describing seven nights of entertainment.

title: The Hillsides of Méry-sur-Oise, Opposite Auvers
sceneContext: The hillsides of Méry-sur-Oise opposite Auvers, painted in 1873 by Daubigny.
whyBigDeal: Daubigny fitted out a studio boat and painted from the river, years before Monet did the same. As a Salon juror he also argued for admitting the young Impressionists and resigned when he was overruled.

title: Nushirwan Listens to the Owls (recto); the Story of Nushirwan and his Minister, "The Third Discourse on Diverse Events and Disorder in Life" (verso) from a Khamsa (Quintet) of Nizami (1141–1209)
medium: opaque watercolor, ink, and gold on paper
sceneContext: Nushirwan listening to the owls, from a manuscript of 1555–65.
whyBigDeal: The owls' conversation is the mechanism by which the king learns what his officials have concealed from him. It is a picture about the difficulty of getting accurate information to a ruler, made for rulers.

title: Reclining Figure
medium: Ink, watercolor, and gold on paper
sceneContext: A reclining figure, painted in Iran about 1630–40.
whyBigDeal: Safavid single-page figures were collected into albums assembled by their owners, mixing paintings, drawings and calligraphy by different hands and dates. The album, not the individual sheet, was the finished object.

title: Composite Camel with Attendant
medium: Opaque watercolor and ink on paper
sceneContext: A composite camel with attendant — the animal's body assembled from other figures — painted in Iran or India in the sixteenth century.
whyBigDeal: Composite animals circulated between Persian and Mughal workshops and are one of the clearest traces of painters moving between the two courts. Artists were recruited across that border throughout the period.

title: Aulad Tied to a Plane Tree, from a Shahnama by Firdausi
medium: opaque watercolor, gold, and silver on paper
sceneContext: Aulad tied to a plane tree, from a Shahnama by Sadiqi Bek, a painter who was also a poet and wrote a treatise on painting.
whyBigDeal: Sadiqi rose to head the royal library-workshop and was removed for what contemporaries described as an impossible temperament. His own writing about painting survives, which is rare — most Persian painters left no account of their practice.

title: Rustam's seventh course: He kills the White Div, folio 124 from a Shah-nama (Book of Kings) of Firdausi (Persian, about 934–1020)
medium: Gum tempera, ink, gold, and silver on paper
sceneContext: Rustam killing the White Div, his seventh and final labour, from a Shahnama of 1522–37 by Abd al-Vahhab.
whyBigDeal: The seven courses are a fixed sequence every illustrated Shahnama includes, so painters were repeatedly reinterpreting the same seven scenes. Comparing versions across two centuries is one of the few controlled ways to trace change in Persian painting.

title: Durham, Connecticut
sceneContext: Durham, Connecticut, painted in 1858.
whyBigDeal: Inness had a commission from a railway company early in his career to paint their line through the Pennsylvania countryside. Nineteenth-century American landscape was frequently funded by the industries that were altering the landscape.

title: Portrait of Genio C. Scott
sceneContext: Genio C. Scott, painted in 1859 by Eastman Johnson.
whyBigDeal: Johnson began as a portrait draughtsman in Washington, drawing Dolley Madison and John Quincy Adams in crayon. He built a national career from a practice that started as something close to reportage.

title: Woman Meditating
sceneContext: A woman meditating, painted after 1868. Corot's late figure paintings were largely unknown until after his death.
whyBigDeal: He sold landscapes and kept the figures in the studio, and they emerged only when the estate was dispersed. Picasso owned several and they visibly informed his own work, so a private body of work reached the twentieth century by accident.

title: Figure in Turkish Costume
medium: oil on paper, glued to canvas
sceneContext: A figure in Turkish costume, painted about 1856–63, drawing on Delacroix's Moroccan notebooks of thirty years earlier.
whyBigDeal: He was still using material from a six-month trip taken in 1832 in the last years of his life. The journey functioned as a permanent stock of imagery rather than as a subject he exhausted.

title: Portrait of Dora Wheeler
sceneContext: Dora Wheeler, painted 1882–83. The sitter was a designer who worked with Louis Comfort Tiffany.
whyBigDeal: The picture was shown in Paris and Munich and made Chase's European reputation. American painters of this generation still needed European exhibition to be taken seriously at home.

title: Portrait of My Daughter Alice
sceneContext: The painter's daughter Alice, about 1895.
whyBigDeal: Chase painted his children constantly, partly from affection and partly because models cost money he did not have. Domestic subjects in this period are often a function of a household budget.

title: Khusrau Surprising Shirin While Bathing
sceneContext: Khusrau surprising Shirin bathing, painted 1550–99. The scene is a set piece of Persian poetry and painting.
whyBigDeal: The two see each other before they meet, each already in love with a description of the other. Persian romance is built on report and reputation rather than encounter, which is why so much of it happens at a distance.

title: Sunset on the River Oise
sceneContext: Sunset on the Oise, painted in 1866 by Daubigny.
whyBigDeal: Monet and Pissarro took refuge in London during the Franco-Prussian war and Daubigny introduced them to the dealer Durand-Ruel, who then sustained Impressionism financially for decades. An older painter's introduction underwrote the movement.

title: View of Schroon Mountain, Essex County, New York, After a Storm
sceneContext: Schroon Mountain after a storm, painted in 1838 by Thomas Cole.
whyBigDeal: Cole made careful drawings on the spot and composed the finished canvases in the studio months later, often rearranging the topography. The pictures document a mood rather than a place, which their titles do not admit.

title: The Cossack
sceneContext: The Cossack, by Sargent.
whyBigDeal: Sargent was born in Florence to American parents, trained in Paris, and lived mostly in London, and he did not visit the United States until he was twenty. The most celebrated American portraitist of his age was American mainly on paper.

title: The Story of Hushang, from a Majma al-tavarikh (A Compendium of Histories) of Hafiz-i Abru (recto)
medium: opaque watercolor and ink on paper
sceneContext: The story of Hushang, a mythical Persian king credited with discovering fire, from a *Majma al-tavarikh* of 1425–50.
whyBigDeal: Hushang throws a stone at a snake, misses, and strikes sparks from rock — so fire enters the world through a failed attempt to kill something. Persian histories begin with legendary kings and slide into documented ones without marking the join.

title: Winding Yarn (Interior of a Nantucket Kitchen)
sceneContext: Winding yarn in a Nantucket kitchen, painted in 1872. Johnson spent summers on Nantucket for years.
whyBigDeal: The island's whaling economy had collapsed and its population was falling fast when he painted these interiors. They record a place emptying out, which the domestic calm does not announce.

title: Leaving the Forest, Fontainebleau: Setting Sun
sceneContext: Leaving the forest at Fontainebleau at sunset, painted in 1851.
whyBigDeal: Rousseau built up thick, dark paint that has cracked badly on many of his canvases. The technical failure is part of why his reputation sits below Corot's and Millet's, and it is a materials problem rather than a judgement about the pictures.

title: Bahram Gur and Azada, from a Shahnama (Book of Kings) of Firdausi (940–1019 or 1025)
artistBio: Iran, Tabriz or Qazvin, Safavid period (1501-1722)
medium: opaque watercolor and gold on paper
sceneContext: Bahram Gur and Azada, painted in the sixteenth century. The king's slave-girl mocks his archery, and he kills her for it.
whyBigDeal: The episode is illustrated constantly despite being an account of a casual murder. Persian painting shows it as an elegant hunting scene, and the disjunction between the beauty of the pictures and the content is not something the tradition tried to resolve.

title: Sunny Autumn Day
sceneContext: A sunny autumn day, painted in 1892 in Inness's last years.
whyBigDeal: He died in 1894 in Scotland, reportedly while watching a sunset. His late pictures dissolve form almost entirely, and they sold better than anything he had painted when his edges were sharp.

title: Saltash with the Water Ferry, Cornwall
sceneContext: Saltash with the water ferry, Cornwall, painted in 1811.
whyBigDeal: Turner toured Britain relentlessly, filling sketchbooks that he mined for finished pictures for decades afterwards. He was a working topographical artist first, and the late atmospheric painting grew out of commercial view-making.

title: A Home in the Wilderness
sceneContext: A home in the wilderness, painted in 1866 by Gifford, who had served in the Union army.
whyBigDeal: Several American landscape painters enlisted, and the clearings and cabins they painted afterwards carry a settlement narrative the war had just decided. The pictures are quiet about a question that had been answered by force.

title: In the Woods
sceneContext: In the woods, painted in 1866.
whyBigDeal: Inness painted the same few motifs — a clearing, a line of trees, a distant storm — for forty years. The consistency is not limited range but a deliberately narrow instrument, which is closer to Cézanne's method than to his American contemporaries'.

title: Groom and Rider
sceneContext: A groom and rider, painted in Iran 1540–50.
whyBigDeal: Horses are rendered with the same precision as human faces in Persian painting, because a court's horses were part of its standing. The care given to an animal's markings is a measure of what the picture was for.

title: Boy Fishing
sceneContext: A boy fishing, painted in the 1860s by Eastman Johnson.
whyBigDeal: American genre painting of the 1860s produced an enormous quantity of untroubled rural boyhood during and immediately after the Civil War. The absence of the war from these pictures is itself a decision.

title: High Tide on the Marshes
sceneContext: High tide on the marshes, painted in 1872 by Heade.
whyBigDeal: Heade painted the salt marshes at Newburyport across four decades, tracking the same flat ground through every light. Marshes were then regarded as waste land, and much of what he painted has since been drained or built over.

title: Apple Blossoms
sceneContext: Apple blossoms, painted in 1873.
whyBigDeal: Heade painted flowers on dark grounds in a manner closer to seventeenth-century still life than to anything American. He never sold well, and his work was rediscovered in the 1940s from pictures found in junk shops.

title: Marshlands
sceneContext: Marshlands, by Théodore Rousseau.
whyBigDeal: The Barbizon painters worked outdoors from the 1830s, two decades before Impressionism, but finished in the studio and kept a dark tonal range. They established the practice the younger painters would take further.

title: The Power of Music
sceneContext: The Power of Music, painted in 1847 by William Sidney Mount. A Black farmhand listens from outside a barn while three white men play within.
whyBigDeal: Mount placed the listener outside the door, excluded from the gathering but given the picture's real attention. It was engraved and widely distributed in the years before the Civil War, and its politics have been argued over ever since.

title: Autumn, a Wood Path
sceneContext: Autumn, a wood path, painted in 1876 by Gifford, the year before he died of malarial fever at fifty-three.
whyBigDeal: Gifford burned or painted over work he thought inadequate and kept a careful list of everything he considered finished. The catalogue he left behind is the reason his output is unusually well documented.

title: The Pond at the Entrance of the Woods
sceneContext: The pond at the entrance of the woods, painted about 1860–75.
