whyBigDeal: Corot's late feathery manner was so popular and so easy to imitate that he is among the most forged painters in history — it was said that of three thousand Corots painted, ten thousand are in America. Authentication of his work remains genuinely difficult.

title: Hungarian Gypsy Girl
sceneContext: Painted in Paris in 1932, when Sher-Gil was nineteen and studying at the École des Beaux-Arts. Her mother was Hungarian, her father a Sikh aristocrat and Sanskrit scholar, and she grew up between Budapest and Shimla.
whyBigDeal: She won a gold medal at the Paris Salon at twenty-one and was told by her teacher that her palette suggested she did not belong in the West. She returned to India the following year and spent the rest of her short career arguing that Indian painting had to be built from Indian subjects rather than European training.

title: Ancient Story Teller
sceneContext: Painted at Saraya in Uttar Pradesh in January 1940, on her husband's family estate, in the last full year of her life.
whyBigDeal: The flattened planes and earth palette come from the Ajanta cave murals and Pahari miniatures she studied on a journey through southern India in 1936–37. She was consciously reaching past three centuries of European influence to a pre-colonial Indian tradition, which is what makes her the pivot between the Bengal School and everything after.

title: Hillside
sceneContext: Painted at Shimla in June 1938, shortly after her marriage to her Hungarian cousin Victor Egan and their move to India.
whyBigDeal: Sher-Gil's landscapes are rare — she painted people almost exclusively, and usually the rural poor. The hills here are handled with the same weight and stillness as her figures, which is a decision about what deserves attention rather than an absence of one.

title: The Swing
sceneContext: Painted at Saraya in February 1940. Sher-Gil died in Lahore in December 1941, aged twenty-eight, days before her first major solo exhibition was to open.
whyBigDeal: The cause of her death has never been established and her mother alleged she had been murdered. The Indian government now classifies her work as a National Art Treasure, which forbids it leaving the country — a status held by only nine artists.

title: Resting
sceneContext: Painted at Saraya in November 1939. The estate belonged to her husband's family and she painted the villagers around it for two years.
whyBigDeal: She wrote that she was 'haunted by an intense longing to return to India' while in Paris, and that she felt she was destined to paint its poor. The subjects are not observed from outside so much as claimed, and Indian critics have argued about that claim ever since.

title: Hill Scene
sceneContext: Painted at Shimla in April 1938, in the hill station where her family kept a house and where she had spent much of her childhood.
whyBigDeal: Shimla was the summer capital of British India, and she painted its surrounding villages rather than its administration. Choosing the servants' hillside over the Viceroy's town was the kind of quiet positioning that runs through all her Indian work.

title: Red Verandah
sceneContext: Painted at Shimla in May 1938.
whyBigDeal: The strong flat colour and compressed space come from Mughal and Pahari miniature painting, which she studied seriously rather than quoting decoratively. She was doing in India what Gauguin and Matisse had done with Japanese and African sources, but with her own tradition.

title: Village Scene
sceneContext: Painted at Shimla in 1938, the year she settled permanently in India after eight years in Europe.
whyBigDeal: Her Paris teachers had trained her in oil and academic modelling, and the Indian work keeps the oil and discards the modelling. It is a technical decision that carries an argument about where she thought painting should come from.

title: Siesta
sceneContext: Painted at Shimla in October 1937, immediately after the journey through south India that produced her South Indian Trilogy.
whyBigDeal: That trip took her to Ajanta, Ellora, Mattancherry and Cape Comorin, and she wrote afterwards that she had found what she was looking for. The change in her painting before and after those months is the clearest turning point in twentieth-century Indian art.

title: Journey's End
sceneContext: A camel collapsed under its load, painted around 1913 by Abanindranath Tagore, nephew of the poet Rabindranath and the central figure of the Bengal School.
whyBigDeal: Abanindranath rejected the academic oil painting the British art schools taught and revived wash technique learned partly from Japanese painters who visited Calcutta. The picture is usually read as an image of exhaustion under empire, though he never said so.

title: Asoka's Queen
sceneContext: Painted in December 1911, showing the empress of the Mauryan emperor Ashoka.
whyBigDeal: The Bengal School built its subjects out of Indian history and myth at the moment when the nationalist movement needed a usable past. Abanindranath's *Bharat Mata*, painted in 1905, became the visual emblem of the anti-partition agitation — art and politics were not adjacent here, they were the same activity.

title: Sita in Captivity in Lanka
sceneContext: Sita held in Ravana's garden, painted in 1908.
whyBigDeal: Abanindranath taught at the Government School of Art in Calcutta under E. B. Havell, a British principal who agreed with him that Indian students should study Indian art rather than plaster casts of Greek statues. The reform came from inside the colonial institution.

title: Siddhas of the Upper Air
sceneContext: Painted in 1907. The siddhas are perfected beings who travel through the air in Indian cosmology.
whyBigDeal: His wash technique — laying thin transparent washes and washing them back — produced a deliberately insubstantial surface, the opposite of the solid oil painting taught in the art schools. The method was as much of a statement as the subject.

title: Dewali, or the Feast of Lamps
sceneContext: Diwali, painted in 1907, two years after the partition of Bengal set off the Swadeshi movement.
whyBigDeal: Abanindranath's students carried the Bengal School across India and into Japan and Britain. Nandalal Bose, his most important pupil, would go on to illuminate the manuscript of the Indian Constitution.

title: Poet's First Flight from London to Paris
sceneContext: Gaganendranath Tagore's view of his uncle Rabindranath's first aeroplane flight, painted in 1921.
whyBigDeal: Gaganendranath was the only Indian painter of his generation to work in a genuinely Cubist manner, and he arrived at it independently, having seen European modernism only in reproduction. It is one of the clearest cases of a modernist language being reinvented from photographs.

title: Dwarkapuri
sceneContext: Krishna's city of Dwarka, painted by Gaganendranath Tagore in the 1920s.
whyBigDeal: He built architecture out of faceted planes of light, using Cubist geometry for a mythological city rather than for a Paris café table. The vocabulary is European and the use is entirely his own.

title: Shaded Flame
sceneContext: Painted in the 1920s, from Gaganendranath's late experimental period.
whyBigDeal: He was also a sharp political cartoonist, publishing three albums of lithographic satire attacking both British rule and the Bengali elite's imitation of it. The same man produced the caricatures and these near-abstract light studies.

title: Brahmin of Kaliyuga
sceneContext: From Gaganendranath's satirical series of 1917, mocking the corrupt priest of the degenerate age.
whyBigDeal: The satire was aimed at his own class and caste, not at the colonial government, and it was published while he was simultaneously funding the nationalist cultural revival. He was attacking the society he was trying to build.

title: Sat-Bhai Champa
sceneContext: An illustration to a Bengali folk tale of seven brothers turned into champa flowers.
whyBigDeal: Gaganendranath illustrated Bengali children's literature alongside his experimental work, and treated both seriously. The folk material was being collected and published in this period as part of the same nationalist project that produced the paintings.

title: City in the Night
sceneContext: Painted in 1925, from the series of nocturnal city interiors that occupied his last productive years.
whyBigDeal: He suffered a stroke in 1930 and stopped painting altogether, eight years before his death. The night pictures, with their staircases and shafts of coloured light, are the last thing he made and the least like anything else in Indian art.

title: Accent on Pink
sceneContext: Painted in 1926, while Kandinsky was teaching at the Bauhaus in Dessau.
whyBigDeal: He wrote *Concerning the Spiritual in Art* in 1911 arguing that colour and form could work like music, without depicting anything. He had synaesthesia and reportedly heard tones when he saw colours, which makes the analogy less metaphorical than it sounds.

title: Autumn in Bavaria
sceneContext: Painted at Murnau in Bavaria in 1908, where Kandinsky and Gabriele Münter had begun spending summers.
whyBigDeal: Murnau is where he moved from representation to abstraction over roughly five years, and the transition is visible canvas by canvas. Few painters have left so complete a record of arriving somewhere new.

title: Impression V (Park)
sceneContext: Painted in 1911, the year Kandinsky co-founded Der Blaue Reiter with Franz Marc.
whyBigDeal: He divided his work into Impressions, Improvisations and Compositions, in ascending order of distance from observation. The taxonomy was published, so he was documenting his own retreat from the visible world as a stated programme.

title: Composition with Red, Blue and Yellow
sceneContext: Painted in 1927, from the years when Mondrian had reduced his vocabulary to horizontals, verticals and three primaries.
whyBigDeal: He broke with his colleague Theo van Doesburg over the diagonal, which van Doesburg introduced and Mondrian considered a betrayal of the principle. The friendship ended over the tilt of a line.

title: Arctic Dew
sceneContext: Painted in 1920, the year Klee joined the Bauhaus faculty.
whyBigDeal: He kept a meticulous catalogue of nearly ten thousand works, numbering each one as he finished it. The archive is so complete that his output can be dated almost to the month, which is unique among major twentieth-century painters.

title: Tropical Forest
sceneContext: Painted in 1915. Klee had travelled to Tunisia the previous year with August Macke.
whyBigDeal: He wrote in his diary in Tunisia that colour had taken possession of him and that he and colour were one. Macke was killed in France weeks after the trip, aged twenty-seven.

title: Castle and Sun
sceneContext: Painted in 1928, from Klee's late Bauhaus years.
whyBigDeal: The Nazis dismissed him from his professorship in 1933, declared his work degenerate and included seventeen of his paintings in the 1937 exhibition of that name. He left for Switzerland and died there in 1940 of a wasting disease.

title: Two Figures in a Landscape
sceneContext: Painted by Malevich after his enforced return to figurative work in the late 1920s.
whyBigDeal: He had invented Suprematism in 1915 with a black square on white, arguing that painting could dispense with objects entirely. Under Stalin abstraction became politically impossible and he went back to painting peasants — sometimes signing them with a small black square.

title: Coast near Lübeck
sceneContext: Painted in 1907, four years before Munch's breakdown and voluntary confinement in a Copenhagen clinic.
whyBigDeal: He left his entire remaining output to the city of Oslo on his death — over a thousand paintings and fifteen thousand prints, much of it stored in his house. The scale of the bequest is why one city holds almost all of him.

title: Still Life with Flowers
sceneContext: Painted in 1911, when Schiele was twenty-one and had recently left the Vienna Academy.
whyBigDeal: He was arrested in 1912 and held for twenty-four days on charges relating to his drawings and his contact with a minor; a judge burned one drawing in court. He died in the influenza pandemic of 1918 at twenty-eight, three days after his pregnant wife.

title: Eduard Kosmack
sceneContext: A portrait of the publisher Eduard Kosmack, painted in 1910.
whyBigDeal: Schiele's sitters are pressed against a blank ground with no room and no furniture, which he arrived at by removing everything Klimt's portraits had put in. The subtraction is the whole method.

title: Herbert Reiner as a Boy
sceneContext: Painted in 1910.
whyBigDeal: Schiele produced roughly three thousand drawings and three hundred paintings in a working life of about ten years. The rate is the reason so much survives from someone who died so young.

title: Reclining Dog (Russi)
sceneContext: Marc's dog Russi asleep in snow, painted in 1909.
whyBigDeal: Marc believed animals saw the world more truthfully than people and painted almost nothing else. He assigned meanings to colours in a letter — blue for the masculine and spiritual, yellow for the feminine and gentle, red for matter — so his animals are coded rather than observed.

title: The Dream
sceneContext: Painted in 1912, the year after Marc co-founded Der Blaue Reiter with Kandinsky.
whyBigDeal: He was killed by a shell splinter at Verdun in 1916, aged thirty-six. The German army had just placed him on a list of artists to be withdrawn from combat; the order had not reached him.

title: Reclining Nude among Flowers
sceneContext: Painted in 1910.
whyBigDeal: Der Blaue Reiter's 1912 almanac put children's drawings, Bavarian glass painting, African masks and Gothic woodcuts beside contemporary work as equals. It was an argument about hierarchy in art, made by juxtaposition rather than in prose.

title: Three Girls in Yellow Straw Hats
artistBio: <span title="German painter of the expressionist group Der
sceneContext: Painted in 1913, the year before Macke's death.
whyBigDeal: Macke was the most straightforwardly pleasurable painter of the group — shop windows, parks, people looking at things. He was killed in Champagne in September 1914, six weeks into the war, aged twenty-seven.

title: Sunny Garden
artistBio: <span title="German painter of the expressionist group Der
sceneContext: Painted in 1908, early in Macke's career.
whyBigDeal: He met Delaunay in Paris in 1912 and took from him the idea that colour alone could structure a picture. The Tunisian watercolours he made two years later with Klee are the result, and they are almost the last work he produced.

title: Coloured Forms
artistBio: <span title="German painter of the expressionist group Der
sceneContext: From Macke's late abstract experiments.
whyBigDeal: His widow Elisabeth preserved and catalogued his work for sixty years after his death and wrote a memoir of the Blaue Reiter circle. A good deal of what is known about the group comes from the widows who outlived it.

title: Lighthouse behind the Bay
sceneContext: Painted in 1912 on Fehmarn in the Baltic, where Kirchner spent several summers.
whyBigDeal: Kirchner co-founded Die Brücke in Dresden in 1905 with three fellow architecture students, none of them trained as painters. The group's roughness was partly a programme and partly the fact that they had taught themselves.

title: Still Life with Calla Lilies
sceneContext: Painted in the 1910s.
whyBigDeal: Kirchner had a breakdown during military training in 1915 and was discharged; he spent the rest of his life in Switzerland. In 1937 the Nazis removed over six hundred of his works from German museums, and he killed himself the following year.

title: Woman's Head with Flowers in Her Hair
sceneContext: Painted around 1913, before Jawlensky was expelled from Germany as a Russian national at the outbreak of war.
whyBigDeal: He had been an officer in the Imperial Russian Guard before turning to painting at thirty. Arthritis crippled his hands in the 1930s and he painted his last small heads by strapping the brush to his wrist.

title: Abstract Head: Symphony in Pink
sceneContext: From the Abstract Heads series Jawlensky began in the early 1920s.
whyBigDeal: He painted essentially one subject — a face reduced to a few lines — for the last twenty years of his life, in hundreds of variations. It is the same method as Monet's haystacks applied to a human face.

title: Still Life with Oil Lamp
sceneContext: Painted in 1907.
whyBigDeal: Jawlensky spent time with Matisse in Paris and brought Fauve colour back to Munich, where it fed directly into Der Blaue Reiter. He was a conduit between the French and German avant-gardes as much as a painter in his own right.

title: No. 1 from The Parsifal Series
sceneContext: Painted in 1916 by Hilma af Klint, a Swedish painter who worked in near-total secrecy.
whyBigDeal: She produced abstract paintings from 1906, several years before Kandinsky, Mondrian or Malevich, and instructed that they not be shown until twenty years after her death. They were not exhibited until 1986, by which time the history of abstraction had been written without her.

title: Buddha's Standpoint in the Earthly Life
sceneContext: Painted in 1920.
whyBigDeal: Af Klint was a trained academic painter who supported herself with conventional portraits and botanical illustration while making this work privately. She was a member of a group of five women who held séances and believed the paintings were directed by other intelligences.

title: Birch
sceneContext: Painted in 1922, from her later, quieter period.
whyBigDeal: Her collected work of over twelve hundred pieces was left to her nephew in crates. The 2018 Guggenheim exhibition of her paintings became the most attended show in that museum's history.

title: Dynamism of a Cyclist
sceneContext: Boccioni's study of a cyclist in motion.
whyBigDeal: The Futurists published manifestos before they had produced much art, declaring that a racing car was more beautiful than the Victory of Samothrace. Boccioni died in 1916 aged thirty-three, thrown from a horse during cavalry training.

title: Charge of the Lancers
sceneContext: Painted in 1915, the year Italy entered the war that the Futurists had spent years demanding.
whyBigDeal: The movement had glorified war as 'the world's only hygiene'. Boccioni and the architect Sant'Elia both enlisted and both were dead within two years, and Futurism as they conceived it did not survive them.

title: Charge of the Lancers (second version)
sceneContext: A second version of the 1915 composition.
whyBigDeal: The painting incorporates a fragment of newspaper reporting the actual cavalry charge. Collage entered Futurism as documentary evidence rather than as formal play.

title: The Hungry Lion Throws Itself on the Antelope
sceneContext: Rousseau's jungle painting, shown at the Salon d'Automne in 1905 in the room that gave the Fauves their name.
whyBigDeal: He never left France. The jungles were assembled from the Paris botanical gardens, a taxidermy display and illustrated magazines, which is why the plants are botanically impossible.

title: Pastoral Landscape with Stream
sceneContext: An early landscape from the 1870s, when Rousseau was working as a toll collector on the edge of Paris.
whyBigDeal: He was self-taught, retired at forty-nine to paint full time, and was mocked at every Salon he entered. Picasso bought one of his canvases for five francs from a dealer selling it as scrap and held a banquet in his honour.

title: The Beauty and the Beast
sceneContext: A late fantasy subject.
whyBigDeal: Rousseau was twice convicted of minor fraud, and at one trial his lawyer secured leniency by showing the court his paintings. Judges found them funny, which was the general verdict of his lifetime.

title: Girl with Small Child
sceneContext: Painted in 1905 at Worpswede, the artists' colony near Bremen.
whyBigDeal: Modersohn-Becker painted the first known female nude self-portraits in Western art. She died of an embolism in 1907, eighteen days after giving birth, aged thirty-one, having sold perhaps three paintings.

title: Two-Trunked Birch in a Landscape
sceneContext: Painted in 1899, early in her time at Worpswede.
whyBigDeal: She made four extended visits to Paris between 1900 and 1907, seeing Cézanne and Gauguin before almost anyone in Germany. Rilke, a close friend, wrote his *Requiem for a Friend* after her death.

title: Man Lying beneath a Blossoming Tree
sceneContext: Painted in 1903.
whyBigDeal: Her journals and letters, published in 1917, became one of the most widely read artist's documents in Germany. She was known as a writer before she was known as a painter.

title: Flowers before the Window
sceneContext: Painted in 1930 by Suzanne Valadon, who began as an acrobat, became an artists' model, and taught herself to paint by watching the people she posed for.
whyBigDeal: She modelled for Renoir, Degas and Toulouse-Lautrec; Degas saw her drawings, bought them and encouraged her. She was the first woman admitted to the Société Nationale des Beaux-Arts.

title: The Artist's Mother
sceneContext: A portrait of Valadon's mother, a laundress who had raised her alone in Montmartre.
whyBigDeal: Valadon was an unmarried mother at eighteen and never named her son's father; the boy became the painter Maurice Utrillo. Three generations of one household worked as artists' models, laundresses and painters in the same few streets.

title: André Utter and His Dogs
sceneContext: Her husband André Utter, a painter twenty-one years her junior whom she married in 1914.
whyBigDeal: She painted male nudes at a time when women were still barred from life classes with male models in most academies. Doing it at all was a professional trespass before it was a subject.

title: Childhood
sceneContext: Painted in 1893 by Ferdinand Hodler, whose parents and all his siblings died of tuberculosis before he was thirty.
whyBigDeal: He built pictures on what he called parallelism — repeated, near-identical figures arranged rhythmically. It was a system meant to express order underlying nature, developed by a man whose own family had been erased.

title: Dying Woman on Her Deathbed
sceneContext: Hodler painted his lover Valentine Godé-Darel through her final illness in 1914–15, in a sequence of dated canvases and drawings.
whyBigDeal: He recorded her decline day by day, then painted the empty bed and the sunrise afterwards. It is one of the very few sustained artistic records of a specific person dying, made by the person closest to her.

title: Aino
sceneContext: Aino from the Finnish national epic *Kalevala*, painted in 1916 by Gallen-Kallela.
whyBigDeal: The *Kalevala* was compiled from oral poetry in the 1830s and became the foundation of Finnish national identity under Russian rule. Gallen-Kallela's illustrations of it were a nationalist programme, and Finland gained independence in 1917.

title: Café in Paris
sceneContext: Painted in 1909.
whyBigDeal: Gallen-Kallela travelled to Kenya in 1909 and painted there for two years, then designed frescoes for the Finnish pavilion in Paris and a mausoleum in Tampere. His range across easel painting, fresco, textiles and stained glass was typical of the national-romantic generation.

title: Madonna
sceneContext: Painted in 1891.
whyBigDeal: He changed his name from the Swedish Axél Gallén to the Finnish Akseli Gallen-Kallela in 1907. Language politics in Finland ran through personal identity, and painters took sides by what they called themselves.

title: Ornament with Peacock Feathers
sceneContext: A decorative panel by Vrubel, painted before 1910.
whyBigDeal: Vrubel worked in ceramics, stage design, mosaic and architecture as readily as in paint, for the Abramtsevo artists' colony outside Moscow. Russian Symbolism was a total-design movement before it was a style of painting.

title: Hamlet and Ophelia
sceneContext: Painted in 1884, early in Vrubel's career.
whyBigDeal: He spent his last years in psychiatric hospitals, painting until he went blind in 1906. Alexander Blok spoke at his funeral, and Russian Symbolist poetry treated him as one of its own.

title: Hansel and Gretel
sceneContext: Painted in 1896.
whyBigDeal: Vrubel's faceted, crystalline handling has no obvious source in Russian painting and predates Cubism by fifteen years. He arrived at it partly from mosaic work he did restoring twelfth-century churches in Kyiv.

title: Barns
sceneContext: Painted in 1904 by Valentin Serov.
whyBigDeal: Serov was the most sought-after portraitist in Russia and resigned from the Academy in 1905 in protest at the shooting of demonstrators on Bloody Sunday. He had painted the Tsar's portrait two years earlier.

title: Interior of the Dormition Cathedral
sceneContext: Painted in 1896.
whyBigDeal: Serov's father was the composer Alexander Serov, and he grew up among musicians. He trained under Repin from the age of nine, which is early even by nineteenth-century standards.

title: Sunset
sceneContext: Painted in the 1890s by Isaac Levitan.
whyBigDeal: Levitan was expelled from Moscow twice under laws restricting where Jews could live, once in 1879 and again in 1892, while he was already a celebrated painter. He continued to define the Russian landscape for Russians throughout.

title: Golden Autumn
artistBio: Isaac Ilyich Levitan (Russian: Исаа́к Ильи́ч Левита́н)
sceneContext: Painted in 1895, five years before Levitan's death at thirty-nine from a heart condition.
whyBigDeal: He was a close friend of Chekhov, and the two men's work is routinely described in the same terms — mood carried by ordinary material, nothing overstated. Chekhov based a character in *The Seagull* partly on him.

title: Albert Pinkham Ryder
sceneContext: Marsden Hartley's posthumous portrait of the painter Albert Pinkham Ryder, painted in 1938.
whyBigDeal: Hartley had met Ryder once and considered the encounter decisive. Painting a portrait of a dead painter you barely knew, as an act of allegiance, is an unusually direct statement of artistic descent.

title: American Indian Symbols
sceneContext: Painted in Berlin in 1914, where Hartley was living when the war broke out.
whyBigDeal: He was drawing on Native American material while in Germany, and simultaneously painting emblems of the German officer he loved, who was killed that year. The two bodies of work were made in the same months by a man displaced from both subjects.

title: Love, Love, Love (Homage to Gertrude Stein)
sceneContext: Painted in 1928 as a poster-portrait of Gertrude Stein, using words and objects instead of a face.
whyBigDeal: Demuth made a series of these portraits of friends, of which the best known is *I Saw the Figure 5 in Gold* for William Carlos Williams. Replacing a likeness with typography was decades ahead of Pop art doing the same thing.

title: Modern Conveniences
sceneContext: Painted in 1921, from Demuth's Precisionist industrial subjects.
whyBigDeal: He had diabetes and was among the first Americans treated with insulin after its discovery in 1922, which extended his life by about a decade. Almost all the mature work was made in that borrowed time.

title: Augusta Wills Buckius Demuth
sceneContext: A portrait of the painter's mother, with whom he lived in Lancaster, Pennsylvania for his entire life.
whyBigDeal: Demuth worked in a small town while remaining central to the New York avant-garde, travelling in and out. He also produced explicit watercolours of bathhouses and sailors that were not exhibited until long after his death.

title: Blackwell's Island, East River
sceneContext: Painted in 1900. The island held a penitentiary, a workhouse and a hospital for the poor.
whyBigDeal: Henri taught that art should come from ordinary life and led the group later called the Ashcan School. He organised the 1910 Exhibition of Independent Artists, which had no jury and no prizes — a direct attack on the academy's control.

title: Cumulus Clouds, East River
sceneContext: Painted around 1901.
whyBigDeal: Henri's book *The Art Spirit*, assembled from his teaching, has stayed in print for a century and shaped more American painters through the classroom than through the canvases. Edward Hopper and Rockwell Kent were among his students.

title: The Skier
sceneContext: Painted in 1911 by Carl Larsson.
whyBigDeal: Larsson's watercolours of his own family home at Sundborn, published as books, effectively invented the Swedish domestic ideal that IKEA later sold to the world. A national style of interior comes out of one painter's house.

title: Elias Sehlstedt and His Muse
sceneContext: Painted in 1892.
whyBigDeal: Larsson grew up in extreme poverty in Stockholm and described his childhood as squalid and frightening. The serene domestic pictures were made deliberately against his own experience, not from it.

title: The Blackcaps
sceneContext: Painted after 1884 by Giovanni Segantini in the Alps.
whyBigDeal: Segantini worked at high altitude, painting outdoors in snow, and used a divided-stroke technique of long threads of pure colour. He died at forty-one of peritonitis in a hut at nearly three thousand metres, having refused to come down.

title: The Water Carrier
sceneContext: A charcoal study.
whyBigDeal: Segantini was born in the Austrian Tyrol and never held citizenship of any country; he was stateless his whole life and could not travel freely. He is claimed today as both an Italian and a Swiss painter.

title: Nature
sceneContext: From Segantini's Alpine triptych of Nature, Life and Death.
whyBigDeal: He planned an enormous panorama of the Engadine for the 1900 Paris Exposition, which was abandoned when funding collapsed. The triptych is what survives of a much larger ambition.

title: Kerala Varma Valiya Koil Thampuran
sceneContext: A portrait of the consort of the Maharani of Travancore, painted around 1880 by Raja Ravi Varma, himself a member of the Travancore royal house.
whyBigDeal: Ravi Varma learned oil painting and European perspective from a visiting Dutch portraitist and applied both to Indian subjects for the first time at this scale. Every argument in Indian art for the next century — including the Bengal School's rejection of him — is a response to what he did.

title: Woman Holding a Fruit
sceneContext: Painted in the late nineteenth century.
whyBigDeal: Ravi Varma set up a lithographic press near Bombay in 1894 to mass-produce his images of gods and heroines as cheap oleographs. Those prints reached households across India and effectively standardised what Hindu deities look like — an iconography now so familiar it is mistaken for ancient.

title: Portrait of a Lady
sceneContext: Painted in 1893, the year Ravi Varma sent ten paintings to the World's Columbian Exposition in Chicago, where he won two awards.
whyBigDeal: He was the first Indian artist to achieve an international reputation on European terms and was attacked at home for exactly that. The Bengal School was founded partly in opposition to him, arguing that he had sold Indian subjects in a borrowed language.

title: Malayali Lady
sceneContext: A woman of Kerala in traditional dress, painted in 1892.
whyBigDeal: Ravi Varma's women became the template for the Indian calendar art, film poster and advertising image that followed. A single painter's sense of an ideal face has shaped Indian popular visual culture for more than a century.

title: The Miser
sceneContext: Painted in 1901, five years before his death.
whyBigDeal: His press went bankrupt and was sold, and he spent his last years in debt despite enormous fame. The oleographs that made his images ubiquitous made very little money for him.

title: Gypsies
sceneContext: Painted in 1893.
whyBigDeal: Ravi Varma travelled across India specifically to find models and costumes for his mythological pictures, treating the whole country as a source. That method — assembling a pan-Indian imagery from regional particulars — was itself a nationalist act, whether or not he intended it.

title: Disappointing News
sceneContext: A woman reading a letter.
whyBigDeal: Ravi Varma painted contemporary domestic subjects alongside the mythological pictures, and these are far less reproduced. The gods sold; the ordinary rooms did not.

title: Lady at Ball Game
sceneContext: Painted around 1894.
whyBigDeal: He was commissioned by the Gaekwad of Baroda and by the Nizam of Hyderabad, and worked for princely courts throughout his career. Indian modern painting begins inside the patronage system of the princely states, not in the colonial cities.

title: Malabar Beauty
sceneContext: Painted before 1906, the year Ravi Varma died at fifty-eight.
whyBigDeal: His reputation collapsed within a decade of his death as the Bengal School's arguments took hold, and was only rebuilt from the 1980s onward. He is now valued at auction above almost any other Indian painter.

title: Allegories of the Fine Arts and Crafts
sceneContext: An early decorative commission from around 1880, when Klimt was still working with his brother and a partner as a firm of architectural decorators.
whyBigDeal: He began as a conventional and successful public decorator and only broke with that career in his thirties. The Secession he founded in 1897 was a revolt by an insider against the system that had already rewarded him.

title: Redheaded Girl in Evening Dress
sceneContext: Painted in 1918, the last year of Modigliani's life.
whyBigDeal: He died of tubercular meningitis in January 1920 aged thirty-five, and his partner Jeanne Hébuterne, nine months pregnant, killed herself the following day. He had held one solo exhibition, closed by the police on its opening day.

title: Woman with Red Hair
sceneContext: Painted in 1917.
whyBigDeal: Modigliani wanted to be a sculptor and worked in stone until the dust became impossible for his damaged lungs. The elongated necks and mask-like faces of the paintings come directly from the carvings he had to abandon.

title: Portrait of a Woman
sceneContext: Painted between 1916 and 1919.
whyBigDeal: He is among the most forged painters in the world, and a 2017 exhibition in Genoa was closed when twenty of the twenty-one works shown were judged fake. The simplicity that makes the pictures recognisable also makes them easy to imitate.

title: The Mendicant
sceneContext: Published in *The Modern Review* in 1914. Nandalal Bose was Abanindranath Tagore's most important pupil.
whyBigDeal: *The Modern Review* carried the Bengal School's work to a national readership as printed plates, which is how the style spread beyond Calcutta. The reproduction, not the original, was the thing most people ever saw.

title: Damayanti Choosing Her Husband
sceneContext: Damayanti's swayamvara from the Mahabharata, published in 1910.
whyBigDeal: Bose later designed the emblems and illuminated every page of the original manuscript of the Constitution of India. The visual identity of the Indian republic was drawn by a painter trained in this idiom.

title: Garuda
artistBio:
Author Sister Nivedita and Ananda Kentish Coomaraswamy

Illustrator  Nandalal Bose
sceneContext: An illustration to *Myths of the Hindus and Buddhists*, published in 1914. The book was written by Sister Nivedita, the Irish disciple of Vivekananda.
whyBigDeal: An Irishwoman's retelling of Hindu myth, illustrated by Indian painters, published in London for a Western readership — the Bengal School was arguing for Indian art in a book aimed abroad. Cultural nationalism here was an export operation.

title: Kirat and Arjuna
artistBio:
Author Sister Nivedita and Ananda Kentish Coomaraswamy 

Illustrator Nandalal Bose
sceneContext: Shiva disguised as a hunter fighting Arjuna, from *Myths of the Hindus and Buddhists*, 1914.
whyBigDeal: Bose taught at Santiniketan under Rabindranath Tagore for over thirty years and shaped Indian art education more than any other individual. His students included Benode Behari Mukherjee and Ramkinkar Baij.

title: Shiva Drinking the World-Poison
artistBio:
Author Sister Nivedita and Ananda Kentish Coomaraswamy 

Illustrator Nandalal Bose
sceneContext: Shiva swallowing the poison churned from the ocean, from the 1914 volume.
whyBigDeal: Bose went to Japan in 1924 and studied with Japanese painters, absorbing brush technique that fed back into the Santiniketan school. The Bengal School's pan-Asianism was practical: painters actually travelled and trained across the region.

title: The Asceticism of Uma
artistBio:
Author Sister Nivedita and Ananda Kentish Coomaraswamy 

Illustrator Nandalal Bose
sceneContext: Uma's penance to win Shiva, from the 1914 volume.
whyBigDeal: Gandhi asked Bose to design the posters and pavilions for the 1938 Haripura session of the Indian National Congress. He produced hundreds of small paintings of ordinary rural occupations for it, which are now among the most reproduced Indian images of the century.

title: Mona Lisa
sceneContext: Begun in Florence for the silk merchant Francesco del Giocondo, whose wife Lisa Gherardini sat for it. Leonardo never delivered it, carried it to France in 1516, and was still adjusting it at his death.
whyBigDeal: Its fame is recent: it was a specialist's picture until a Louvre handyman stole it in 1911 and the empty wall drew larger crowds than the painting had. Leonardo built the face from dozens of glazes each a fraction of a millimetre thick, leaving no visible brushstroke or outline anywhere.

title: Lady with an Ermine
sceneContext: Cecilia Gallerani was sixteen and the mistress of Ludovico Sforza, Duke of Milan, who employed Leonardo. The ermine puns on her name in Greek and on Ludovico's own emblem, the Order of the Ermine.
whyBigDeal: The sitter turns as if someone has entered the room behind her, which almost no portrait before this had attempted — the convention was a static profile. The animal is anatomically observed rather than heraldic, and its paw is drawn with the same tendon-by-tendon attention as her hand.

title: Ginevra de' Benci
sceneContext: Painted in Florence when Leonardo was in his mid-twenties, probably to mark the marriage of Ginevra de' Benci, daughter of a banking family. The panel was later cut down; the lower third with her hands is lost.
whyBigDeal: The reverse carries a painted wreath and the motto 'Beauty adorns virtue' — the picture was made to be handled and turned over, not hung. The juniper bush behind her head is another pun on her name, and its needles are picked out with a brush of a few hairs.

title: Virgin of the Rocks
sceneContext: Commissioned by a Milanese confraternity for a chapel altarpiece, with a contract specifying the subject in detail. Leonardo delivered something so unlike the commission that a twenty-year legal dispute followed and a second version was eventually painted.
whyBigDeal: The grotto geology is drawn from his own field notes on rock strata and erosion, not from studio convention. He lit the group from a single source in a dark cavern, an effect other painters copied for a century before Caravaggio pushed it further.

title: Saint John the Baptist
sceneContext: Leonardo's last painting, made in Rome and France in his final years, when his right hand was partly paralysed and he was working slowly with assistants around him.
whyBigDeal: The figure emerges from total darkness with no landscape, no attributes beyond a reed cross, and a smile that contemporaries found unsettling on a desert ascetic. It is the furthest he took sfumato — the transitions are so gradual that no edge in the face can be located precisely.

title: The Garden of Earthly Delights
sceneContext: Painted in 's-Hertogenbosch for a private patron, probably Engelbert II of Nassau, for a palace rather than a church. It was recorded in a Brussels palace in 1517 and taken to Spain by Philip II.
whyBigDeal: The outer wings, painted in grey, show the world on the third day of creation as a flat disc inside a sphere — so the triptych begins closed, as a globe, and opens into the world's history. Bosch signed almost nothing and left no writings, so every reading of the centre panel is inference.

title: The Haywain Triptych
sceneContext: Made late in Bosch's life in 's-Hertogenbosch, where he belonged to a conservative religious brotherhood. Philip II of Spain bought it in 1570 and hung it in the Escorial.
whyBigDeal: It illustrates a Netherlandish proverb — the world is a haystack and each takes what he can grab — with popes and emperors riding behind the cart and ordinary people crushed under its wheels. Bosch put social rank into a moral image at a moment when religious painting rarely named who was culpable.

title: The Temptation of St Anthony
sceneContext: The hermit Anthony's desert torments were a standard subject, popular partly because ergot poisoning from infected rye was called St Anthony's fire and its victims hallucinated.
whyBigDeal: Bosch's demons are assembled from real parts — a fish's body on bird legs, a funnel for a hat — rather than invented wholesale, which is why they read as plausible rather than decorative. Sixteenth-century Spanish collectors valued him precisely for this, and copies were produced in quantity.

title: The Hunters in the Snow
sceneContext: One of six panels on the months painted for the Antwerp merchant Niclaes Jonghelinck's dining room. The winter of 1564–65 was among the harshest on record in the Low Countries.
whyBigDeal: The hunters return with a single fox, which makes the picture a record of a poor season rather than a seasonal decoration. Bruegel put the horizon high and ran a diagonal of trees down to the frozen ponds, a device landscape painters used for the next three centuries.

title: Netherlandish Proverbs
sceneContext: Painted in Antwerp for the open market rather than a commission, at a time when collections of proverbs — Erasmus's among them — were bestsellers in the Low Countries.
whyBigDeal: More than a hundred proverbs are staged simultaneously in one village, including several whose meaning is now lost because the sayings died out. It is a picture that assumes its viewer will stand close and take a long time, which is not how altarpieces were meant to be seen.

title: The Peasant Wedding
sceneContext: Bruegel was a cultivated Antwerp and Brussels townsman with humanist friends, not a villager; he visited country festivals to observe them, and his patrons were urban collectors.
whyBigDeal: The bride sits under the paper crown doing nothing while everyone else eats — and the groom cannot be identified with certainty, which has kept the picture argued over for four centuries. The bagpiper watching the food go past is the one figure whose hunger Bruegel makes explicit.

title: The Tower of Babel
sceneContext: Bruegel had crossed the Alps to Italy around 1552 and seen the Colosseum, whose tiers of arches he gave to the tower. Antwerp at the time was Europe's boom port, crowded with languages.
whyBigDeal: The tower is already failing as it rises: the lower arches are subsiding and the upper storeys tilt off the vertical, so the building's collapse is structural rather than divine punishment. Bruegel drew working cranes, scaffolding and treadwheels accurately enough that engineers still cite the panel.

title: The Triumph of Death
sceneContext: Painted a generation after the Low Countries had lived through repeated plague, famine and the beginnings of religious war, when danse macabre imagery was already old and familiar.
whyBigDeal: Bruegel replaced the medieval procession of individual skeletons with an army — organised, using nets, coffins and a cart, working as infantry. Death here is administrative rather than personal, which is a distinctly sixteenth-century horror and one no earlier version had staged.

title: Las Meninas
sceneContext: Painted in the Alcázar in Madrid, in a room Velázquez used as a studio, in the year he was angling for admission to the Order of Santiago. The red cross on his chest was added after his death.
whyBigDeal: The mirror on the back wall shows the king and queen, which places them where the viewer stands and makes the painting's real subject a person outside it. Velázquez painted himself at work at full height beside the royal family, an assertion of the painter's rank that was the point of the picture.

title: Las Hilanderas
sceneContext: Painted for a royal huntsman's collection. The foreground shows women working in the Santa Isabel tapestry workshop in Madrid; the lit chamber behind shows a tapestry of Titian's Rape of Europa.
whyBigDeal: The subject is Arachne's contest with Athena, but Velázquez put the myth in the back room and the wage labour in front, at full scale. The spinning wheel's spokes are painted as a blur, one of the earliest attempts anywhere to render motion rather than describe it.

title: Rokeby Venus
sceneContext: Almost certainly painted in Italy or just after Velázquez's return. Female nudes were effectively banned by the Spanish Inquisition, and this is the only surviving one by him.
whyBigDeal: The mirror is angled so that the face reflected in it could not be hers from that position — Velázquez gives her a blurred, generic reflection instead of a likeness, which keeps her anonymous. A suffragette slashed the canvas in 1914; the repairs are still visible in raking light.

title: The Triumph of Bacchus
sceneContext: Painted for Philip IV just before Velázquez's first trip to Italy, when he was still the young court painter and had been criticised for being able to paint only portraits.
whyBigDeal: He staged a classical god among recognisably drunk Madrid labourers who look straight out at the viewer, so the mythology is a pretext for painting faces from the street. The picture is known in Spain simply as Los Borrachos — the drinkers — which is what the court took from it.

title: Pope Innocent X
sceneContext: Painted in Rome during Velázquez's second Italian journey, as a demonstration piece to establish his standing there. He warmed up first by painting his enslaved assistant Juan de Pareja.
whyBigDeal: Innocent reportedly called it 'troppo vero' — too truthful. Velázquez declined to soften a suspicious, hard face, and built almost the whole picture from variations of a single red, so that the sitter's expression is the only incident in it.

title: The Third of May 1808
sceneContext: Painted six years after the event, once the French had gone, when Goya proposed to the restored Spanish government that he record the uprising. He had been court painter under the French occupation too.
whyBigDeal: The firing squad is a faceless machine and the lantern on the ground, not heaven, supplies the light. The man in white throws his arms out in a crucifixion pose with a stigma-like mark on his palm — martyrdom without any promise that it means anything.

title: The Second of May 1808
sceneContext: The companion piece, showing the Madrid crowd attacking Napoleon's Egyptian Mamluk cavalry in the Puerta del Sol — the revolt that the executions of the following morning punished.
whyBigDeal: Goya gives the rebels no heroism: it is a knife-fight around horses' legs, painted as confusion rather than as a battle with a shape. Pairing it with the executions turns the two canvases into cause and consequence, which history painting had almost never done.

title: Saturn Devouring His Son
medium: Mixed media on plaster, transferred to canvas
sceneContext: Painted directly onto the walls of the Quinta del Sordo, the house outside Madrid where Goya lived, deaf and ill, after a near-fatal illness. He never exhibited these works or wrote about them.
whyBigDeal: It was a private mural in his own dining room, not a commission, and was only moved to canvas fifty years after his death. The paint is applied with almost no drawing underneath, and the figure's eyes are the most finished thing in a picture that is otherwise nearly formless.

title: The Clothed Maja
sceneContext: Painted for Manuel Godoy, the Spanish prime minister, who kept it and its nude twin in a private cabinet with a mechanism that let one slide in front of the other.
whyBigDeal: The Inquisition seized both and interrogated Goya about them in 1815. The clothed version was painted later over the same pose, so the pictures work as a pair about being looked at rather than as two studies of a model.

title: The Dog
medium: Mixed media on plaster, transferred to canvas
sceneContext: Another of the Black Paintings from the walls of Goya's own house, made in his mid-seventies during a period of political repression under Ferdinand VII.
whyBigDeal: Almost the entire surface is empty ochre, with a dog's head at the bottom edge looking up at nothing that is depicted. Painters from Manet onwards treated it as the first picture whose subject is the space it refuses to fill.

title: The Scream
sceneContext: Munch wrote of walking at sunset near Ekeberg outside Kristiania when the sky turned blood red and he felt an infinite scream passing through nature. There was a slaughterhouse and an asylum, where his sister was confined, on that road.
whyBigDeal: The figure is not screaming but blocking out a scream it hears — Munch's own note says the shriek came from the landscape. He made it as a painting, a pastel and a lithograph, treating the image as something to reissue rather than a unique object, which is closer to modern practice than to 1893.

title: Madonna
sceneContext: Painted in Berlin, where Munch was part of a circle of writers around Strindberg that met at a wine bar called The Black Piglet and argued about sex, degeneration and the unconscious.
whyBigDeal: He titled a nude at the moment of conception 'Madonna', collapsing sacred and sexual imagery in a way that got the picture attacked as blasphemous. Some versions carry a painted border of sperm and a foetus, making the biology explicit rather than symbolic.

title: The Sick Child
sceneContext: Munch's sister Sophie died of tuberculosis at fifteen when he was fourteen; their mother had died of it earlier. He returned to this scene in six painted versions across forty years.
whyBigDeal: He scraped the surface back repeatedly and let the paint run, so the canvas records its own revision — critics in 1886 called it unfinished and it was the scandal of the Oslo autumn exhibition. He said afterwards that most of what he did later began here.

title: Puberty
sceneContext: Painted in Berlin during the same years as The Scream and Madonna, as part of the sequence Munch called the Frieze of Life, which he intended to be hung together as one work about love and death.
whyBigDeal: The shadow behind the girl is not cast by her body — it has its own bulk and shape, and Munch used it as a mood rather than as optics. That single decision to let a shadow lie is why the picture reads as psychological rather than observed.

title: Anxiety
sceneContext: Painted in Berlin, reusing the blood-red sky and the fjord bridge from The Scream of the year before, but filling the bridge with a crowd in mourning clothes.
whyBigDeal: Munch recycled his own setting deliberately, treating a composition as a reusable stage. The faces are drained to the same mask, which turns the earlier picture's single private terror into something collective and social.

title: The Starry Night
sceneContext: Painted from the barred window of his room in the asylum at Saint-Rémy-de-Provence, where van Gogh had admitted himself after the breakdown in Arles. He was allowed to paint only in a ground-floor studio, so this was worked up from memory and drawings.
whyBigDeal: The village below is invented — there is no such church spire in Provence, and its shape is Dutch. He thought the picture a failure and told Theo the stars were exaggerated; the cypress in the foreground is the plant Provençal graveyards were planted with.

title: Bedroom in Arles
sceneContext: Painted in the Yellow House at Arles while van Gogh waited for Gauguin to arrive and share it. He wrote to Theo that the picture was meant to express absolute rest and that he had chosen flat colour to do it.
whyBigDeal: The walls are now pale blue because the red lake pigment in the original violet has faded — he described the walls as violet in his letter, so the painting we see is not the one he described. He made three versions, the later two after the room was already lost to him.

title: Café Terrace at Night
sceneContext: Painted on the Place du Forum in Arles over several nights, working outdoors under gaslight. He told his sister he had an enormous need for religion and had gone out to paint the stars.
whyBigDeal: He used no black anywhere in it, building the night entirely from blues and violets against the gas-lit yellow — a claim he made explicitly in a letter. The café still stands, and the paving and terrace can be matched to the picture.

title: The Night Café
sceneContext: Painted in the all-night café at Arles where van Gogh had been lodging, over three consecutive nights while he stayed up and slept during the day.
whyBigDeal: He wrote that he had tried to express the idea that the café is a place where one can ruin oneself, go mad or commit a crime, using red and green to convey 'the terrible passions of humanity'. The floor tilts up and the gas lamps have haloes — distortion used deliberately as feeling, ahead of the Expressionists.

title: Potato Eaters
sceneContext: Painted in Nuenen in the Dutch Brabant, where van Gogh was living with his parents and drawing local weavers and farm labourers. He had had almost no formal training and was five years from his death.
whyBigDeal: He deliberately made the hands and faces coarse, writing that he wanted it clear the diggers had eaten their potatoes with the same hands they had put in the earth. His friend Van Rappard's harsh criticism of it ended their friendship, and van Gogh still called it his best work years later.

title: Almond Blossom
sceneContext: Painted at Saint-Rémy as a gift for his brother Theo and sister-in-law Jo, who had just had a son and named him Vincent. The almond is the first tree to flower in Provence.
whyBigDeal: He cropped the branches against flat blue with no ground and no horizon, taking the device straight from the Japanese prints he collected. It is the only picture he made as a present for a birth, and he had a relapse shortly after finishing it that stopped him painting for two months.

title: The Birth of Venus
sceneContext: Painted in Florence for a Medici cousin's country villa, probably alongside Primavera. Canvas rather than panel was cheap and portable — this was domestic decoration, not an altarpiece.
whyBigDeal: It is the first monumental female nude in Western painting since antiquity that is not Eve and not a sinner. Botticelli drew her contour as a continuous line and used real gold on the hair, techniques already old-fashioned in 1485, while Leonardo was dissolving outlines entirely.

title: Primavera
sceneContext: Made for the Medici, hung in a Florentine townhouse near a bedchamber. Its programme probably came from a humanist in the circle of Marsilio Ficino, who was reviving Plato under Medici patronage.
whyBigDeal: Botanists have identified around 190 plant species in the meadow, most of them Tuscan and flowering in spring, painted accurately enough to key out. No contemporary document explains the subject, so the story it tells has been argued about since the nineteenth century.

title: Venus and Mars
sceneContext: A long horizontal panel of a kind set into furniture — a bench back or a chest — for a bedroom, probably a wedding gift. The wasps at Mars's ear may pun on the Vespucci family.
whyBigDeal: Botticelli has the satyrs blowing a conch in Mars's ear without waking him, making the joke that love exhausts war rather than the reverse. The fruit the small satyr holds is a datura, a hallucinogen, which has kept the picture's reading unsettled.

title: Girl with a Pearl Earring
sceneContext: Painted in Delft, where Vermeer produced perhaps three pictures a year and never left the town. This is a tronie — a study of a type or costume rather than a portrait of a named sitter.
whyBigDeal: Recent imaging shows there was a green curtain behind her that Vermeer painted out, leaving the black void that gives the picture its force. The pearl is two strokes of white lead over grey, with no outline at all, and is probably too large to be a real pearl.

title: The Art of Painting
sceneContext: Vermeer kept this picture rather than selling it, and his widow tried to shield it from creditors after his death by transferring it to her mother. Hitler later acquired it for his planned museum at Linz.
whyBigDeal: The map on the back wall shows the Netherlands before the split between north and south, already politically obsolete when painted — a deliberate archaism. The painter wears fifteenth-century dress, so Vermeer staged his own trade as something historical rather than contemporary.

title: The Astronomer
sceneContext: Delft in the 1660s was a short ride from Leiden's university and Antonie van Leeuwenhoek, the microscopist, lived in the town and was appointed executor of Vermeer's estate.
whyBigDeal: The celestial globe is identifiable as Jodocus Hondius's of 1600 and the book on the table is open at a specific page of Adriaan Metius on astronomy, recommending divine inspiration as a guide to the science. Vermeer painted instruments precisely enough to date them, which is rare in genre painting.

title: View of Delft
sceneContext: Painted from a first-floor room across the harbour, six years after a gunpowder magazine exploded and destroyed a large part of Delft, killing Carel Fabritius.
whyBigDeal: Vermeer moved buildings that do not line up that way in reality, so the 'view' is composed. Proust called it the most beautiful painting in the world and gave his dying novelist a passage about its 'little patch of yellow wall', which is a real and locatable passage of paint.

title: Arnolfini Portrait
sceneContext: Painted in Bruges, then the banking and luxury-goods capital of northern Europe, for Giovanni di Nicolao Arnolfini, an Italian merchant trading silk there.
whyBigDeal: Van Eyck signed the back wall 'Jan van Eyck was here 1434' in legal handwriting, and the convex mirror shows two extra figures in the doorway — witnesses. Whether it records a marriage is still disputed, but the mirror frame's ten scenes of the Passion are each about a centimetre across and fully legible under magnification.

title: The Ghent Altarpiece (wings closed)
sceneContext: Begun by Hubert van Eyck and finished by his brother Jan for a chapel in Saint Bavo's, Ghent, paid for by a wealthy merchant and his wife, who appear kneeling on the outer wings.
whyBigDeal: It has been stolen or looted seven times, dismantled by Napoleon, sold to Berlin, hidden in an Austrian salt mine by the Nazis, and one panel taken in 1934 has never been recovered. Van Eyck's oil glazes hold their intensity after six centuries in a way tempera does not.

title: The Ambassadors
sceneContext: Painted in London, where Holbein worked for the French embassy and later for Henry VIII. Jean de Dinteville was in England on a mission during Henry's break with Rome; his friend Georges de Selve was a bishop.
whyBigDeal: The smear across the floor is a skull in anamorphic projection, correct only from the lower right edge, so the picture requires you to move to complete it. The lute has a broken string and the hymn book is open at Luther — the objects are an argument about discord, not a display of learning.

title: The Raft of the Medusa
sceneContext: The French frigate Méduse ran aground off Senegal in 1816 through the incompetence of a captain appointed by political favour; 147 people were put on a raft and 15 survived. Géricault interviewed two survivors and had a scale model of the raft built in his studio.
whyBigDeal: He shaved his head so he could not go out, worked for eight months, and brought corpses and severed limbs from a nearby hospital to study decomposition. Exhibiting a contemporary government scandal at the scale of history painting was the provocation — the Salon hung it high and the critics understood exactly what it accused.

title: Portrait of a Kleptomaniac
sceneContext: One of a series of ten portraits of asylum patients, each labelled with a monomania, painted for a physician friend, Étienne-Jean Georget, at the Salpêtrière. Five survive.
whyBigDeal: They were made as clinical documents at a moment when psychiatry was arguing that madness was specific and partial rather than total. Géricault painted the sitters at eye level with the dignity of a commissioned portrait, and declined to make the illness legible in the face.

title: Liberty Leading the People
sceneContext: Painted within months of the July Revolution that put Louis-Philippe on the throne. Delacroix did not fight; he wrote to his brother that if he had not fought for his country, at least he would paint for it.
whyBigDeal: Liberty is an allegory with real armpit hair and dirty feet, standing on actual corpses in recognisable Paris — the collision of allegorical figure with reportage is what shocked the Salon. The state bought it and then kept it out of sight for most of the next two decades as too inflammatory.

title: Death of Sardanapalus
sceneContext: Taken from Byron's play about an Assyrian king who, facing defeat, has his possessions, horses and concubines destroyed in front of him before his own death.
whyBigDeal: The Salon of 1827 attacked it so comprehensively that the state warned Delacroix his commissions were at risk. There is no stable perspective or ground plane — the bed tips the whole scene toward the viewer, which was the technical scandal underneath the moral one.

title: The Massacre at Chios
sceneContext: The Ottoman reprisal on Chios in 1822 killed or enslaved most of the island's population and was a live cause across Europe; Byron died at Missolonghi the year this was shown.
whyBigDeal: Delacroix saw Constable's Hay Wain in Paris while the picture hung at the Salon and repainted the background in a few days with broken colour. He gave the victims the foreground and the composition no hero, which is why Gros called it 'the massacre of painting'.

title: Luncheon on the Grass
sceneContext: Rejected by the Salon and shown instead at the Salon des Refusés, which Napoleon III set up that year in response to complaints about the jury. The model is Victorine Meurent; the men are Manet's brother and his future brother-in-law.
whyBigDeal: The pose is lifted from a Raphael composition known through an engraving, so the offence was not nudity but a nude woman with contemporary clothed men, looking out. The background bather is the wrong size for her position — Manet flattened the space deliberately and critics read it as incompetence.

title: A Bar at the Folies-Bergère
sceneContext: Manet's last major painting, made in the studio from a model, Suzon, who worked at the Folies-Bergère, with the bar reconstructed around her. He was dying of complications of syphilis and could barely stand to paint.
whyBigDeal: The reflection is wrong: the barmaid's back appears far to the right and the customer she faces is not in front of her. Manet knew — he shifted the mirror deliberately, and the argument over why has run for over a century.

title: The Execution of Emperor Maximilian
sceneContext: Napoleon III installed the Habsburg Maximilian as emperor of Mexico, then withdrew French troops and left him to be shot in 1867. Manet worked from newspaper reports and photographs across three large versions.
whyBigDeal: He put the firing squad in French-style uniforms, making the picture an accusation against his own government, and it was barred from exhibition and from being reproduced as a print in France. The composition quotes Goya's Third of May directly, but drains the drama out.

title: The School of Athens
sceneContext: Painted on the wall of Julius II's private library in the Vatican, while Michelangelo was at work on the Sistine ceiling a short walk away. Raphael was twenty-six and had been in Rome barely a year.
whyBigDeal: The philosophers are portraits of living artists — Plato is generally read as Leonardo, and the brooding figure on the steps was added late and resembles Michelangelo, whose ceiling Raphael had just been shown. The architecture is a design for the new St Peter's, then under construction.

title: Sistine Madonna
sceneContext: Commissioned by Julius II for a church in Piacenza. Augustus III of Saxony bought it in 1754 and it went to Dresden, where it became the most discussed painting in Germany.
whyBigDeal: The two bored cherubs at the bottom edge were cut from the picture in the nineteenth century and reproduced on everything from biscuit tins to postcards, independent of the painting. The curtain and the parapet make the whole image a stage revealed, which is why the Virgin appears to step toward the viewer.

title: Transfiguration
sceneContext: Raphael's last painting, commissioned by Cardinal Giulio de' Medici, and unfinished at his death at thirty-seven. It was carried at the head of his funeral procession.
whyBigDeal: He combined two moments that scripture separates — Christ on the mountain and the disciples failing to heal a possessed boy below — so the lower half is chaos lit by nothing and the upper half is light with no source. Painters treated the lower group as the beginning of Mannerism.

title: The Creation of Adam
sceneContext: Part of the Sistine ceiling, painted lying back on scaffolding over four years for Julius II. Michelangelo considered himself a sculptor and had tried to refuse the commission.
whyBigDeal: God is carried in a shape that anatomists since 1990 have argued matches a cross-section of the human brain, though Michelangelo left no note about it. What is certain is the gap: the two fingers do not touch, and every earlier creation scene had shown contact.

title: Doni Tondo
sceneContext: Painted in Florence for the wedding of Agnolo Doni, a wealthy cloth merchant, who then tried to pay less than agreed. Michelangelo demanded double and got it.
whyBigDeal: It is the only finished panel painting securely by him. The Virgin's twisting pose and the muscular nudes lounging behind her are a sculptor's picture — he treated paint as a way of showing bodies in torsion, and Florentine Mannerists took the pose directly.

title: Wanderer above the Sea of Fog
sceneContext: Painted in Dresden shortly after Friedrich married, from studies made in the Elbe Sandstone Mountains. The rocks in it are identifiable individual outcrops, assembled into a view that does not exist.
whyBigDeal: The figure has his back turned, so the picture withholds the face and offers his position instead — the device Friedrich used repeatedly and that made him the emblem of German Romanticism. He was almost forgotten for a century and only recovered around 1900.

title: The Sea of Ice
sceneContext: Painted after Friedrich studied ice floes on the Elbe in the winter of 1820–21, and prompted by reports of William Parry's expedition searching for the Northwest Passage.
whyBigDeal: A ship's stern is crushed under the slabs at the right, almost hidden, so the wreck is a detail rather than the subject. Nobody bought it in his lifetime; it was read as unsellably bleak and stayed in his studio.

title: The Monk by the Sea
sceneContext: Exhibited in Berlin in 1810 with The Abbey in the Oakwood; the Prussian crown prince bought both. X-rays show Friedrich painted out two sailing ships that had been on the horizon.
whyBigDeal: Removing the ships left a picture that is roughly four-fifths empty sky above an almost featureless sea, with a figure a few centimetres high. Kleist wrote that looking at it was like having one's eyelids cut away — no European painting had previously offered so little to look at.

title: The Abbey in the Oakwood
sceneContext: The companion to The Monk by the Sea, based on the ruins of Eldena Abbey near Friedrich's birthplace at Greifswald, which he drew repeatedly throughout his life.
whyBigDeal: A funeral procession carries a coffin through the ruined portal toward an open grave, at a scale that makes the monks nearly illegible. Friedrich painted the ruin of a church as the only architecture left standing, which the Prussian court read as devotional and later critics as the opposite.

title: Two men contemplating the Moon
sceneContext: A later version of a composition Friedrich first painted in 1819; he made several. He told a visitor the figures were 'engaged in demagogic intrigues', a joke about the political surveillance of the period.
whyBigDeal: The two men wear old German dress, which had been banned as a nationalist symbol, so a quiet moonlit picture carries a political marker in the costume. Friedrich repeated his own compositions as variants rather than treating each canvas as unique.

title: The Tempest
sceneContext: Painted in Venice for a private collector. Giorgione died of plague around 1510 in his early thirties, leaving fewer than a dozen securely attributed pictures and no documented explanation of any of them.
whyBigDeal: X-rays show a seated female nude where the standing soldier now is, so Giorgione changed the cast entirely as he worked — evidence that there was no fixed subject to illustrate. It is generally taken as the first European painting in which landscape and mood, rather than a story, are the content.

title: Sleeping Venus
sceneContext: Left unfinished at Giorgione's death and completed by Titian, who painted the landscape and, according to a sixteenth-century account, a Cupid that was later painted out.
whyBigDeal: It established the reclining female nude asleep in a landscape as a subject, and Titian's Venus of Urbino, Manet's Olympia and a long line after them all answer this pose. Her eyes are closed, which removes the exchange of looks that later versions put back.

title: The Three Philosophers
sceneContext: Recorded in a Venetian collection in 1525 as three philosophers contemplating the sun's rays, with no further identification. It was probably cut down on the left at some point.
whyBigDeal: The three figures have been read as the ages of man, the three Magi, and Greek, Arab and Renaissance learning, with no way to settle it. The dark rock face occupying the left third is painted with more attention than the men, which suggests the subject may be the cave itself.

title: Niccolò Mauruzi da Tolentino at the Battle of San Romano
sceneContext: One of three panels of a minor 1432 Florentine skirmish, painted for the Bartolini Salimbeni family and later taken — effectively seized — by Lorenzo de' Medici for his palace bedchamber.
whyBigDeal: Uccello laid the broken lances on the ground in a deliberate perspective grid, using a battlefield as a demonstration of the new geometry. Vasari wrote that he stayed up all night at it and told his wife perspective was a sweet thing; the horses are consequently rocking-horse rigid.

title: The Hunt in the Forest
sceneContext: One of Uccello's last works, a long horizontal panel made for a piece of domestic furniture, painted when he was in his seventies and, by Vasari's account, poor and reclusive.
whyBigDeal: All the hunters, dogs and stags converge on a vanishing point deep in the wood, so the perspective construction is doing the work a horizon normally does at night. The trees are set out on a regular grid, which turns a forest into a measured space.

title: The Baptism of Christ
sceneContext: Painted for a priory in Piero's home town of Borgo San Sepolcro. He was also a mathematician who wrote treatises on perspective and on the five regular solids.
whyBigDeal: The dove is painted as a flat white shape at exactly the width of the clouds behind it, so a bird and a sky formation occupy the same plane. Piero built the whole panel on a grid of squares and circles, and the daylight falls with no drama at all — the opposite of what religious painting was moving toward.

title: Flagellation of Christ
sceneContext: A small panel from Urbino whose commission and subject are undocumented. Kenneth Clark called it the greatest small painting in the world; nobody agrees who the three men in the foreground are.
whyBigDeal: The flagellation happens in the middle distance, correctly scaled and half-ignored, while three unidentified contemporaries talk in front at full size. Piero's perspective is exact enough that the building's floor plan and dimensions have been reconstructed from it.

title: Portrait of Federico da Montefeltro
sceneContext: Federico, Duke of Urbino, was a mercenary commander who lost his right eye and the bridge of his nose in a tournament, and had the bridge surgically cut back to widen his remaining field of vision.
whyBigDeal: He is shown in strict profile from the left for that reason — the damaged side is simply never depicted. Piero painted the broken nose and the moles precisely, so the profile is both a heraldic convention and a clinical record.

title: Venus of Urbino
artistBio: Italian, Pieve di Cadore ca. 1488–1576 Venice
sceneContext: Painted for Guidobaldo della Rovere, later Duke of Urbino, who referred to it in letters simply as 'the naked woman'. The classical title came later and did not come from Titian.
whyBigDeal: The setting is a contemporary Venetian bedroom with servants at a cassone in the back, so the mythological alibi is thin to non-existent. Mark Twain called it the foulest painting in the world; Manet used its pose exactly for Olympia three centuries on.

title: Bacchus and Ariadne
artistBio: Italian, Pieve di Cadore ca. 1488–1576 Venice
sceneContext: One of a set of mythologies for Alfonso d'Este's private study in Ferrara, a room designed to be seen by a handful of people. Titian took the commission over after Raphael died before starting it.
whyBigDeal: The sky is ultramarine ground from lapis lazuli, more expensive by weight than gold, used across a large area purely for a background. Bacchus is caught leaping out of his chariot in mid-air with no support, a moment of arrested motion that Baroque painters spent the next century pursuing.

title: The Flaying of Marsyas
artistBio: Italian, Pieve di Cadore ca. 1488–1576 Venice
sceneContext: Painted in Titian's last years in Venice, when he was in his eighties and working almost entirely for himself. It was found in his studio after his death in the plague of 1576.
whyBigDeal: He worked the paint with his fingers as much as with brushes — contemporaries described him smearing and dragging it — so the surface breaks up at close range. The old man watching, chin on hand, is generally read as Titian's self-portrait, present at a scene of a musician being skinned alive.

title: The Calling of Saint Matthew
sceneContext: Caravaggio's first public commission, for the Contarelli Chapel in San Luigi dei Francesi in Rome, won at twenty-eight through a cardinal's patronage after years of painting small pictures for private buyers.
whyBigDeal: The tax collectors wear contemporary Roman dress and sit in a bare room lit by a single hard raking light with no halo, no architecture and no sky. Which figure is Matthew is still disputed — the bearded man may be pointing at himself or at the youth beside him.

title: Judith Beheading Holofernes
sceneContext: Painted in Rome for a Genoese banker. Caravaggio worked from a live model and, unusually for the subject, had almost certainly watched the public execution of Beatrice Cenci in Rome in 1599.
whyBigDeal: He shows the sawing mid-stroke with arterial spray, and gives Judith an expression of distaste rather than resolve — she is leaning away from her own hands. Artemisia Gentileschi's version answers this one directly and puts the strength back into the arms.

title: Supper at Emmaus
sceneContext: Painted in Rome for the nobleman Ciriaco Mattei shortly after the Contarelli Chapel had made Caravaggio's name, when he was living in the Mattei household and being paid well for the first time in his life.
whyBigDeal: The fruit basket tips over the table edge into the viewer's space, and the fruit is out of season and partly rotten — painted from what was in front of him rather than what the story required. Christ is beardless and young, which broke the recognisable type so completely that the picture is about not recognising him.

title: David with the Head of Goliath
sceneContext: Painted in Naples in the last months of Caravaggio's life, while he was under a papal death sentence for killing a man in a brawl and was seeking a pardon through Cardinal Scipione Borghese.
whyBigDeal: The severed head is his own self-portrait, and the picture was probably sent to Borghese as a plea — an offer of his own head. David looks at it with pity rather than triumph, which no earlier version of the subject had done.

title: The Entombment of Christ
sceneContext: Painted for the Chiesa Nuova in Rome, for a chapel of the Oratorians, a reforming order that wanted directness and plainness in religious art.
whyBigDeal: The stone slab juts out of the picture at the viewer's eye level so that the body is being lowered into the altar itself, and by extension into the church floor. It was the most admired of his altarpieces in his own lifetime, and both Rubens and Cézanne made copies of it.

title: The Anatomy Lesson of Dr. Nicolaes Tulp
sceneContext: Rembrandt was twenty-five and newly arrived in Amsterdam when the surgeons' guild commissioned it. Public dissections were ticketed winter events, held on executed criminals — this one on a robber hanged that morning.
whyBigDeal: Group portraits of guilds were traditionally rows of faces paid for by the sitter; Rembrandt gave them a single action to attend to and staggered them into a pyramid. The dissected forearm is anatomically wrong, apparently copied from a textbook plate rather than the body on the table.

title: The Return of the Prodigal Son
sceneContext: One of Rembrandt's last paintings, made after bankruptcy, the loss of his house and collection, and the deaths of his partner Hendrickje and his son Titus.
whyBigDeal: The father's two hands are painted differently — one broad and male, one slighter — and the asymmetry appears deliberate rather than careless. The son's head is shaved and his shoe is falling apart, details of destitution rendered with more paint than the faces of the watching figures.

title: Belshazzar's Feast
sceneContext: Painted in Amsterdam, where Rembrandt lived in the Jewish quarter. He took the Hebrew inscription from his neighbour Menasseh ben Israel, a rabbi and printer he knew.
whyBigDeal: The letters are correct Hebrew but written in vertical columns rather than right to left, which is the arrangement Menasseh had published to explain why the king's own scholars could not read the writing. It is a rare case of a painting incorporating a specific scholarly argument as its central device.

title: The Storm on the Sea of Galilee
sceneContext: Rembrandt's only seascape, painted in his late twenties during his most commercially successful years in Amsterdam, when he was running a busy studio and taking in pupils at a considerable fee.
whyBigDeal: It was cut from its frame in the 1990 Isabella Stewart Gardner Museum robbery and has never been recovered; the empty frame still hangs in the gallery. Fourteen figures are on a boat that historically held thirteen — one of them, looking out at the viewer and holding his cap, is Rembrandt.

title: The Fighting Temeraire
sceneContext: The Temeraire had fought at Trafalgar and was being towed up the Thames to be broken up at Rotherhithe. Turner was sixty-four and refused to sell the picture for the rest of his life.
whyBigDeal: The masts were actually removed before the tow, and the ship could not have looked like this — Turner reinstated them. He also put the sunset in the wrong part of the sky for a westward tow, so the image is arranged rather than witnessed.
