title: Rain, Steam and Speed – The Great Western Railway
sceneContext: The Great Western line over Maidenhead Bridge was Brunel's, and the bridge's flat brick arches were then the widest and shallowest ever built, widely predicted to collapse.
whyBigDeal: A hare is running on the track ahead of the locomotive, nearly invisible, racing it. Turner was sixty-nine and had reportedly put his head out of a train window in a storm for nine minutes to see what it looked like.

title: The Slave Ship
sceneContext: Exhibited with lines from Turner's own unfinished poem, and prompted by the Zong case, in which a captain threw sick enslaved people overboard because insurance covered drowning but not death from illness.
whyBigDeal: Ruskin's father bought it and Ruskin, who called it the finest thing Turner ever did, eventually sold it because he could not live with the subject. The chained legs and the fish in the foreground are the only figuration in what is otherwise almost pure colour.

title: The Death of Marat
sceneContext: Marat was stabbed in his bath by Charlotte Corday in July 1793; David had visited him the previous day and was a deputy in the Convention that had just voted for the king's execution. He organised Marat's funeral.
whyBigDeal: The skin disease that kept Marat in the bath is entirely omitted, and the packing-crate desk is inscribed as a tombstone — David made a political martyr's icon within months of the death. It hung in the Convention hall until Robespierre fell, then was returned to David as an embarrassment.

title: The Oath of the Horatii
sceneContext: Painted in Rome on a royal commission and shown at the Paris Salon of 1785, four years before the Revolution. David deliberately exhibited it late so it would hang alone.
whyBigDeal: The oath itself is not in Livy or Corneille — David invented the scene. Three arches divide the canvas so the men occupy two and the collapsed women one, and the swords meet at the exact centre; the composition's rigidity was read immediately as a political style.

title: Napoleon Crossing the Alps
sceneContext: Commissioned by the King of Spain. Napoleon refused to sit, telling David that nobody knew whether the portraits of great men resembled them and that it was enough for the genius to live.
whyBigDeal: He crossed the pass on a mule, led by a guide, in fair weather. David put him on a rearing charger in a storm and carved HANNIBAL and KAROLVS MAGNVS into the rock beneath BONAPARTE — a lineage claim made in stone within the picture.

title: The Coronation of Napoleon
sceneContext: David attended the ceremony at Notre-Dame in 1804 and worked from sketches, a wax model of the cathedral and posed mannequins, over nearly three years, on a canvas about ten metres wide.
whyBigDeal: Napoleon crowned himself and then his wife; David initially drew the self-coronation and changed it to Josephine's, which was less arrogant to look at. Napoleon's mother is prominent in the stands and was not present at all — she had boycotted it.

title: A Burial at Ornans
sceneContext: Courbet painted his own village's funeral, using actual residents of Ornans as models and naming them, on a canvas over six metres wide — the size reserved for history painting.
whyBigDeal: Nobody in it is idealised, the grave is an empty hole at the front, and there is no visible sign of consolation or heaven. Critics called it the burial of Romanticism; Courbet said he had painted a burial at Ornans and it happened to be the burial of Romanticism too.

title: The Painter's Studio
sceneContext: Rejected by the Exposition Universelle of 1855, so Courbet built his own shed nearby, called it the Pavilion of Realism, charged admission and hung this at the centre. It was the first artist's solo protest exhibition of its kind.
whyBigDeal: He subtitled it 'a real allegory summing up seven years of my artistic and moral life', which is a deliberate contradiction in terms. Napoleon III is present as the poacher on the left, unnamed and unmistakable.

title: The Stone Breakers
sceneContext: Courbet saw two men breaking stones on a road near Ornans, asked them to come to his studio, and painted them at life size. The canvas was destroyed in the Allied bombing of Dresden in 1945.
whyBigDeal: Neither man's face is shown — one is too old for the work and one too young, and the picture makes a point of their being a dead end rather than a pair. Proudhon read it as socialism; Courbet insisted he had simply painted what he saw.

title: The Kiss
medium: Oil and gold leaf on canvas
sceneContext: Painted at the height of Klimt's golden period, after a trip to Ravenna where he saw the Byzantine mosaics at San Vitale. Vienna's Ministry of Education bought it before it was even finished.
whyBigDeal: The two figures' robes carry different ornament — rectangles for him, circles and flowers for her — so the gender distinction is carried entirely by pattern rather than by body. They are kneeling at the edge of a drop, with her feet curling over it, which most reproductions crop out.

title: Judith I
sceneContext: Klimt's model was probably Adele Bloch-Bauer, a Viennese banker's wife whose portrait he later painted twice. The gold frame, made by his brother, names the subject because viewers kept calling her Salome.
whyBigDeal: Holofernes's severed head is pushed almost out of the frame at the lower right and cropped, so the picture is about her face instead. Klimt gave a biblical heroine an expression of open sexual pleasure, which is why Vienna insisted on reading her as the wrong woman.

title: Death and Life
sceneContext: Klimt reworked it after winning a prize in Rome in 1911, replacing a gold background with grey and adding to the group of the living.
whyBigDeal: The living are packed into a single mass in which no figure is separable, while Death stands alone with space around him. Klimt painted no ground for either group — they float, and the gap between them is simply empty canvas.

title: Impression, Sunrise
sceneContext: Painted from a hotel window overlooking the port of Le Havre, Monet's home town, probably in a single session. He gave it its title offhandedly when asked for one for the catalogue.
whyBigDeal: A critic took the title and coined 'Impressionists' as an insult in a review of the 1874 show, and the group adopted it. Astronomers have used the tide, smokestacks and sun angle to date it to around 7.35am on 13 November 1872.

title: Rouen Cathedral
sceneContext: Monet rented rooms opposite the cathedral's west front and worked on more than thirty canvases at once, switching between them as the light moved and finishing them later in the studio at Giverny.
whyBigDeal: The subject is a fixed object chosen precisely because it could not change, so the entire content of the series is the light. He exhibited twenty of them together in 1895, which made the series rather than the single picture the unit of work.

title: Self-Portrait
sceneContext: Dürer was twenty-six and had returned from Italy, where painters were treated as gentlemen rather than as members of a craft guild as they were in Nuremberg.
whyBigDeal: He painted himself in expensive Italian dress with kid gloves, at a window with an Alpine view, and inscribed that he had made it from his own appearance. Northern artists did not do this — the self-portrait as a claim to social standing effectively starts here.

title: Great Piece of Turf
sceneContext: A watercolour study made in Nuremberg, of a patch of ground with the roots and soil visible in section, at a time when such studies existed to be quarried for details in finished works.
whyBigDeal: The species — dandelion, yarrow, greater plantain, meadow grass — are identifiable to botanists, and Dürer painted them at eye level from the ground rather than looking down. He never used it in another picture; it is a finished work about ordinary weeds, two centuries before that was a category.

title: The Four Horsemen, from The Apocalypse
sceneContext: One of fifteen woodcuts Dürer cut, printed and published himself in 1498, with an eye on the widespread expectation that the world would end in 1500.
whyBigDeal: He financed and sold the series himself rather than working for a publisher, which made him one of the first artists in Europe to control his own distribution. He also compressed the four riders into a single overlapping charge — earlier illustrations had given them separate compartments.

title: Woman with a hat
sceneContext: Shown at the 1905 Salon d'Automne in the room a critic christened the cage aux fauves — the wild-beast cage. The sitter is Matisse's wife Amélie, who in fact wore black.
whyBigDeal: The public tried to scratch the paint off, and Matisse nearly withdrew it. Gertrude and Leo Stein bought it, which gave him the money to keep working; the green and vermilion in the face are unmixed and applied next to each other rather than blended.

title: The Green Stripe
sceneContext: Painted in Collioure on the Mediterranean coast in the summer Matisse spent working alongside Derain. It is again a portrait of Amélie Matisse.
whyBigDeal: The green band down the centre of the face is not a shadow but a divider, splitting the head into a warm and a cool half and doing the job modelling normally does. Matisse used colour as structure rather than description, which is the single move Fauvism amounts to.

title: The Dessert: Harmony in Red (The Red Room)
sceneContext: Commissioned by the Moscow collector Sergei Shchukin, who bought Matisse in quantity when almost nobody in France would. Matisse repainted it after delivery had been agreed.
whyBigDeal: It was begun as a blue painting and then a green one before Matisse overpainted the whole surface red, and the tablecloth pattern runs up the wall so that table and wall become one plane. Shchukin accepted the change without seeing it first.

title: The Joy of Life
sceneContext: Matisse's largest painting to date, made in the studio from studies at Collioure and shown at the 1906 Salon des Indépendants, where it was the main target of the year's abuse.
whyBigDeal: Signac, who had championed Matisse, hated it and said he had gone to the dogs. Picasso saw it at the Steins' and began Les Demoiselles d'Avignon within months, largely as an answer to it.
